text: **Wallenberg (lateral medullary) syndrome**: PICA/vertebral thrombosis infarcts the lateral medulla: vertigo, nystagmus, vomiting, ipsilateral Horner syndrome, dysphagia and hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus), ipsilateral ataxia with falling toward the lesion, and crossed sensory loss (ipsilateral face, contralateral body pain/temperature). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 36)

**Vertebrobasilar insufficiency and subclavian steal**: VBI causes vertigo with other brainstem signs (diplopia, dysarthria, visual change, hemiparesis) and drop attacks without loss of consciousness provoked by neck motion; isolated hearing loss/tinnitus is unusual. Subclavian steal (stenosis proximal to the vertebral origin) gives arm-exercise-provoked vertigo, occipital headache and visual symptoms, with an interarm blood pressure difference. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 32, 51)

topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
text: **Heerfordt syndrome**: Uveoparotid fever: a sarcoidosis variant with fever, bilateral parotid enlargement and uveitis, frequently with facial nerve palsy. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 16)

**Trotter syndrome**: Nasopharyngeal tumor invading the sinus of Morgagni gives the tetrad of V3 neuralgia (mandibular), conductive hearing loss from eustachian tube obstruction, ipsilateral palatal immobility, and trismus (pterygoid invasion). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 35)

topic: Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Marjolin ulcer**: An SCC arising in a chronic burn scar (or other chronic wound); typically well differentiated yet aggressive with early metastasis, so chronic nonhealing ulcers in scars warrant biopsy. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 41)

topic: Cranial Nerve Examination / Skull Base Localization
text: **Raeder paratrigeminal syndrome**: Ipsilateral ptosis and miosis with V1-distribution pain but preserved facial sweating, localizing to postganglionic sympathetic fibers along the internal carotid or the anterior middle cranial fossa (a 'partial Horner' that spares sweating). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 29)

**Ortner (cardiovocal) syndrome and dysphagia lusoria**: Left recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy from cardiac enlargement (especially left atrial dilation in mitral stenosis) compressing the nerve near the aortopulmonary window is Ortner syndrome. Dysphagia lusoria is esophageal compression by an aberrant right subclavian artery, which also implies a nonrecurrent right laryngeal nerve. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 4, 25)

**Semon law**: With progressive compressive injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve the abductor (posterior cricoarytenoid) fails before the adductors, and on recovery the adductors return before the abductor. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 43)

**Gardner syndrome**: Autosomal dominant (APC) syndrome of multiple osteomas of the skull, mandible and paranasal sinuses with soft-tissue fibromas, epidermoid cysts and colonic polyps that almost inevitably become malignant; multiple craniofacial osteomas should prompt GI evaluation. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 14)

**Ondine curse**: Loss of automatic respiratory drive with apnea/hypoventilation most evident in sleep (congenital or acquired central alveolar hypoventilation). Patients breathe adequately only when awake and voluntarily. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 24)

**Lermoyez syndrome**: A Ménière variant in which fluctuating hearing loss and tinnitus worsen first and then improve after the vertigo attack (the reverse of the usual pattern). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 20)

**Toynbee law**: Intracranial complications of mastoiditis tend to involve the lateral (sigmoid) sinus and cerebellum, whereas attic cholesteatoma tends to cause temporal-lobe (cerebral) complications. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 44)

topic: Systemic Disease of the Nose / Sinuses
text: **Lethal midline granuloma differential**: Midline destructive lesions of the nose and palate include extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma (formerly polymorphic reticulosis), granulomatosis with polyangiitis, cocaine-induced midline destructive lesion and idiopathic midline destructive disease. Localized lymphoma has historically been treated with radiation (about 50 Gy) and disseminated disease with chemotherapy. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 20)

**Goldenhar syndrome (oculoauriculovertebral spectrum)**: A nonhereditary first/second arch variant of hemifacial microsomia: malar/maxillary/mandibular hypoplasia, microtia or canal atresia, preauricular tags and pits, epibulbar dermoids, vertebral anomalies, and cardiac/renal defects with usually normal intelligence. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 15)

topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
text: **Sturge-Weber syndrome**: V1-distribution port-wine stain with ipsilateral leptomeningeal venous angiomatosis causing seizures, hemiparesis, glaucoma and tram-track intracranial calcifications. Oral and nasal mucosal angiomatous involvement may bleed during surgery. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 32)

topic: CF / Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia Sinonasal Disease
text: **Kartagener triad and ciliary defect**: Kartagener = situs inversus, chronic sinusitis and bronchiectasis; cilia and sperm flagella lack the dynein arms of the A-tubules, causing impaired mucociliary clearance and infertility in both sexes. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 18)

**AASM sleep-study levels**: Level 1 is attended in-lab PSG (needs about 6 hours of recording at 70% or better sleep efficiency; EEG, EOG, ECG, airflow, SaO2, effort belts, limb leads, position, snore) and can be run split-night with CPAP titration. Level 2 is the same channels unattended at home (more data loss). Level 3 is a limited-channel home study (airflow/SaO2/effort/snore) now commonly used first-line. Level 4 is oximetry alone, insufficient for treatment planning, with false positives in COPD and false negatives in OSA with mild desaturation. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 2, p 59-60)

**Screening questionnaires**: The Epworth Sleepiness Scale rates likelihood of dozing in 8 situations (0-3 each, total 24); a score above 10 indicates excessive sleepiness, but it is not specific for OSA. The Berlin questionnaire is a more OSA-specific screening tool. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 2, p 56)

**Mueller maneuver versus DISE**: In the awake Mueller maneuver the patient inhales forcefully against a closed mouth and pinched nose while the scope views retropalatal and retrolingual collapse; it is cheap but has poor inter- and intrarater reliability and low predictive value for surgical success. Observing collapse at end-expiration is more reproducible. DISE (propofol or midazolam, VOTE scoring) is reserved for discordant exam and PSG findings, failed prior surgery, or before major surgery; very severe OSA and morbid obesity are relative contraindications. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 2, p 57-58)

**Uvulopalatal flap and CAPSO**: The uvulopalatal flap denudes the lingual surface of the uvula/palate and folds the uvula back onto the soft palate, sparing muscle so pain and velopharyngeal dysfunction are less than UPPP. Avoid in a thick palate (the bulky flap causes gagging). Cautery-assisted palatal stiffening (CAPSO) removes a diamond-shaped mucosal strip in the office to scar and stiffen the palate. It helps snoring but not OSA. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 2, p 62)

**UPPP outcomes and complications**: Unselected UPPP succeeds in about 50%. With Friedman-guided selection, success is much higher: K.J. Lee quotes over 85% long term for tonsils 2-4 with palate position I-II, while Friedman's own stage I data (palate position I-II, tonsils 3-4, BMI under 40) show about 80%. Complications include velopharyngeal insufficiency and nasopharyngeal stenosis from over-resection of posterior pillar/levator tissue. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 2, p 62)

**Tongue and hyoid suspension, genioglossus advancement**: Tongue suspension anchors a suture loop through the tongue base to a screw on the inner genial tubercle (risk of altered swallow and foreign-body sensation). Hyoid suspension advances the hyoid to the thyroid cartilage after strap transection. Genioglossus advancement moves a rectangular geniotubercle window forward and rotates it (risks: tooth root injury, mental nerve injury, mandible fracture, hematoma). The last two are adjuncts rather than stand-alone procedures. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 2, p 63-64)

**Tongue-base radiofrequency and midline glossectomy**: Radiofrequency tongue-base reduction places about 4-6 paired intramuscular lesions that scar and shrink the tongue with less pain than cautery (risks: ulceration, taste change, infection). Midline glossectomy (Coblation, microdebrider or TORS) risks lingual artery bleeding, hypoglossal injury, abscess and dysphagia. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 2, p 63)

**Postoperative monitoring after OSA surgery**: Routine ICU admission for all OSA surgery is not supported. Monitored admission is reserved for severe symptomatic OSA with very high AHI, significant cardiovascular comorbidity, or major tongue-base surgery. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 2, p 65-66)

**Defining surgical success**: Success should combine an AHI reduction to less than 50% of baseline with improvement in bed-partner reported apneas/snoring, validated daytime sleepiness scores, comorbidities such as hypertension, and quality-of-life measures. Most surgical studies use the Sher criterion: an AHI reduction of 50% or more to an AHI below 20. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 2, p 66)

**Laser physics and tissue interaction**: Stimulated emission in a resonant cavity (one fully and one partially reflective mirror) requires population inversion and yields monochromatic, coherent, collimated light. Only absorbed light affects tissue. The wound has a central vaporization zone, a necrosis zone and a rim of reversible thermal damage. Surgeon-controlled variables are power, spot size and exposure time, and tissue effect tracks energy density (J/cm2). Short high-energy pulses shorter than the tissue thermal relaxation time limit collateral heat. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 3, p 68-69)

**Chromophore targeting by wavelength**: Hemoglobin peaks at 405-420 nm with secondary peaks at about 540 and 577 nm, so vascular lasers use KTP 532, copper vapor 578 and pulsed dye 585 nm. Melanin targets (hair, pigment, tattoo) use red wavelengths where hemoglobin does not compete: ruby 694 and alexandrite 755 nm. Water absorption rises through the infrared and peaks at 2.94 µm (Er:YAG). Longer wavelength means deeper penetration in the visible range, but CO2 and Er:YAG are exceptions because water absorbs them superficially. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 3, p 70)

**Delivery and laser-specific properties**: CO2 (10.6 µm, invisible, needs a coaxial helium-neon aiming beam) cannot travel through standard optical fiber and uses articulated arms or hollow flexible waveguides. It is precise with good small-vessel hemostasis. Nd:YAG (1.064 µm) passes through fibers and flexible scopes, coagulates about 4 mm deep (good for palliating obstructing tracheobronchial/esophageal tumors and vascular/lymphatic malformations) but is imprecise. Er:YAG cuts cleanly with minimal thermal spread but poor hemostasis. KTP is fiber-deliverable with excellent hemostasis. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 3, p 69-71)

**Eye injury depends on wavelength**: Visible and near-infrared light (KTP, Nd:YAG) passes the clear media and burns the retina, whereas far-infrared CO2 light is absorbed by water and injures the cornea and lens. Patients get moist saline eye pads and staff wear wavelength-specific eyewear. Also lower FiO2 to the minimum and avoid nitrous oxide when lasing in the airway, use laser-specific or metal tubes rather than PVC, and evacuate plume. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 3, p 73)

**Ablative laser resurfacing: CO2 versus Er:YAG**: CO2 removes roughly 50-100 µm per pass, coagulates small vessels for a nearly bloodless field and reepithelializes in about 2 weeks. Er:YAG removes only about 25-30 µm, bleeds more, suits mild epidermal aging and heals in 5-7 days. Nonablative rejuvenation (for example 1.32 µm Nd:YAG) heats the dermis to stimulate fibroblasts without ablating epidermis. Give perioperative HSV antiviral prophylaxis (eg, valacyclovir starting the day before and continuing to about day 10). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 3, p 72)

**Laser resurfacing contraindications and complications**: Avoid ablative resurfacing after isotretinoin within the prior 1-2 years, in scleroderma, active acne, prior facial burns, or prior head and neck radiation (all impair reepithelialization). This is the book view. The 2017 ASDS consensus found insufficient evidence to delay superficial peels, nonablative lasers or fractional ablative lasers after isotretinoin, but still advises against fully ablative laser and mechanical dermabrasion on or soon after it. Complications are prolonged erythema, scarring and dyschromia, with higher pigmentary risk in Fitzpatrick III and darker skin. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 3, p 72)

**Lingual neurovascular bundle location**: During tongue-base radiofrequency or resection, the hypoglossal nerve-lingual artery bundle lies about 2.7 cm deep and 1.6 cm lateral to the foramen cecum. Staying near the midline protects it. Tongue-base and palatal radiofrequency yields about a 45% long-term RDI reduction and can be repeated. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 3, p 74)

**Radiofrequency (Coblation) mechanism**: Radiofrequency energy in a conductive medium creates an ionized plasma layer that breaks molecular bonds at roughly 40-100 °C, removing or shrinking tissue with less thermal spread than electrocautery. Coblation tonsillectomy has pain and hemorrhage outcomes comparable to or better than electrocautery. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 3, p 73)

topic: ENT Perioperative Anesthesia / Difficult Airway Planning
text: **IV induction agents**: Propofol (1.5-2.5 mg/kg, GABA-A) gives rapid induction and emergence with less PONV but drops arterial pressure about 20-30% and causes apnea. Etomidate preserves hemodynamics and lowers ICP but suppresses adrenal steroid synthesis. Ketamine (NMDA antagonist) is a dissociative, analgesic bronchodilator that keeps airway reflexes and drive but raises ICP and heart rate and causes emergence dysphoria. Dexmedetomidine (alpha-2 agonist) sedates while preserving respiration, useful for awake airway work, but a rapid load causes bradycardia and hypotension. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 4, p 77-78)

topic: ENT Perioperative Anesthesia / Difficult Airway Planning
text: **Aspiration pneumonitis (Mendelson syndrome)**: K.J. Lee links high risk to gastric contents over 200 mL with pH under 2.5, but the classic risk threshold is over 25 mL (about 0.4 mL/kg) with pH under 2.5. Aspiration occurs past cuffed tubes in up to 5%. Lavage does not help, and care is supportive. Sodium citrate and H2 blockers raise gastric pH preoperatively. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 4, p 92)

topic: ENT Perioperative Anesthesia / Difficult Airway Planning
text: **Epinephrine limit under volatile anesthesia**: Volatile agents sensitize myocardium to catecholamines; keep injected epinephrine to about 10 mL of 1:100,000 (100 µg) per 10 minutes. Epinephrine with tricyclics or MAO inhibitors can precipitate hypertensive crisis; treat tachycardia/hypertension with short-acting beta blockade (esmolol). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 4, p 83, 92)

topic: ENT Perioperative Anesthesia / Difficult Airway Planning
text: **Extubation planning and difficult-airway registry**: The UK NAP4 audit found many airway losses at extubation from failure to plan for failure, so extubation deserves the same backup planning as induction. Patients with a known difficult airway should be told in writing, flagged in the record, and may enroll in the MedicAlert difficult airway registry; difficult airway response teams improve rescue. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 4, p 91-92)

topic: ENT Perioperative Anesthesia / Difficult Airway Planning
text: **Airway regional anesthesia for awake procedures**: Internal superior laryngeal nerve block: walk a 25-gauge needle about 1 cm below the greater cornu of the hyoid to the thyrohyoid membrane and inject about 3 mL. Transtracheal block: puncture the cricothyroid membrane in the midline, confirm air aspiration and instill about 4 mL (cough spreads it below the cords). Topical anesthesia of the piriform sinuses blocks the same internal branch; tracheal mucosa absorbs local anesthetic almost like an IV dose. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 4, p 82, 93-94)

topic: Pain Management in the Head & Neck Patient
text: **Opioid and nonopioid specifics**: Hydromorphone is about 5 times morphine potency and causes less pruritus and nausea (preferred PCA). Morphine releases histamine and its glucuronides accumulate in renal failure. Codeine needs CYP2D6 activation: ultrarapid metabolizers (1-2%) risk toxicity and poor metabolizers (5-10%) get no effect. For this reason the FDA contraindicates codeine and tramadol in children under 12 and after tonsillectomy or adenoidectomy in anyone under 18. Meperidine is avoided (serotonin syndrome with MAOIs) except low-dose for shivering. Ketorolac is limited to short courses and avoided with renal failure, bleeding risk and AERD. Liposomal bupivacaine lasts up to 72 h but interferes with postoperative nerve assessment. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 4, p 86-89)

topic: Pain Management in the Head & Neck Patient
text: **PONV prophylaxis**: PONV affects about one third of untreated patients. Risk factors are female sex, prior PONV/motion sickness, nonsmoking, younger age (<40) and postoperative opioids. Each prophylactic class lowers risk about 20-25%, so high-risk patients get multimodal prophylaxis: dexamethasone, 5-HT3 antagonist before emergence, transdermal scopolamine placed hours before surgery, NK-1 antagonists (aprepitant), opioid sparing and gastric suctioning of swallowed blood. Low-dose droperidol needs ECG monitoring for QT prolongation. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 4, p 89-90)

**Local anesthesia pitfalls in middle ear surgery**: Inject at the bony-cartilaginous junction of the canal (for example at 6 points around the canal so each later stick is already numb). Lidocaine that diffuses into the middle ear can cause transient facial paralysis via a dehiscent facial nerve, or violent vertigo with nystagmus about 45 minutes later through the oval or round window. Both resolve, but avoid infiltrating bony canal skin for simple myringotomy. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 4, p 97-99)

topic: Hemostasis / Coagulopathy / Antithrombotic Management in ENT
text: **Bleeding pattern localizes the defect**: Primary hemostasis defects (von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited one; thrombocytopenia the most common acquired) bleed from mucosa and skin: epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia, petechiae. Secondary (coagulation factor) defects produce deep hematomas, hemarthrosis and delayed bleeding. Primary hemostasis works even in hemophilia, which is why hemophiliacs may not bleed immediately. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 5, p 104-105)

topic: Hemostasis / Coagulopathy / Antithrombotic Management in ENT
text: **Three-question bleeding history**: Ask (1) prior surgery or dental extraction without bleeding (a recent uneventful operation is a hemostatic stress test), (2) what they take for pain (aspirin/NSAIDs) plus supplements such as garlic, vitamin E and fish oil, and (3) family history of bleeding. Routine PT/aPTT screening does not predict tonsillectomy bleeding, bleeding time misses von Willebrand disease, and no routine test measures fibrinolysis. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 5, p 105-106)

topic: Hemostasis / Coagulopathy / Antithrombotic Management in ENT
text: **Heparin pharmacology and reversal**: IV unfractionated heparin clears in about 4 hours; protamine 1 mg neutralizes about 100 units of recently given heparin (give slowly over 1-3 min to avoid hypotension/bradycardia) and fully reverses UFH. LMWH (anti-Xa:anti-IIa over 4) does not prolong the aPTT, is monitored with anti-Xa levels in obesity over 150 kg, renal insufficiency and pregnancy, and is only about 60% reversed by protamine (1 mg per 1 mg enoxaparin given in the last 8 h). Fondaparinux has no reliable reversal. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 5, p 107-110)

topic: Hemostasis / Coagulopathy / Antithrombotic Management in ENT
text: **Warfarin kinetics and supratherapeutic INR**: Warfarin blocks vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX and X; full antithrombotic effect needs about 5 days (factor II half-life about 50 h), so acute VTE requires a 5-day heparin overlap. For INR elevation without bleeding, hold warfarin (add low-dose oral vitamin K, up to 2.5 mg, if INR over 8 or other bleeding risk); with bleeding stop warfarin and give vitamin K (about 5 mg), adding PCC for major bleeding. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 5, p 108, 111)

topic: Hemostasis / Coagulopathy / Antithrombotic Management in ENT
text: **DOAC hold times**: For standard-risk procedures hold rivaroxaban, apixaban and edoxaban about 24 h (48 h if CrCl under 50 for rivaroxaban/apixaban) and dabigatran about 48 h (it is 80% renally cleared). DOACs need no bridging. Low-risk procedures (skin biopsy, endoscopy without biopsy, dental work) usually proceed on aspirin or clopidogrel. Otherwise the book stops antiplatelets 7-10 days before elective surgery, while current ACCP 2022 guidance stops clopidogrel about 5 days (prasugrel 7) before surgery and often continues aspirin, in coordination with cardiology. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 5, p 110-113)

topic: Hemostasis / Coagulopathy / Antithrombotic Management in ENT
text: **Coronary stents and antiplatelet interruption**: Do not interrupt clopidogrel shortly after a stent (the book cites 3 months, with 3-6 months before planned surgery); recently placed stents (within 1 year) are high thrombotic risk, so coordinate with cardiology. Current ACC/AHA guidance generally delays elective surgery at least 6 months after a drug-eluting stent (12 months after ACS) and keeps aspirin through surgery when possible. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 5, p 113, 116)

topic: Hemostasis / Coagulopathy / Antithrombotic Management in ENT
text: **Platelet receptors**: Adhesion uses platelet GPIb with von Willebrand factor; aggregation uses activated GPIIb/IIIa bridging fibrinogen; release of thromboxane A2, ADP and serotonin recruits more platelets. Bernard-Soulier (GPIb) and Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GPIIb/IIIa) are the receptor-defect disorders. The extrinsic (tissue factor-VIIa) and intrinsic pathways converge at factor Xa. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 5, p 104-105, 114)

topic: Facial Pain / Headache vs Rhinogenic Disease
text: **Primary headache criteria**: Migraine: attacks of 4-72 hours with two of unilateral, pulsating, moderate-severe, or worsened by activity, plus nausea/vomiting or photophobia and phonophobia; aura is usually visual. Tension-type: bilateral pressing/tightening (bifrontal or occipitonuchal), mild-moderate, not worsened by activity, without nausea or photo/phonophobia, lasting up to 7 days. Imaging is unnecessary with a stable pattern and normal neurologic exam; MRI is preferred over CT outside emergencies. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 120-122)

topic: Facial Pain / Headache vs Rhinogenic Disease
text: **Migraine abortive and preventive therapy**: Abortives (triptans, ergots, NSAIDs, combination analgesics, antiemetics) work best within about 15 minutes of onset. Avoid opioids and butalbital as first line and limit OTC analgesic overuse. Prophylaxis is indicated for frequent attacks (more than 2 per month or abortives more than twice weekly), prolonged or disabling attacks, or abortive failure. Options are antiepileptics (topiramate), beta blockers, tricyclics, calcium channel blockers and botulinum toxin (for chronic migraine), and supplements include magnesium, riboflavin and coenzyme Q10. The book predates CGRP-targeted drugs: current AHS guidance adds CGRP monoclonal antibodies for prevention and gepants for acute treatment and prevention. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 121)

topic: Facial Pain / Headache vs Rhinogenic Disease
text: **Cluster headache**: Severe strictly unilateral orbital/temporal pain lasting 15-180 minutes, up to 8 times a day, often nocturnal, with ipsilateral tearing, conjunctival injection, congestion, rhinorrhea, sweating, miosis and ptosis. The episodic form has remissions of at least 3 months, and the chronic form does not. Abort attacks with 100% oxygen or triptans (intranasal or injected). K.J. Lee gives oxygen at about 8 L/min for 10 min, but current AHS guidance uses 12-15 L/min by non-rebreather mask for about 15 minutes. Verapamil is the main preventive, with lithium and topiramate. Refractory cases may get occipital nerve block, sphenopalatine ganglion stimulation or hypothalamic deep brain stimulation. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 122-123)

**Dural arteriovenous fistula**: A dural AV shunt, often after transverse/sigmoid sinus thrombosis, presenting with pulsatile tinnitus, proptosis, papilledema or hemorrhage. Retrograde cortical venous drainage marks high hemorrhage risk and needs urgent treatment (Borden I drains to a sinus, about 2% aggressive, II adds cortical reflux, about 39%, III drains directly into cortical veins, about 79%). Hemorrhage carries roughly 30% mortality. Pulsatile tinnitus workup should include vascular imaging (CTA/MRA or angiography) for this. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 130-131)

**Idiopathic intracranial hypertension evaluation**: IIH (typically obese women of childbearing age) is papilledema with elevated ICP (opening pressure over about 25 cm H2O) and no mass or hydrocephalus on MRI with MR venography; formal ophthalmology assessment is needed because blindness from optic atrophy is the main risk and does not track symptom duration. Treat with weight loss and acetazolamide (or furosemide), then optic nerve sheath fenestration or CSF shunting if medical therapy fails; suspect IIH in any spontaneous CSF leak. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 133)

topic: Endoscopic Pituitary / Anterior Skull Base Approach
text: **Postoperative diabetes insipidus monitoring**: After transsphenoidal surgery, check urine specific gravity and sodium about every 6 hours; DI is suggested by dilute urine (SG under 1.003) with rising sodium over 145. On MRI a microadenoma is a hypointense nonenhancing focus within the brightly enhancing gland on T1. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 135)

topic: Endoscopic Pituitary / Anterior Skull Base Approach
text: **Craniopharyngioma**: A WHO grade 1 Rathke cleft tumor of the sellar/suprasellar region with bimodal ages: children (adamantinomatous, calcified, cystic, T1 bright from protein/cholesterol) and middle-aged adults (papillary, T1 isointense). After surgery expect endocrinopathy: permanent DI in about 90%, cortisol and thyroid replacement in about 90%, GH replacement in about 50%, and hypothalamic obesity in about 50%. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 134)

**Meningioma imaging signs**: Meningiomas are extra-axial, dural-based, T1 isointense and T2 hyperintense with homogeneous enhancement, a dural tail, a CSF cleft at the brain interface, adjacent hyperostosis, and a prolonged venous-phase angiographic blush ('mother-in-law' sign). About 7% are WHO grade 2 and 2.4% grade 3. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 135-136)

**Craniovertebral junction anomalies**: Chiari I is cerebellar tonsillar descent at least about 5-6 mm below the foramen magnum, obstructing CSF flow and causing downbeat nystagmus, occipital headache and lower cranial neuropathies. Platybasia (skull-base angle over about 143 degrees) and basilar invagination (odontoid migrating into the foramen magnum) occur with Down syndrome, Klippel-Feil and rheumatoid arthritis; treatment is decompression and/or fusion depending on reducibility. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 133)

**ABR generators and lesion patterns**: Classic (Jewett) generators are wave I distal eighth nerve, II proximal nerve or cochlear nucleus, III superior olivary complex, IV lateral lemniscus and V inferior colliculus. Intraoperative recordings (Moller) revise this: wave II is the proximal nerve, III mainly the cochlear nucleus, IV the superior olivary complex and V the lateral lemniscus where it ends at the inferior colliculus. Vestibular schwannomas typically prolong I-III (nerve to caudal pons), whereas MS more often prolongs III-V. ABR is abnormal in about 90% of vestibular schwannomas and a third of MS patients. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 129)

**Blunt cervical artery dissection**: Vertebral or carotid dissection from blunt trauma or transverse foramen fracture can cause posterior circulation or hemispheric stroke. K.J. Lee gives heparin then warfarin for about 3 months, with antiplatelet therapy when bleeding risk is high. **Current view**: trials (CADISS, TREAT-CAD) and trauma guidelines show antiplatelet therapy, usually aspirin, works as well as anticoagulation, so it is the usual first-line choice. Endovascular stenting or sacrifice is reserved for selected lesions, and most heal within about 6 weeks. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 131-132)

**Osmotic demyelination**: Correcting chronic hyponatremia too fast causes central pontine myelinolysis (dysarthria, dysphagia, pseudobulbar palsy, quadriparesis, coma); limit correction to about 12 mmol/L in 24 hours (many now target 8-10). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 128)

topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
text: **Multiple sclerosis in ENT**: Relapsing CNS demyelination (peak about 35 years, women) presenting to ENT as trigeminal neuralgia in a young patient, vertigo, sudden hearing loss or internuclear ophthalmoplegia. MRI shows T2/FLAIR periventricular lesions perpendicular to the ventricles (Dawson fingers) with open-ring enhancement. CSF shows oligoclonal bands and IgG index over 0.7. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 126-127)

topic: ENT Perioperative Anesthesia / Difficult Airway Planning
text: **A-a gradient to sort hypoxemia**: Estimate alveolar PO2 at sea level on room air as about 148 - 1.2 x PaCO2; an A-a gradient under about 20 mm Hg means hypoventilation alone (eg, opioid or anesthetic effect), which corrects when ventilation is restored. A widened gradient means V/Q mismatch (improves with supplemental oxygen) or true shunt (does not improve with oxygen). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 7, p 145)

topic: ENT Perioperative Anesthesia / Difficult Airway Planning
text: **Preoperative spirometry and weaning numbers**: Normal FEV1 and FVC are at least 80% predicted with FEV1/FVC above about 0.70-0.75; a 15-20% improvement after bronchodilator indicates reversible obstruction, and such patients should be bronchodilated before surgery. A rapid shallow breathing index (rate/tidal volume in L) under 105 during a spontaneous breathing trial predicts about 85% extubation success. Breathing 100% oxygen for about 7 minutes washes out roughly 90% of nitrogen and buys several minutes of apnea tolerance. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 7, p 141, 144-145, 147, 149)

**Apnea after relief of chronic obstruction**: A patient with chronic CO2 retention from upper airway obstruction may depend on hypoxic drive. Sudden relief with tracheotomy and oxygen can remove that drive and cause apnea (CO2 narcosis), so be ready to ventilate until CO2 falls. Pneumomediastinum and pneumothorax are classic early tracheotomy complications. In children the innominate artery crosses at the sternal notch, higher than in adults, and about 10% of people have a thyroidea ima artery ascending on the anterior trachea. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 7, p 148-150)

**Tracheobronchial and mediastinal landmarks**: Adult trachea is 10-12 cm long with 16-20 rings and bifurcates at T4-T5 about 6 cm below the sternal notch. The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical. The right upper lobe bronchus lies above the right pulmonary artery. The esophagus narrows at the cricopharyngeus, aortic arch, left main bronchus and diaphragm. Approximate rigid bronchoscope sizes: 3 mm premature, 3.5 mm at 6 months, 4 mm at 18 months, 5 mm at 5 years, 6 mm at 10 years, 7 mm adult. In mediastinoscopy dissect deep to the pretracheal fascia. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 7, p 149-151, 154)

**Thoracic causes of left vocal fold paralysis**: Imaging for unexplained paralysis must extend to the chest: the left recurrent nerve loops under the aortic arch with the ligamentum and lies near the left main bronchus and tracheobronchial nodes. Apical (Pancoast) lung tumors invade the lower brachial plexus, sympathetic chain, phrenic and recurrent laryngeal nerves, giving shoulder/inner arm pain, intrinsic hand wasting and Horner syndrome. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 7, p 148, 150)

**Mediastinal mass by compartment**: About one third of mediastinal tumors are malignant, lymphoma most often. Anterior/superior: thymoma, teratoma/dermoid, substernal thyroid, parathyroid, lymphoma. Middle: bronchogenic and pericardial cysts, lymphoma, carcinoma. Posterior: neurogenic tumors and enteric cysts. Superior vena cava syndrome (facial/neck/arm edema and cyanosis, distended chest wall veins, normal leg venous pressure) is usually malignant. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 7, p 154)

**Chronic cough big four**: With a normal chest radiograph, cough over 8 weeks is usually from upper airway cough syndrome (sinonasal disease), asthma, GERD and ACE inhibitors; about a third have more than one cause. Difficult-to-treat asthma often has unrecognized sinonasal disease (proposed links: nasobronchial reflex, eosinophil activation, postnasal seeding, nasal obstruction), and vocal fold dysfunction mimics refractory asthma. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 7, p 144)

**Nose as the main airway resistor**: The nose contributes about 79% of total airway resistance on inspiration and about 75% on expiration (larynx about 3-6%, bronchial tree 15-23%), explaining why nasal obstruction drives mouth breathing and dependence on oral airflow. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 7, p 149)

**Nutritional markers and their half-lives**: Albumin (half-life about 21 days; under 3.0 g/dL predicts perioperative morbidity), transferrin (about 7 days; under 150 mg/dL indicates malnutrition, affected by iron status) and prealbumin (2-3 days; best for short-term change, falsely high in renal failure). CRP over 10 signals an inflammatory cause of low visceral proteins. Total lymphocyte count under 1700/µL is associated with about a fivefold increase in wound infection. Physical findings (temporal and orbital fat loss, proximal muscle wasting, cheilosis) remain more reliable than any single lab. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 8, p 161-162)

**Cancer cachexia versus malnutrition**: Up to 50% of head and neck cancer patients are malnourished at presentation and up to 80% during chemoradiation. Cachexia (weight loss over 5% in 6 months or BMI under 20) is cytokine-driven (IL-1, IL-6, TNF) sarcopenia with insulin resistance, anemia and high CRP that does not reverse with feeding alone; options include megestrol acetate, corticosteroids and omega-3 supplements. Obese patients can have sarcopenic obesity and still be malnourished. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 8, p 160, 162)

**Enteral access and prophylactic gastrostomy**: NG tubes are easiest but cause discomfort, reflux and alar necrosis; gastrostomy is better tolerated long term; jejunostomy reduces reflux/vomiting but prevents bolus feeds. Prophylactic gastrostomy before chemoradiation is commonly used with over 10% weight loss, severe dehydration, aspiration/dysphagia or intensive multimodality therapy, but keeping patients swallowing by mouth lowers long-term tube dependence. TPN needs a central line and is reserved for nonfunctional gut or refractory high-output chyle leak. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 8, p 163-164)

**Maintenance fluid math**: Total body water is about 60% of weight (42 L in a 70-kg man: 28 L intracellular, 14 L extracellular, of which about 4 L plasma). Adults need roughly 35 mL/kg/day; children use 100/50/20-25 mL/kg/day for the first 10 kg, next 10 kg and each kg above (4-2-1 mL/kg/h); add about 500 mL/day per degree above 38.3 °C. Avoid routine hypotonic maintenance fluid, which causes hospital-acquired hyponatremia. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 8, p 165-166)

**Calcium disorders**: Correct total calcium by about 0.8 mg/dL for each 1 g/dL that albumin is below 4.0. Symptomatic hypocalcemia: 1 ampule (10 mL of 10%) calcium gluconate IV over 10-15 minutes with cardiac monitoring; chronic replacement with oral calcium plus calcitriol starting about 0.25 µg/day. Hypercalcemia is mostly primary hyperparathyroidism or malignancy: aggressive saline first, then furosemide only after volume repletion, calcitonin for rapid effect, bisphosphonate (slow, days), and steroids for granulomatous causes. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 8, p 168)

**Acid-base compensation and anion gap**: Anion gap = Na - (Cl + HCO3), normal about 10. High-gap acidosis: ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, toxins (aspirin, ethylene glycol), renal failure; normal-gap: diarrhea, fistulas/drains, RTA. Expected compensation: metabolic acidosis lowers PaCO2 about 1.3 per 1 mEq/L HCO3 drop; acute respiratory acidosis raises HCO3 about 1 per 10 mm Hg PaCO2. Metabolic alkalosis after vomiting or NG suction is chloride- and potassium-responsive and corrects with saline and KCl. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 8, p 169-171)

**Resistance mechanisms**: Beta-lactamase hydrolysis is the most common resistance mechanism. MRSA carries mecA, encoding PBP2a with low beta-lactam affinity. D-Ala-D-Lac substitution confers vancomycin resistance; gyrase/topoisomerase IV mutations confer fluoroquinolone resistance; Pseudomonas reduces porins and gram-negatives upregulate efflux pumps. Biofilm matrix can be about nine times the bacterial mass, slows bacterial growth and blocks antibiotic penetration, explaining CRS and tube otorrhea persistence. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 9, p 174-175)

**High-yield drug spectra and toxicities**: Ciprofloxacin is the oral fluoroquinolone with the best Pseudomonas activity (tendon rupture, QT prolongation, arthropathy); moxifloxacin adds anaerobes. Clindamycin covers streptococci, MSSA, many CA-MRSA and anaerobes but drives C. difficile. Amoxicillin causes rash in about 30% of patients with EBV mononucleosis. Linezolid causes cytopenias, serotonin syndrome and optic neuritis. Vancomycin causes red man (infusion) reactions and nephrotoxicity. Ceftaroline is the cephalosporin with MRSA activity; ertapenem lacks Pseudomonas coverage; posaconazole and amphotericin cover Mucorales while voriconazole does not. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 9, p 175-182)

**AOE microbiology and follow-up**: Pseudomonas aeruginosa and S. aureus cause most AOE; under 2% is fungal, viral or eczematous. Use acidifying/antiseptic or topical antibiotic drops with aural toilet and a wick for canal edema, nonototoxic preparations if the TM may not be intact, and reassess at 48-72 hours if not improving. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 9, p 186)

**AOM pathogens and beta-lactamase rates**: S. pneumoniae about 50%, nontypeable H. influenzae about 45% (a third to half produce beta-lactamase) and M. catarrhalis about 10% (over 90% beta-lactamase positive). Amoxicillin is first line; observation for 48 hours is an option for nonsevere unilateral AOM at 6-23 months and nonsevere AOM over 2 years; cefdinir, cefuroxime, cefpodoxime or ceftriaxone for non-severe penicillin allergy; acute tube otorrhea gets topical fluoroquinolone drops alone. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 9, p 186)

**Intranasal steroid and anticholinergic specifics**: Intranasal steroids cause epistaxis and rarely septal perforation but no meaningful cataract or IOP effect. Mometasone, fluticasone furoate and triamcinolone are approved from age 2, fluticasone propionate from 4, and budesonide from 6. Budesonide has the most favorable pregnancy data. Mometasone and exhalation-delivered fluticasone (Xhance) carry US nasal polyp indications. Ipratropium (0.03% or 0.06%) is the only nasal anticholinergic and treats watery rhinorrhea (vasomotor, viral, gustatory) without affecting congestion. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 10, p 192-193)

topic: Hemostasis / Coagulopathy / Antithrombotic Management in ENT
text: **Desmopressin and topical hemostatic agents**: DDAVP releases von Willebrand factor and factor VIII from endothelium: useful for type 1 vWD, mild hemophilia A and uremic platelet dysfunction (it also releases tPA). Aminocaproic acid (lysine analog) blocks fibrinolysis. Topicals: fibrin sealants (thrombin plus fibrinogen), gelatin plugs, gelatin-thrombin matrix (FloSeal), oxidized regenerated cellulose (Surgicel), microfibrillar collagen (Avitene, activates intrinsic pathway), and cyanoacrylate for skin. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 10, p 196)

**Other ototoxic drug classes**: Loop diuretics (furosemide, ethacrynic acid) cause usually transient loss via the stria vascularis. Give infusions slowly rather than as boluses and beware synergy with aminoglycosides. Salicylates (typically over about 2.7 g/day of aspirin) cause reversible flat hearing loss and tinnitus that resolve with clearance. Quinine/chloroquine cause cochlear vasculitis and can cause congenital SNHL in exposed fetuses. Cisplatin and carboplatin cause permanent 4-8 kHz loss in over half of patients. Monitor including ultra-high frequencies. Aminoglycoside susceptibility is markedly increased by the mitochondrial 12S rRNA A1555G mutation. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 10, p 196-198)

**Xerostomia pharmacotherapy**: When residual gland parenchyma exists, cholinergic agonists pilocarpine or cevimeline increase saliva but cause sweating, diarrhea and bronchorrhea; otherwise use frequent water, sugar-free sialagogues and cellulose-based substitutes. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 10, p 200)

**Recurrent aphthous stomatitis**: Affects 20-50% of people. Potent topical steroids (0.05% clobetasol or fluocinonide) outperform triamcinolone. Tetracycline rinses reduce ulcer size and pain. Amlexanox 5% paste speeds healing without preventing recurrences. Viscous lidocaine for pain. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 10, p 200)

topic: Systemic Therapy Foundations in Head & Neck Cancer
text: **Cetuximab toxicities**: Cetuximab (anti-EGFR) causes acneiform rash, fatigue and hypomagnesemia. It can be given with radiation, with platinum, or as monotherapy after platinum failure. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 10, p 189-190)

topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
text: **Biologics for vasculitides**: Rituximab (anti-CD20, B-cell depletion) is now standard for moderate-severe granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Mepolizumab (anti-IL-5) is approved for eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Tocilizumab (anti-IL-6 receptor) for giant cell arteritis. Infliximab (anti-TNF) is used in relapsing polychondritis. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 10, p 190)

topic: Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Sunscreen counseling**: UVB (290-320 nm) damages DNA directly and UVA (320-400 nm) indirectly through reactive oxygen species. Sunscreen lowers photodamage, actinic keratoses and SCC (evidence for BCC and melanoma is weaker); apply 30 minutes before exposure and every 2 hours; inorganic blockers (zinc, titanium oxide) give broader, more durable protection than organic absorbers. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 10, p 198)

topic: CF / Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia Sinonasal Disease
text: **CFTR mutations and modulators**: Autosomal recessive CFTR chloride channel defect. Delta F508 accounts for about 70% of alleles and G551D (a gating mutation, about 5%) is the original target of the potentiator ivacaftor, which improves lung function and exacerbation rates. Elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor (FDA 2019) now treats patients with at least one F508del allele, and it also improves sinonasal symptoms and CT findings. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 10, p 201)

**HIV parotid disease: BLEC and DILS**: Benign lymphoepithelial cysts are the most common parotid lesion in HIV (about 75% of HIV parotid masses), bilateral in up to 80%, with cervical adenopathy in up to 90%, and can mimic bilateral Warthin tumor; treat with ART (regression), serial aspiration, doxycycline sclerotherapy or radiation, reserving parotidectomy for disfigurement or suspected malignancy. Diffuse infiltrative lymphocytosis syndrome (about 1% of HIV patients) mimics Sjögren with diffuse parotid enlargement and sicca, but the infiltrate is CD8-predominant and half have lymphocytic interstitial pneumonitis. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 11, p 206-207)

**Oral candidiasis forms and treatment threshold**: Four forms: pseudomembranous (thrush, wipes off to raw red base, most common), atrophic/erythematous (red depapillated tongue), angular cheilitis, and hyperplastic (thick plaque that does not wipe off, rarest). Confirm with KOH or PAS. With CD4 over 200 use topical nystatin. Under 200 use systemic fluconazole, watching for azole resistance after repeated courses. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 11, p 208)

**HIV periodontal disease and oral histoplasmosis**: Linear gingival erythema (fiery marginal band out of proportion to plaque) and necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis/periodontitis strongly suggest HIV. Treat with chlorhexidine, debridement and dental care, and biopsy when bone loss exceeds mucosal disease (lymphoma, bacillary angiomatosis). Oral histoplasmosis (Ohio River valley) produces painful granulomatous ulcers, is AIDS-defining, and needs biopsy/culture and amphotericin or itraconazole. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 11, p 208-209)

**Kaposi sarcoma**: HHV-8-driven angioproliferative tumor in about 5% of HIV patients (variants: AIDS-associated, classic Mediterranean, endemic African, transplant). Up to 70% of AIDS-KS involves the head and neck, especially hard palate, gingiva and tongue, as violaceous nonblanching lesions; biopsy shows spindle cells, slit-like vascular channels and extravasated RBCs; up to 25% have visceral disease. Treatment centers on ART, with radiation, intralesional or systemic chemotherapy, laser or palliative surgery for local control. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 11, p 210-211)

**HIV-associated lymphomas**: Lymphoma is the second most common HIV malignancy (up to 19%): diffuse large B-cell most common, then Burkitt (doubling time 24-48 h, unrelated to CD4 count, rarely jaw-based outside endemic Africa). Plasmablastic lymphoma typically arises in the oral cavity of HIV patients and should trigger HIV testing. Prognosis is poor. HIV Hodgkin lymphoma presents later with mixed cellularity or lymphocyte-depleted histology. Open biopsy is preferred to define subtype. Treatment is chemotherapy (R-CHOP or R-EPOCH) with concurrent ART. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 11, p 211-213)

topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
text: **EGPA (Churg-Strauss) criteria**: Asthma typically precedes vasculitis by 3-9 years, progressing through allergic, eosinophilic (Loeffler-type) and vasculitic phases. About 70% have sinonasal disease. pANCA/MPO is positive in only about 50%. ACR 1990 criteria (4 of 6): asthma, eosinophils over 10%, mononeuropathy/polyneuropathy, migratory pulmonary infiltrates, paranasal sinus abnormality, and extravascular eosinophils on biopsy. The 2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria now replace the 1990 set: obstructive airway disease +3, nasal polyps +3, mononeuritis multiplex +1, eosinophils at least 1×10⁹/L +5, extravascular eosinophilic inflammation on biopsy +2, cANCA/PR3 −3 and hematuria −1, with a score of 6 or more classifying EGPA. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 12, p 220)

topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
text: **Lupus and Behçet in the head and neck**: SLE can cause laryngotracheal perichondritis with vocal fold thickening, nasal crusting and septal perforation. Discoid lupus affects only skin/mucosa. Specific serology is anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm. Behçet disease requires recurrent oral aphthae (3 or more per year) plus two of genital ulcers, uveitis, skin lesions (erythema nodosum) or a positive pathergy test. It can cause progressive SNHL and vasculitis of vessels of any size. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 12, p 221-222)

topic: Systemic Disease of the Nose / Sinuses
text: **Septal perforation site clues and other infections**: Syphilis classically perforates the bony septum, whereas most other causes (cocaine, GPA, trauma) involve cartilage. Leprosy (Mycobacterium leprae, grows best at 27-33 °C) favors cool tissues and causes early nasal disease and saddle nose. Treat with dapsone plus rifampin and clofazimine. Rhinosporidiosis (South India, Sri Lanka) causes friable 'strawberry' nasal polyps requiring excision. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 12, p 227, 229, 231)

**Otosyphilis and tuberculous otitis**: Otosyphilis causes fluctuating, often bilateral SNHL with tinnitus and vertigo, sometimes with a positive Hennebert sign and Tullio phenomenon. Screen with RPR/VDRL and confirm with FTA-ABS. K.J. Lee reserves IV penicillin for tertiary/neurosyphilis, but current CDC guidance treats otosyphilis at any stage as neurosyphilis (IV aqueous penicillin G for 10-14 days), usually with steroids, and the case is reported. Tuberculous otitis gives painless watery otorrhea with multiple TM perforations and pale granulation. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 12, p 228-230)

**Granulomatous laryngitis**: Laryngeal tuberculosis typically involves the posterior glottis/interarytenoid area with ulceration and granulation and can produce a turban-shaped epiglottis; it mimics carcinoma, so biopsy plus AFB culture and chest imaging are needed. Blastomycosis and histoplasmosis also produce ulcerative laryngeal or oral lesions with pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia that can be misread as SCC. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 12, p 228, 230-231)

**Chronic granulomatous disease and phagocyte disorders**: CGD (about two thirds X-linked, one third autosomal recessive) impairs phagocyte oxidative killing, causing recurrent abscesses and granulomas from catalase-positive bacteria and fungi. Diagnose it with neutrophil function testing (dihydrorhodamine or nitroblue tetrazolium). Long-term care is directed by immunology and includes interferon gamma, avoidance of live vaccines (including BCG), and stem cell transplant for cure. Chédiak-Higashi (autosomal recessive: albinism, neutropenia, neuropathy) and Job (hyper-IgE with recurrent staphylococcal cold abscesses) belong in this differential. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 12, p 231-232)

**Lobular capillary hemangioma (pyogenic granuloma)**: A friable, bleeding, noninfectious lobular capillary proliferation of gingiva, lip, tongue or nasal septum, often after trauma and hormonally driven in pregnancy (pregnancy lesions usually regress postpartum). Otherwise excise, cauterize or laser, completely to prevent recurrence. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 12, p 225)

**Named surgical landmarks**: Körner septum (petrosquamous lamina) separates squamous from petrous air cells and can be mistaken for the antrum medial wall, leaving disease unopened. The ponticulus is the ridge between the oval window niche and sinus tympani. The subiculum lies between the round window niche and sinus tympani. Notch of Rivinus is the superior gap in the tympanic ring medial to which lies the pars flaccida. The solid angle is formed by the three semicircular canals. Citelli angle is the sinodural angle. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 13, p 234-236)

**Fissures and canals that spread disease**: Foramen of Huschke is a persistent defect in the anterior-inferior tympanic plate opening the canal to the parotid/TMJ (route for infection or tumor spread, and for salivary fistula). Fissures of Santorini perforate the cartilaginous canal floor to the parotid. Huguier canal carries the chorda tympani anteriorly out of the temporal bone. Hyrtl fissure, open in young infants, runs from the hypotympanum near the round window to the subarachnoid space and can spread otitis to the meninges. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 13, p 235-236, 248)

**Temporal bone numbers**: Only about one third of people have a pneumatized petrous apex. Tympanic facial nerve dehiscence is reported in 20-30%. Absent stapedius tendon/pyramidal eminence about 1%. IAC diameter upper limit about 8 mm. Cochlear aqueduct averages 6.2 mm, connecting the basal-turn scala tympani to the posterior fossa subarachnoid space. TM area is about 70-80 mm2 with an effective vibrating area of about 55 mm2. Stapes footplate about 1.4 x 3 mm. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 13, p 236-237, 248)

**Ossicular ligaments, joints and middle ear muscles**: The malleoincudal and incudostapedial joints are diarthrodial, while the stapediovestibular joint (annular ligament) is a syndesmosis. Tensor tympani runs from the cochleariform process to the medial manubrium (V3) and pulls the malleus medially. Stapedius from the pyramidal process usually inserts on the posterior stapes neck (VII). The anterior malleal ligament passes through the petrotympanic fissure. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 13, p 238-239)

**Ossicular and canal embryology**: Malleus head/neck and incus body/short process derive from Meckel (first arch) cartilage. The manubrium and long process of incus from Reichert (second arch) cartilage. The stapes superstructure from the second arch around the stapedial artery, while the footplate vestibular surface and annular ligament come from otic capsule mesenchyme. The canal forms from a solid ectodermal core that canalizes from about week 21 to 28, so a normal auricle with canal atresia indicates a late (about 28-week) insult after ossicles have formed, whereas microtia signals an early arch defect with likely middle ear and facial nerve anomalies. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 13, p 243-245, 248)

**Inner ear developmental timeline**: The otic placode appears in week 3 and becomes the otocyst by week 4. The endolymphatic duct/sac appears first and is the last to stop growing. Semicircular canals and utricle (pars superior) are formed by week 8, before the saccule and cochlea (pars inferior). The cochlea reaches 2.5 turns by about weeks 8-12 (sources differ) and the membranous labyrinth is complete by about week 15. The otic capsule ossifies from 14 centers between weeks 15 and 23, with the fissula ante fenestram the last area (and may stay cartilaginous, the classic otosclerosis site). Labyrinthine anomalies are rare because the structure is phylogenetically old. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 13, p 246-248)

**Speech audiometry cross-checks**: SRT (spondees repeated 50% of the time) should agree within 10 dB of the 500/1000/2000 Hz pure-tone average (use the best two-frequency average in steep configurations). Word recognition is tested about 25-35 dB SL above SRT to find the maximum score: 90-100% normal, 76-88% slight, 60-74% moderate, 40-58% poor, under 40% very poor difficulty. Conversational speech is about 50-60 dB HL, so presentation level matters when comparing scores. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 14, p 272-273)

**Tuning fork details**: Use a 512-Hz fork struck gently (lower forks are felt as vibration). Rinne turns negative only once the air-bone gap reaches roughly 20 dB or more. Bing: occluding the canal makes the tone louder (occlusion effect) in normal or SNHL ears but not with conductive loss. Schwabach compares the patient's bone conduction duration with the examiner's: prolonged in conductive loss, shortened in SNHL. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 14, p 263-264)

**Behavioral site-of-lesion tests**: Largely replaced by MRI and ABR but still tested: tone decay over 25 dB, rollover ratio of 0.30 or more on the performance-intensity function, and acoustic reflex decay (amplitude falls by half within 5 seconds at 10 dB above reflex threshold, usually at 1000 Hz) suggest retrocochlear disease. Historic: SISI score of 70% or more indicates cochlear and 30% or less neural lesion; ABLB recruitment indicates cochlear; Békésy type III/IV indicates neural and type V pseudohypacusis. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 14, p 280-281, 292)

**Normative values and reflex rules**: Adult norms: static admittance 0.3-1.7 mL, tympanometric width 50-114 daPa, ear canal volume 0.9-2.0 mL (children 3-10 y: 0.25-1.05 mL, 80-160 daPa, 0.3-0.9 mL). A broad width marks reduced mobility, and type C is peak pressure below -100 daPa (adults) or -150 daPa (children). Reflex thresholds are normally 70-100 dB HL (about 70 dB SL). A reflex is absent if there is any significant conductive loss in the probe ear or over about 65 dB HL loss in the stimulated ear. Ossicular discontinuity can give an Ad tracing with a high-frequency-predominant conductive loss. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 14, p 274-276)

**ABR technical variables**: Newborns show mainly waves I, III and V with prolonged latencies that mature by about 18 months; females have slightly shorter latencies. Temperature outside 36-38 °C alters latency; rates over 30/s prolong latencies (mostly wave V) and over 55/s degrade morphology; dropping from 80 to 20 dB shifts wave V latency about 2 ms; sedation does not affect ABR. I-III and III-V intervals are each about 2.2 ms; a prolonged I-III suggests eighth nerve/lower brainstem lesion, prolonged III-V a rostral lesion, and interaural wave V difference over about 0.5 ms (book's limit) suggests retrocochlear pathology once peripheral asymmetry is excluded. Correct for conductive loss by subtracting the air-bone gap. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 14, p 281-283)

**OAE facts**: Spontaneous OAEs occur in about 35-60% of normal ears, so their absence is nondiagnostic and they rarely explain tinnitus. TEOAEs imply cochlear thresholds no worse than about 30-40 dB HL; DPOAEs may persist with moderate loss and give frequency-specific information. Any middle-ear disorder usually abolishes OAEs; normal OAEs with absent/abnormal ABR suggests auditory neuropathy. OAE screening takes only about 5-10 minutes per ear without sedation. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 14, p 283-284, 288)

**Behavioral audiometry by developmental age**: Behavioral observation audiometry for developmental age up to about 6 months (unconditioned, gives minimal response levels above true threshold, unreliable). Visual reinforcement audiometry or conditioned orienting response from about 6 to 30 months (localizing to the correct side requires hearing symmetric within about 30 dB). Conditioned play audiometry from about 30 months, usually with insert earphones. Use a 1000-Hz probe tone for tympanometry under 6 months. A present reflex with a normal tympanogram excludes severe SNHL. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 14, p 285-288)

**Screening details and risk indicators**: About 50% of congenital hearing loss has no risk indicator, hence universal screening. Well babies may be screened with OAE or AABR, but NICU infants must be screened with ABR because of auditory neuropathy risk. JCIH risk indicators include caregiver concern, family history, NICU stay over 5 days, ECMO, ventilation, ototoxic drugs or loop diuretics, hyperbilirubinemia needing exchange transfusion, in utero TORCH/CMV infection, craniofacial anomalies, syndromic stigmata (white forelock), neurodegenerative disease, culture-positive meningitis, temporal bone fracture and chemotherapy. Children with delayed-onset risk factors need surveillance even after passing. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 14, p 289-290)

**Auditory processing disorder**: Suspected when speech understanding in quiet or noise is worse than the audiogram predicts (mishearing, poor attention, trouble in noise, poor auditory memory, reading/spelling problems). Rule out peripheral loss first (pure tones, word recognition, reflexes, ABR), then use monotic and dichotic degraded-speech batteries. Management improves signal-to-noise ratio (preferential seating, acoustics, FM/remote microphone systems) plus auditory training. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 14, p 293-294)

**Ototoxicity monitoring criteria**: Significant change (ASHA) is a shift of 20 dB or more at one frequency, 10 dB or more at two adjacent frequencies, or loss of response at three consecutive frequencies previously measured, confirmed within 24 hours after excluding middle ear change. Monitoring includes ultra-high-frequency (10-20 kHz) testing, which detects change before the speech frequencies are affected. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 14, p 293)

**Hearing aid circuitry and fitting terms**: Gain is output minus input; maximum output is OSPL90/SSPL. Peak clipping limits output but distorts; compression limiting reduces gain at high inputs with less distortion; wide dynamic range compression progressively lowers gain as input rises to substitute for lost outer hair cell compression. Venting and open-fit receiver-in-canal devices reduce occlusion and low-frequency gain (ideal for high-frequency loss with good lows) but raise feedback risk; directional microphones improve signal-to-noise; telecoils couple to phones and loops. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 14, p 296-297)

**Outer and middle ear acoustics**: The ear canal resonates around 2000-5500 Hz (peak about 2700 Hz); the middle ear transmits best at 500-3000 Hz. The impedance match comes from the area ratio of the vibrating TM (about 55 mm2) to footplate (about 3.2 mm2), roughly 17:1, times the ossicular lever (about 1.3:1), giving about 22:1 or roughly 25 dB, plus a small (about 4 dB) round-oval window phase effect. About 95% of afferent fibers innervate inner hair cells; the eighth nerve has about 25,000 fibers; the central pathway is remembered as E-COLI (eighth nerve, cochlear nucleus, olivary complex, lateral lemniscus, inferior colliculus) then medial geniculate and cortex. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 14, p 260-263)

**Decibel references**: dB SPL = 20 log (measured pressure/20 µPa); dB HL is referenced to average normal thresholds at each frequency (0 dB HL equals about 26.5 dB SPL at 250 Hz but 7.5 dB SPL at 1000 Hz), and dB SL is referenced to the individual's own threshold. Sustained exposure over about 90 dB SPL risks damage and over about 140 dB SPL causes pain. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 14, p 257-259)

**ECoG technique and SP/AP cutoffs**: ECoG records the cochlear microphonic (AC, outer hair cells; distinguishes auditory neuropathy when present with absent ABR), summating potential (DC, hair cells) and compound action potential (N1 equals ABR wave I). An abnormal SP/AP ratio depends on electrode: over 50% with canal TIPtrode, over 35% with tympanic membrane electrode, over 30% transtympanic (promontory needle, best amplitudes). It detects about 65-70% of Ménière ears with roughly 5% false positives; alternating polarity cancels the CM. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 15, p 303-304)

**ABR interpretation patterns**: Conductive loss delays all waves including wave I with normal interpeak intervals; cochlear (sensory) loss gives a small or absent wave I, poor morphology and normal or shortened I-V; neural (retrocochlear) loss gives a normal wave I with prolonged I-III/I-V and poor morphology. Abnormal criteria cited: interaural wave V difference of 0.4 ms or more and wave V rate-latency shift of 0.8 ms or more. Click ABR detects eighth nerve tumors with about 90% sensitivity but misses small tumors (stacked ABR improves this); threshold ABR estimates about 10-20 dB above behavioral thresholds, with clicks reflecting about 1-4 kHz and tone bursts giving frequency-specific data. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 15, p 305-307)

**ASSR and cortical potentials**: ASSR uses amplitude/frequency-modulated carrier tones (500-4000 Hz) with automated detection; it can estimate severe-profound thresholds beyond click/tone-burst ABR limits, but needs a still or sedated patient, may overestimate near-normal thresholds, and cannot separate profound loss from auditory neuropathy. Middle-latency responses (10-50 ms) assess thalamocortical pathways and are affected by sedation and state; P300 (oddball paradigm) and mismatch negativity are endogenous cognitive potentials used in research on central processing and aging. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 15, p 307-309)

**ENoG mechanics**: Supramaximal stimulation at the stylomastoid foramen with recording at the nasolabial fold; % response = involved/uninvolved amplitude x 100 and % degeneration = 100 minus that. It is valid from day 3 (after Wallerian degeneration) to about day 21, repeated every 3-5 days to plateau; it cannot distinguish axonotmesis from neurotmesis. A response of 10% or less of the normal side (90% or more degeneration) predicts over 50% chance of incomplete recovery; ENoG predicts spontaneous recovery with 80-100% accuracy. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 15, p 312-313)

**Closed treatment and condyles**: closed reduction with 4 to 6 weeks of MMF suits nondisplaced fractures within the dentition when teeth can hold an arch bar and the patient will comply. Watch for fragment shift or infection, which call for conversion to ORIF. When condylar fractures are treated closed with MMF, release it after 10 to 14 days and start physiotherapy early, or skip MMF in favor of immediate physiotherapy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 20, p 308)

**Atrophic edentulous mandible**: thin atrophic bone with atherosclerotic inferior alveolar supply contraindicates load-sharing repair. Use a long, strong load-bearing reconstruction plate with multiple bicortical screws on each side (locking designs help). In panfacial injuries, open reduction of subcondylar (especially bilateral) fractures restores ramus height, which guides overall facial height. (Cummings 7e, Ch 20, p 291, 309)

**CT vs panoramic radiograph**: with high-resolution 1-mm helical CT, sensitivity for mandible fractures was 100%, compared with 86% for panoramic tomography. Thick-slice (3 to 5 mm) CT missed fractures that panorex caught, so slice thickness matters. Coronal CT with 3D reconstruction best shows the proximal fragment position in subcondylar fractures. (Cummings 7e, Ch 20, p 294)

**Universal tooth numbering (US)**: there are 32 adult teeth, numbered 1 to 32. Tooth 1 is the right maxillary third molar. Numbering runs across the upper arch to tooth 16 (left maxillary third molar), then drops to 17 (left mandibular third molar) and runs back to 32 (right mandibular third molar). **Overjet** is horizontal overlap and **overbite** is vertical overlap of the maxillary incisors over the mandibular incisors. (Cummings 7e, Ch 20, p 291-292)

**Why small zygoma shifts matter**: the lateral orbital rim, formed largely by the zygoma, sits near the equator of the globe. The other rims sit in front of the globe. So small zygomatic displacements change the globe's front-to-back position, and enophthalmos is the most common globe malposition after inadequate ZMC/orbital repair. Multiple fixation points are needed to resist masseter pull, with focus on the usually mobile zygomaticomaxillary buttress. (Cummings 7e, Ch 20, p 287, 301, 309)

**Buttress gaps and condylar seating**: a buttress gap under 5 mm can be bridged by a plate. Larger gaps need bone graft, commonly split calvarium, which can serve as a biologic plate fixed with lag screws. Le Fort I and II fractures are typically fixed with 1.5- to 2-mm L/J plates with at least two screws on each side of every fracture. Make sure the condyles are seated during MMF. Otherwise the maxilla is fixed to a distracted mandible, and an anterior open bite appears when MMF is released. (Cummings 7e, Ch 20, p 303-304)

**Locating the tendon intraoperatively**: if the medial canthal tendon is hard to find, push a hemostat placed in the caruncle medially. From the deep side, the tendon lies at the resulting bulge (protect the cornea). A transnasally fixed tendon or central fragment that is not positioned and fixed correctly slowly lateralizes into late telecanthus, which may not be apparent early. (Cummings 7e, Ch 20, p 306, 309)

**Access details**: when a long pericranial flap may be needed, for frontal sinus obliteration or anterior fossa repair, keep the coronal incision superficial to the pericranium. Then incise the pericranium further back to create a long, anteriorly based flap. A supraorbital nerve running through a true foramen, rather than a notch, must be freed by osteotomizing the foramen's lower lip. A 6-foot Caldwell radiograph can serve as a template for an osteoplastic flap. Paired frontal sinuses are present in only about 85% of people, because one or both may be absent or hypoplastic. (Cummings 7e, Ch 20, p 287, 293, 296-297)

**Facial crumple zones**: the facial skeleton absorbs energy to protect vital organs. The medial orbital wall and floor blow out to spare the globe and optic nerve. The frontal sinus cushions the anterior cranial fossa. The condylar necks fracture to keep the condyle out of the middle cranial fossa. This is why blowout fractures far outnumber globe ruptures. (Cummings 7e, Ch 20, p 290-291)

**CT technique**: 3D reconstructions give a helpful overview but contain fill-in artifacts. Do not build them from scans thicker than 1.5 mm, and base decisions on the direct axial/coronal images. Progressive vision loss means rising intraorbital pressure or optic nerve injury and needs emergency management. Cheek and lateral nasal numbness (V2) may be the only clue to a zygoma fracture and should prompt CT. (Cummings 7e, Ch 20, p 292-293)

**Pedicle and thinning details**: the paramedian forehead flap pedicle can be as narrow as about 1.2 cm. A narrow pedicle gives more effective length and less standing cone. Free the corrugators bluntly near the brow to protect the supratrochlear vessels. Distal subcutaneous fat can be thinned to about 1 mm under the dermis. Divide the pedicle about 3 weeks later under local anesthesia, returning its base to restore the normal interbrow distance. (Cummings 7e, Ch 21, p 319-320)

**Geometry numbers**: a rhombic flap suits defects with roughly 60/120-degree angles. Draw it from the 120-degree corner toward adjacent laxity. In a bilobed flap, the first lobe can be up to about 20% smaller than the defect and the second about 20% smaller than the first. On the cheek, base it inferiorly and orient scars in natural lines. A random transposition flap is classically limited to 3:1 length:width, but rich facial vascularity often allows more. Scalp rotation flaps must be large relative to the defect because scalp is inelastic. (Cummings 7e, Ch 21, p 313, 325-326)

**Cheek and forehead repair**: an island subcutaneous-pedicle V-Y cheek advancement flap is designed with a surface area 1.5 to 2 times the defect. It can advance 2 to 3 cm, with 2 cm of undermining at the margins. Superiorly based melolabial transposition flaps recruit lower medial face laxity. For forehead defects, preserve brow symmetry and hairlines and prefer horizontal scars (except midline). Bilateral advancement (H-plasty) and O-T / A-T closures are standard. Large defects may need 6 to 12 weeks of tissue expansion before excision. (Cummings 7e, Ch 21, p 327-329)

**Hair cycle numbers**: the scalp has about 100,000 hairs. About 90% are in anagen (growth, about 3 to 4 years), about 1% in catagen (involution, about 2 weeks), and about 10% in telogen (rest, 3 to 4 months), followed by exogen (shedding). Normal shedding is 50 to 100 hairs per day. Density must fall by about 50% before thinning becomes visible. (Cummings 7e, Ch 22, p 331)

**Scarring alopecia is a transplant trap**: lichen planopilaris, frontal fibrosing alopecia, pseudopelade of Brocq, discoid lupus and folliculitis decalvans destroy the pilosebaceous unit. Look for itching, perifollicular erythema, scale, and later shiny skin without follicular openings. Biopsy any suspicious area. Transplant only after 2 to 5 years of documented inactivity, since grafts can be lost in later flares. (Cummings 7e, Ch 22, p 333)

**Hairline design**: a natural hairline is convex, with its lowest central point about 7 to 10 cm above the glabella. The apex of each frontotemporal triangle sits on a vertical line above the lateral canthus. Grafts exit at about 15 to 20 degrees at the hairline, 30 to 45 degrees in the midscalp, and flat (5 to 10 degrees, inferiorly directed) in the temples. Use single-hair units in the hairline zone and 2- to 4-hair units behind it. Placing the hairline too low (often at patient request) is a lasting error. (Cummings 7e, Ch 22, p 337, 342-343)

**Donor harvest**: candidates with fewer than about 50 follicular units/cm² in the donor area are poor candidates. Recipient density of 20 to 40 FU/cm² usually looks full. Strip harvest is up to 24 to 30 cm long, taken from the safe zone and staying above about 2 cm from the nape. A tension-free closure is required, and trichophytic closure lets hair grow through the scar. FUE uses 0.8- to 1-mm punches to avoid a linear scar, at the cost of transection risk. Older age is not a contraindication; young patients need conservative planning because their final pattern is unknown. (Cummings 7e, Ch 22, p 336-342)

**Postoperative timeline**: grafts are vulnerable to dislodgement in the first week. Transplanted hairs shed at 2 to 6 weeks, new growth starts at 3 to 4 months, and growth runs about 1/2 inch per month. Judge results and plan another session only after 12 months. Shock loss (surgical telogen effluvium of native hair) usually recovers by about 3 months. Cysts and ingrown hairs are the most common problems at 8 to 12 weeks, and infection occurs in under 1%. Donor dominance (Orentreich) means grafts keep their donor-site behavior. (Cummings 7e, Ch 22, p 337, 343-344)

**Flaps, reductions and expansion**: scalp reductions are rarely done now; the midline pattern can leave a 'slot' deformity, corrected with Frechet rotational flaps. Scalp expansion starts about 2 weeks after placement, filling 2 to 3 times a week with 20 to 50 mL until blanching or pain, over about 6 to 8 weeks. The temporoparietal-occipital (Juri-type) flap is based on the posterior branch of the superficial temporal artery. It is about 3 to 4 cm wide and 28 cm long, starts about 3 cm above the helical root, and suits isolated frontal baldness. (Cummings 7e, Ch 22, p 344-346)

**Peel contraindications**: These include confirmed malignancy (except very superficial BCC), unstable psychiatric status and true allergy. For phenol, add cardiac, hepatic or renal disease. In the book, isotretinoin taken within the prior 6 months contraindicates dermabrasion, because it reduces the pilosebaceous units needed for healing, and some wait a full year before any facial resurfacing. The 2017 ASDS consensus still advises against mechanical dermabrasion on or soon after isotretinoin but found no evidence to delay superficial peels. Telangiectasias and large pores do not improve and may look worse. Nevi can darken. Port-wine stains, hemangiomas and neurofibromas do not respond. (Cummings 7e, Ch 23, p 352-353, 360)

**Peel preparation**: give tretinoin nightly starting 4 to 6 weeks before medium/deep peels and stop it about 2 weeks before. Tretinoin thins the stratum corneum and deepens a peel, so avoid it right before a Baker phenol peel. Use 4% hydroquinone for Fitzpatrick III or higher before and after. Give antiviral prophylaxis to every medium/deep resurfacing patient (e.g., acyclovir 800 mg three times daily), starting before the procedure and continuing until reepithelialization. Use SPF 30 or more for 9 to 12 months. (Cummings 7e, Ch 23, p 353, 359)

**Expected sequelae vs complications**: pigment change, usually hypopigmentation, is the most common peel sequela and usually appears in the first 3 months. Treat early hyperpigmentation with tretinoin 0.1%, hydroquinone 4% and triamcinolone. Withhold estrogens 4 weeks before and 6 to 8 weeks after a peel. Wait at least 4 months to repeat a deep peel and 1 year to repeat a medium peel. Multiple superficial peels do not equal one medium or deep peel. A breakthrough herpetic outbreak is treated with high-dose acyclovir. (Cummings 7e, Ch 23, p 356, 358-359)

**Nonablative and maintenance options**: nonablative devices heat the dermis to about 65 to 75°C to denature collagen without wounding the epidermis. They need multiple sessions (every 4 to 12 weeks) but avoid hypopigmentation and scarring. Microdermabrasion causes only stratum corneum turnover. Tretinoin is the best-proven topical antiphotoaging agent. Laser resurfacing can also treat widespread actinic keratoses. (Cummings 7e, Ch 23, p 366-370)

**Septum and fat anatomy**: in white patients, the upper-lid septum fuses with the levator aponeurosis about 3 mm above the tarsus; it fuses lower in Asian lids, which gives a low or absent crease and fuller lid. The lower-lid septum joins the capsulopalpebral fascia about 5 mm below the tarsus. The upper lid has medial and central fat pads, with the lacrimal gland laterally (pink and firm, do not resect). The lower lid has medial, central and lateral pads. The inferior oblique separates the medial and central pads and must be protected. The levator runs about 36 mm to Whitnall's ligament. (Cummings 7e, Ch 26, p 406-407)

**Upper blepharoplasty marking**: marking is the most important step. Place the lower incision in the natural crease or 1 mm above it (about 8 to 10 mm from the margin). Stop medially at the punctum, and taper both ends at about 30 degrees. Leave about 20 mm of skin between the lid margin and the brow to avoid lagophthalmos. Remove only fat that prolapses with gentle globe pressure. A common error is leaving the medial fat pad. In ptosis repair, identify and advance the levator aponeurosis, not the septum or Müller muscle, to avoid contour irregularities. (Cummings 7e, Ch 26, p 411-412)

**Lower blepharoplasty approaches**: the transconjunctival approach (preseptal or postseptal) avoids an external scar and lowers malposition risk. Mild skin excess can be pinched out or resurfaced. The subciliary skin-muscle flap starts 2 mm below the lashes and runs from 1 mm lateral to the punctum to about 10 mm past the lateral canthus. Excise skin conservatively to avoid scleral show and ectropion. Avoid strong traction on fat, which communicates with deep orbital fat. (Cummings 7e, Ch 26, p 412-413)

**Ear growth and dimensions**: about 85% of auricular growth is done by age 3, and cartilage growth is nearly complete by age 5. The adult ear is 5.5 to 6.5 cm long, with width 50% to 60% of length. It is rotated about 15 to 30 degrees posteriorly, from brow level to subnasale. Normal helix-to-scalp distances are about 10 to 12 mm superiorly, 16 to 18 mm at the mid helix, and 20 to 22 mm at the lower helix. On frontal view, the helix should sit about 2 to 5 mm lateral to the antihelix. Ears beyond 40 to 45 degrees are abnormal. The conchomastoid and conchoscaphal angles are normally about 90 degrees. (Cummings 7e, Ch 28, p 433-434)

**Technique details**: Mustardé antihelical sutures are permanent horizontal mattress sutures. Each takes a 4- to 6-mm bite through cartilage and anterior perichondrium, usually 1 to 3 sutures. Furnas sutures anchor the concha to mastoid periosteum. Place conchomastoid sutures before the Mustardé sutures, and rotate the bowl so it does not narrow the external canal. Partial-thickness scoring bends cartilage away from the scored side (Stenström principle). Incisionless percutaneous suture otoplasty is an option. Treat the lobule with a cauda helicis cut or skin excision. (Cummings 7e, Ch 28, p 434-435)

**Airflow numbers**: at rest, flow speeds up to about 16 m/s through the nasal valve, then slows about fourfold in the nasal cavity, which creates the mixing needed to condition air. About 50% of inspired air travels along the nasal floor, so floor and crest deviations matter. Decongestion cuts normal nasal resistance by about a third, and wide alar retraction by about two-thirds. The nose senses turbulent flow as low flow, which feels like stuffiness. (Cummings 7e, Ch 29, p 444)

**Septoplasty technique specifics**: the Killian incision is about 1 to 2 cm behind the caudal margin. A hemitransfixion incision can convert to a full transfixion. Preserve at least a 1-cm dorsal and 1-cm caudal L-strut, including the nasal spine. Before removing bony septum, make a superior cut so twisting the perpendicular plate does not fracture the cribriform plate. Reset cartilage displaced off the maxillary crest into the groove and suture it to the spine periosteum. A one-sided crest spur can be shaved with a 2-mm osteotome. Use crushed cartilage as an interposition barrier, close even unilateral flap tears, and quilt with 5-0 plain to prevent hematoma. (Cummings 7e, Ch 29, p 447-450)

**Caudal and high-septal deviations**: in the tongue-in-groove maneuver (Rethi/Kridel), the caudal septum is set between the medial crura and fixed with a transcutaneous columellar-septal suture. This fixes the caudal septum in the midline and avoids aggressive caudal trimming, but it can change tip projection and rotation.
