Correct high dorsal bowing with spreader grafts or a Boccieri crossbar graft on the concave side, scoring, or shaving. Release the upper lateral cartilages from the septum when straightening a crooked dorsum. Trim the caudal septum only when it is too crooked to straighten or so long it pushes the columella down. (Cummings 7e, Ch 29, p 450-451, 454)

**Turbinates and postoperative care**: medical therapy is first-line for mucosal turbinate hypertrophy from rhinitis. Never perform total turbinectomy, because it predisposes to empty nose syndrome with drying and crusting. Prefer conservative submucosal or partial resection (e.g., a modified Mabry approach). After septoplasty, suction gently on days 5 to 10, allow gentle nose blowing after week 3, and avoid strenuous exercise for 6 weeks. Soft Silastic splints are optional. Many insurers require 6 weeks of failed nasal steroid therapy before approving septoplasty. (Cummings 7e, Ch 29, p 445, 455-456)

**Exam pearls**: watch the sidewalls during quiet and forced breathing. Habitual 'sniffers' collapse their sidewalls regardless of valve competence. The Cottle maneuver has many false positives. Lifting the upper lateral cartilage with a cotton applicator or curette is more specific for internal valve narrowing. Tip ptosis can itself obstruct airflow. A previously fractured bony pyramid can hold the dorsal septum off midline, and septoplasty alone will not fix that. On acoustic rhinometry, the first notch is the valve and the second is the anterior inferior/middle turbinates. (Cummings 7e, Ch 29, p 441, 445)

**Septal C-fracture**: cadaver studies show frontal and lateral blows both cause a consistent C-shaped fracture through the cartilaginous septum and perpendicular plate (Murray). An unreduced septal fracture is the most common reason closed reduction fails in the first week to 10 days. After 2 weeks, fibrous tissue and early bony remodeling are the cause of failure. Incomplete cartilage fractures release interlocked stresses that keep deforming the nose. (Cummings 7e, Ch 30, p 459, 465)

**Imaging and exam evidence**: plain nasal films had a 66% false-positive rate (suture lines, vascular grooves). Only about 15% of nasal fractures heal by ossification, so films cannot date injuries, and they miss cartilage. In a series of 100 patients, films never changed management. Brown-Gruss maneuvers press the upper, middle and lower vaults to expose infrastructure instability. Lower-vault compression showing tip hyperrotation suggests caudal septal or tip-support disruption. Photograph in the Frankfort horizontal. Recheck smell after swelling resolves, since post-traumatic anosmia occurs in up to about 5% of head injuries. (Cummings 7e, Ch 30, p 460-461)

**Domestic violence screen**: about 30% to 60% of women with facial trauma from assault are victims of domestic violence, so a nasal or facial fracture from assault should prompt screening. Loss of nasal length with a raised nasolabial angle suggests telescoping. Nostril collapse suggests the lower lateral cartilage has separated from the upper lateral cartilage. (Cummings 7e, Ch 30, p 460-461)

**Outcome data for closed reduction**: across 13 studies, 79% of patients were satisfied with their appearance, while surgeons rated only 37% of reductions successful. Prospective series report 85% to 91% patient satisfaction, with only 3% to 9% later seeking septorhinoplasty. Residual deformity on examiner scoring was 30% to 40%. Open reduction has not been shown to give better long-term results for most fractures, so use the least invasive adequate treatment and correct residual deformity by delayed rhinoplasty at 6 months or more. (Cummings 7e, Ch 30, p 462, 466)

**Traumatic leak with nasal/NOE injury**: confirm with beta-2 transferrin and localize with high-resolution CT. Most traumatic leaks close with bed rest, head elevation and, if needed, lumbar drainage. Repair leaks that persist beyond about 1 week of conservative care to prevent meningitis. (Cummings 7e, Ch 30, p 468)

**Tip recoil test and approach selection**: pressing the tip toward the lip tests how well the tip support springs back. Weak tips with thin skin and thin sidewalls need support preserved or added. Nondelivery approaches (cartilage-splitting or retrograde eversion) suit minimal refinement. Delivery approaches (bipedicle chondrocutaneous flaps) suit moderate bulbosity, with refinement using transdomal and interdomal sutures. The open approach suits revision cases, asymmetric or twisted noses, cleft-lip noses and markedly over- or underprojected tips. (Cummings 7e, Ch 31, p 471, 486)

**Profile targets and timeline**: aim for the tip-defining point about 1 to 2 mm above the cartilaginous dorsum, which creates a supratip break. A gentle 2 to 3 mm slope is acceptable. In women, a slightly more open nasolabial angle and a subtle columellar double break are desirable. Shape columellar struts with a gentle curve and stop them short of the tip skin to avoid a tent-pole look. The final result takes about 12 to 18 months to settle. Remove the external splint at 5 to 7 days. (Cummings 7e, Ch 31, p 500-502, 509)

**Open approach and dorsum steps**: a stair-step or inverted-V transcolumellar incision joins bilateral marginal incisions along the caudal edge of the lower lateral cartilages. Elevate directly on the perichondrium to preserve the venous and lymphatic drainage of the tip. Close the columella with 6-0 nonabsorbable sutures and the marginal incisions with 4-0 chromic. Lower the cartilaginous dorsum in 1- to 3-mm increments before the bony hump. Smooth bony irregularities with a rasp and suction away the debris. Limit lateral periosteal elevation so the bones stay stable after osteotomy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 31, p 497, 502-506)

**Costal cartilage handling**: harvest straight segments from the 6th to 8th ribs (inframammary incision in women). Carve concentrically from the central core, or use oblique symmetric cuts, to limit warping, the main complication. Soak in saline for about 30 minutes to reveal warping before placement. The ideal age for rib grafting is about 30 to 50 years. Younger cartilage is softer but warps more, and older cartilage may be calcified. Save perichondrium for camouflage. Irradiated homologous rib is an alternative. A warped rib graft usually needs replacement or recarving rather than observation. (Cummings 7e, Ch 33, p 534, 542) (Cummings 7e, Ch 34, p 546)

**Twisted nose principles**: straighten the septum, including the caudal septum fixed to the spine through sutures or a burr hole. Make complete osteotomies (including intermediate cuts and cuts up to the radix when needed). Use long, wide spreader grafts for cartilaginous dorsal deviation, and remove the hump asymmetrically, taking more from the longer side. Score along the existing angles, and use transseptal coaptation sutures. A hanging or retracted columella is corrected by addressing the caudal septum (trim, set back, or extension graft or plumping graft). The ideal columellar show on lateral view is 2 to 4 mm. (Cummings 7e, Ch 32, p 511-514, 517); (Cummings 7e, Ch 34, p 552)

**Unified airway numbers**: most asthmatics have allergic rhinitis, but only about 10% to 40% of allergic rhinitis patients have asthma. Allergic rhinitis is a risk factor for developing asthma. Treating it helps both conditions, and allergen immunotherapy lowers later asthma development. Other associations include atopic dermatitis, eustachian tube dysfunction/otitis media, eosinophilic esophagitis, laryngeal disease and OSA. The hygiene (biodiversity) hypothesis links falling infections and microbiome changes to rising allergy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 35, p 567, 584)

**Drug-specific facts**: first-generation antihistamines sedate about 20% of patients. H1 antihistamines are inverse agonists, not true antagonists. Intranasal azelastine mainly causes bitter taste. Ipratropium controls watery rhinorrhea but not sneezing or congestion. Cromolyn 4% is very safe in children but needs dosing 4 to 6 times a day. Montelukast is approved for seasonal and perennial allergic rhinitis, but since 2020 it has carried an FDA boxed warning for neuropsychiatric events, so it is reserved for patients with inadequate response to or intolerance of other therapies. Oral phenylephrine performed no better than placebo in a meta-analysis. Phenylpropanolamine was withdrawn for hemorrhagic stroke risk. Limit topical decongestants to short courses. (Cummings 7e, Ch 35, p 579-580)

**Intranasal steroid details**: for known seasonal disease, start about a week before the pollen season and recheck at 2 weeks. Epistaxis (blood-flecked mucus) occurs in about 4% to 8%, and septal perforation is rare. Biopsies after 1 year of continuous fluticasone or mometasone show no mucosal atrophy. Avoid intramuscular depot steroids for seasonal allergic rhinitis because they lower resistance to infection for 4 to 6 weeks after injection. Omalizumab (anti-IgE) reduces symptoms but is FDA-indicated for asthma, not rhinitis alone. (Cummings 7e, Ch 35, p 580-581)

**Intradermal and MQT criteria in Cummings**: skin-prick lancets penetrate about 1 mm and are read at 15 to 20 minutes. A single intradermal test is read at 10 minutes and is positive with a wheal of 7 mm or more that is at least 2 mm wider than the negative control. Modified quantitative testing (MQT) combines a prick test with one or two intradermal dilutions to find an endpoint, confirmed when the next stronger concentration produces a wheal at least 2 mm larger. MQT is faster and cheaper than full dilutional testing. (Cummings 7e, Ch 35, p 577)

**Newer diagnostics**: component-resolved diagnosis measures IgE to individual allergen molecules. For example, Can f 5 is a prostatic protein made only by male dogs, and up to 38% of dog-allergic patients react only to it, so they may tolerate female dogs. The basophil activation test detects CD63/CD203c by flow cytometry and can help diagnose local allergic rhinitis. Nasal provocation testing helps when systemic tests are negative but suspicion is high. Nasal cytology separates allergic rhinitis (eosinophils, mast cells, basophils) from NARES and other rhinitides. Total IgE mainly flags atopy when markedly elevated. (Cummings 7e, Ch 35, p 578-579)

**SCIT logistics**: build-up uses weekly escalating injections over weeks to months, then maintenance injections less often. Accelerated (cluster or rush) schedules give several injections per visit about 30 minutes apart. Most systemic reactions occur within 30 minutes, so patients are observed for 30 minutes in a supervised facility. Therapy usually lasts 3 to 5 years. SLIT tablets for grass and ragweed matched intranasal steroids in pooled analyses and beat montelukast and antihistamines. Grass tablets are started about 16 weeks before the season. SLIT side effects are mainly oral itching and swelling, and epinephrine use is rare. Intralymphatic immunotherapy (ultrasound-guided inguinal node injection) is investigational. (Cummings 7e, Ch 35, p 582-583)

**Mechanism sequence**: AIT first desensitizes FcεRI-bearing mast cells and basophils (possibly via histamine-2 receptor upregulation). It then induces peripheral T-cell tolerance through IL-10- and TGF-beta-secreting regulatory T cells (Tr1, FoxP3+CD25+), shifting the immunoglobulin profile toward IgG4. Healthy people have mostly IL-10-producing Tr1 cells for common allergens, while allergic people have more IL-4-producing Th2 cells. (Cummings 7e, Ch 35, p 581)

**Control instruments**: the Rhinitis Control Assessment Test (RCAT) has 6 items scored 1 to 5 (total 6 to 30, higher means better control). A score of 21 or less identifies poorly controlled rhinitis. The ARIA/MASK app uses visual analog scales from 0 to 100. (Cummings 7e, Ch 35, p 584)

**Peripheral olfactory physiology**: the olfactory epithelium covers about 2 to 5 cm², and less than 15% of inspired air reaches it during quiet breathing, so sniffing matters. Odorants dissolve in an about 50-µm mucus layer from Bowman glands. Odorant binding activates G-olf, adenylyl cyclase and cAMP, which open cyclic nucleotide-gated cation channels (Ca²⁺/Na⁺ influx). Calcium-gated chloride efflux then amplifies depolarization. Calcium feedback causes adaptation, which is the basis for trials of intranasal calcium buffers. Receptor neuron axons synapse on mitral and tufted cells in bulb glomeruli. (Cummings 7e, Ch 36, p 587-588)

**Etiology breakdown**: about 200 causes exist. Excluding age, about two-thirds of specialist-clinic cases are sinonasal, postinfectious or posttraumatic. Postinfectious loss accounts for about 18% to 45% of series and drug/toxin causes for 4% to 6%. Idiopathic loss (0% to 32%) is likely overdiagnosed. Parosmia and phantosmia occur in about 5% to 10% of patients with olfactory loss and usually accompany quantitative loss. Phantosmia may be a deafferentation phenomenon and suggests worse prognosis, while parosmia can occur during recovery. (Cummings 7e, Ch 36, p 591-592, 594, 596)

**Prognosis by cause**: in one prospective cohort, postinfectious loss improved meaningfully in about 46% of anosmic and 35% of hyposmic patients. Younger age, female sex, nonsmoking and parosmia predict better recovery. Post-traumatic loss follows 5% to 10% of adult head injuries and is often complete anosmia that does not fluctuate. It may be worse after occipital blows (coup-contrecoup) and is usually immediate but can be delayed. Some recovery occurs in only about 30%. Mechanisms are obstruction, shearing of olfactory fila at the cribriform plate, and contusion of the bulb or frontal lobe. MRI lesion patterns predict severity. (Cummings 7e, Ch 36, p 592-593)

**Psychophysical testing specifics**: UPSIT is a self-administered, 40-item microencapsulated forced-choice identification test. Sniffin' Sticks measure threshold, discrimination and identification (TDI). The composite TDI score is more sensitive than any single subtest, and threshold is thought to reflect peripheral function more. Hyposmia is defined below the 10th percentile of healthy young normative scores, and functional anosmia by a separate empirical cutoff. Tests must be validated for culture and age and can be used from about age 5. Grade the olfactory cleft with Lund-Kennedy. MRI uses coronal T2 through the bulbs plus axial whole-brain images. Electro-olfactography and chemosensory EEG are research tools. (Cummings 7e, Ch 36, p 597-599)

**Treatment evidence**: olfactory training uses four odors (flowery, fruity, spicy, resinous, classically rose, lemon, clove, eucalyptus) twice daily for months. A meta-analysis of 13 studies showed gains in threshold, discrimination and identification for postinfectious, post-traumatic and idiopathic loss. Consensus guidance (PPOD) does not recommend systemic corticosteroids for non-CRS smell loss. Intranasal calcium buffers (e.g., sodium citrate) and topical vitamin A with training have limited supportive data. For intractable phantosmia, options escalate from saline drops and topical cocaine to excision of olfactory epithelium or bulbectomy as a high-risk last resort at major centers. (Cummings 7e, Ch 36, p 599-602)

**Peak nasal inspiratory flow (PNIF)**: a facemask Wright-type meter measures maximal forced nasal inspiration from residual volume. Take the best of 2 to 3 tries after practice. Typical adult norms are about 143 L/min (men) and 122 L/min (women), and about 80 L/min in children 6 and older. PNIF falls with age and rises with height and male sex. It is cheap, portable and reproducible, but effort- and lung-dependent (check peak expiratory flow), and alar collapse can lower it falsely. (Cummings 7e, Ch 37, p 607-608)

**Rhinomanometry standards**: anterior active rhinomanometry (one nostril taped with a pressure tube while the other breathes) is the most common method. Nasal airway resistance is pressure divided by flow, reported in Pa/cm³/s (0.1 Pa/cm³/s = 1 cm H₂O/L/s). The international standard reports flow or resistance at 150 Pa or at radius 2. Normal unilateral resistance is about 0.24 to 0.26 Pa/cm³/s. On the pressure-flow plot, obstructed airways lie closer to the pressure axis, and distal flattening suggests valve collapse. Four-phase rhinomanometry (Vogt) reports vertex and effective resistance without needing a target pressure. (Cummings 7e, Ch 37, p 609-610)

**Acoustic rhinometry**: reflected sound measures cross-sectional area along about the first 6 cm. The first notch is the nasal valve and the second the inferior turbinate head. One of these is the minimal cross-sectional area (MCA, about 0.5 to 0.6 cm² in adults, about 0.3 cm² at age 3 to 6). It needs only breath-holding, so it suits children, and it correlates with CT. It is unreliable past a severe narrowing, and nosepiece seal, swallowing and palate motion add error. (Cummings 7e, Ch 37, p 612)

**Physiologic modifiers of nasal resistance**: the dependent nostril congests when recumbent. Exercise decongests the nose like oxymetazoline: resistance falls within 30 seconds, is lowest at about 5 minutes, and stays down for up to 30 minutes, through sympathetic vasoconstriction, alar muscle activity and hyperventilation. Menthol, camphor and eucalyptol make the nose feel more open without lowering resistance. (Cummings 7e, Ch 37, p 606-607)

**CT patterns and secretions**: in 500 screening CTs, Babbel found an infundibular pattern in 26% (maxillary only), an ostiomeatal-unit pattern in 25% (maxillary, frontal and anterior ethmoid), a sphenoethmoidal recess pattern in 6%, and a polyposis pattern in 10%. Acute secretions measure about 10 to 25 HU on CT and chronic inspissated secretions about 30 to 60 HU. On MRI, T2 signal falls as protein concentration rises; secretions above about 30% protein can appear as signal voids that mimic air. Fungal ball and allergic fungal mucin are T2-dark. Up to a third of asymptomatic people show mucosal thickening on CT, and symptom severity does not track CT extent. (Cummings 7e, Ch 38, p 625-627)

**Awake injection details**: avoid a superior laryngeal nerve block, which paralyzes the cricothyroid and distorts voice feedback; target anterolateral to the vocal process at the level of the inferior medial edge of the fold (about 0.5–1.0 mL of micronized dermis); slightly overinject resorbable materials such as fat or micronized dermis because resorption is expected. Avoid fat or PTFE when recovery is likely. (Cummings 7e, Ch 62, p 909)

**Mucosal leak check**: before seating the implant, fill the wound with saline while the patient phonates. Bubbling means the endolaryngeal mucosa has been breached and the implant should not be placed (extrusion/infection risk). Early postoperative intubation can displace the implant or erode the mucosa. (Cummings 7e, Ch 62, pp 914–915)

**Disposition**: isolated thyroplasty can usually be done as an outpatient. Overnight observation is advised for bilateral procedures, obstructive sleep apnea, anticoagulation requiring bridging, other high-risk comorbidity, and thyroplasty combined with arytenoid adduction (higher airway-edema risk). Airway compromise is the most serious complication. (Cummings 7e, Ch 62, pp 910, 914)

**Stroboscopy caveat**: the mucosal wave is a passive phenomenon driven by fold tension and subglottic pressure, so an absent or asymmetric wave does not prove denervation. LEMG is the only test of motor-unit integrity. Immobility with normal voluntary EMG suggests synkinesis, cricoarytenoid ankylosis or a scar web, separated by palpating the vocal process at direct laryngoscopy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 62, p 907)

**Joint biomechanics**: the cricoarytenoid joint is a shallow multiaxial ball-and-socket joint; the adduction (LCA) axis is nearly vertical and helical, so medial movement of the vocal process also moves it caudally, whereas the abduction (PCA) axis is nearly horizontal (about 60 degrees different), moving the vocal process laterally and upward. A paralyzed fold that looks 'short' on endoscopy is usually an optical illusion from a vocal process tilted out of the glottic plane (level mismatch). (Cummings 7e, Ch 63, pp 917–918)

**Key steps**: horizontal incision at the lower thyroid border; dissect lateral to the strap muscles and rotate the larynx with a hook on the superior cornu; divide the inferior constrictor along the posterior thyroid ala; reflect the piriform mucosa (having the awake patient say 'puppy' distends it) to expose the PCA, whose fibers converge on the white muscular process. Pass a permanent suture through cartilage (not muscle), tunnel it through the paraglottic space and tie over the inferior strut of a thyroplasty window. Local anesthesia allows voice and endoscopic monitoring; avoid disrupting the cricothyroid joint. (Cummings 7e, Ch 63, pp 919–920)

**Adjuncts**: with an atrophic, concave thyroarytenoid a gap remains anterior to the vocal process, so add a rigid thyroplasty implant (preferred over Gore-Tex ribbon because the dissected paraglottic space is large). A forward-sagging arytenoid is corrected with a posterior suspension (abduction) suture or adduction arytenoidopexy. After vagal injury (e.g., skull base surgery) add cricopharyngeal myotomy, because the bilaterally innervated cricopharyngeus keeps its tone while the ipsilateral constrictors are weak. Results are poorer in long-standing paralysis and central causes. Observe overnight; paraglottic bleeding is the main cause of airway obstruction, so use a drain and control cough and blood pressure. (Cummings 7e, Ch 63, pp 918–920)

**Why trunk repair gives synkinesis**: adductor and abductor motor fibers are intermixed in the RLN trunk until they branch inside the larynx (first branches to the PCA, then interarytenoid, then LCA and TA), so suture of a divided RLN or a trunk-level transfer restores tone and bulk without coordinated motion. The interarytenoid is innervated bilaterally. The PCA fires with inspiration slightly before the diaphragm, which is why the phrenic nerve is the best abductor donor; the thyrohyoid branch (C1) is an adductor donor. Reinnervated muscle takes on the fiber-type behavior of the donor nerve. (Cummings 7e, Ch 64, pp 923–925)

**Selective reinnervation options**: the neuromuscular pedicle (ansa branch to the omohyoid with a 2–3 mm muscle block sutured to the PCA, with a tracheotomy) gave airway improvement in a large majority in Tucker's series (about 74% long-term decannulation), but only about half of patients qualify; cricoarytenoid fixation (about one-third) is the most common contraindication and CNS causes do poorly (40–50%). Phrenic nerve-to-PCA transfer (with a graft to the contralateral PCA and C1 to adductors) can restore inspiratory abduction. Trunk-level reinnervation is not used for bilateral paralysis because it cannot produce coordinated motion. (Cummings 7e, Ch 64, pp 925–927)

**Menu of other procedures**: narrow-field laryngectomy (preserves hyoid, straps and pharyngeal mucosa; definitive, can be done under local); subperichondrial cricoidectomy (removes the cricoid except the posterior lamina and closes the subglottis as a pouch; simple, irreversible); epiglottic flap closure (reversible, keeps swallowing, but controls aspiration in only about half because of dehiscence); Biller vertical laryngoplasty (tubes the supraglottis, used after total glossectomy, posterior dehiscence common); Montgomery glottic closure via thyrotomy (very effective but essentially irreversible); endolaryngeal stents (short-term only). (Cummings 7e, Ch 65, pp 934–936)

**Conservative limits**: nasogastric tubes reduce but do not prevent aspiration and may blunt laryngeal reflexes; gastrostomy alone does not reduce aspiration in neurologically impaired patients; a cuffed tracheotomy tube (even low-pressure) does not prevent aspiration. Medialization thyroplasty ± arytenoid adduction improved swallowing in about 94% of high vagal lesions and allowed decannulation in 79%. In neurologically impaired children with sialorrhea, four-duct ligation or ultrasound-guided botulinum toxin injection of the salivary glands reduces aspiration pneumonitis. Cerebrovascular accident (especially brainstem) is the most common adult cause of intractable aspiration. (Cummings 7e, Ch 65, pp 931–933)

**Numbers**: external laryngeal trauma is rare (about 1 in 137,000 adults); hoarseness is the most common presenting feature (about 85%), then dysphagia, pain, dyspnea and hemoptysis. Concomitant cervical spine fracture occurs in roughly 10–13%, so any but the most trivial laryngeal injury counts as a distracting injury requiring CT clearance of the spine (plain films insufficient). About 40% can be managed without surgery, and roughly a quarter have long-term morbidity. (Cummings 7e, Ch 66, pp 939–941)

**Repair details**: mucosal tears closed with 5-0/6-0 absorbable suture; posterior commissure defects resurfaced with piriform, supraglottic or postcricoid advancement flaps to prevent stenosis; the anterior vocal fold ends are resuspended to the thyroid cartilage/outer perichondrium at the correct height; thyroid fractures plated (the cricoid arch never fully calcifies and is sutured). Stents (soft Silastic, fixed with a transcartilage suture) mainly for comminution or bilateral fold epithelial loss, removed at 10–14 days. After cricotracheal separation repair, keep the neck flexed for about 7 days; RLN exploration is rarely needed because at least one fold usually recovers. Voice rest 48–72 hours, NG tube until swallowing is safe, antireflux therapy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 66, pp 944–946)

**Laryngeal involvement and airway**: the larynx is involved in about 40% of caustic ingestions; alkali causes deep liquefaction necrosis that worsens over time, acid causes coagulation necrosis. Admit for at least 24 hours of airway observation; facial burns, oral soot and laryngeal edema predict need for airway intervention. Translaryngeal intubation after caustic laryngeal injury was associated with later tracheotomy for stenosis in every case in one series, so tracheotomy is preferred when an airway is needed. Endoscopy should be done within 24 hours, before edema and ulceration make instrumentation riskier. Inhalation burns affect about 30% of burn patients and increase mortality sixfold. (Cummings 7e, Ch 66, pp 948–949)

**Traumatic cervical esophageal injury**: present in about 14% of laryngotracheal trauma and about 6.5% of penetrating neck trauma. If recognized early, nonoperative care (nothing by mouth, broad-spectrum antibiotics, nutrition) for about 8–10 days, then a water-soluble contrast swallow, is the cornerstone; delayed presentation with sepsis needs exploration and drainage. Survival is 90–100%. (Cummings 7e, Ch 66, p 949)

**Endoscopic vs open selection**: endoscopic treatment suits Myer-Cotton I–II, short-segment lesions with an intact cricotracheal framework. It fares poorly with vertical scar over 1 cm, circumferential cicatricial scar, tracheomalacia or cartilage loss, prior severe tracheostomy infection, or posterior inlet scar with arytenoid fixation. Tracheal/cricotracheal resection gives excellent decannulation but is less successful for stenosis longer than about six rings, where augmentation laryngotracheoplasty is preferred. Idiopathic stenosis needs fewer reoperations (about 25%) than intubation/trauma cases (35–54%). Stage circumferential endoscopic resections 2–4 weeks apart to avoid a circumferential raw surface. Mitomycin C evidence is mixed. Stabilize autoimmune disease (e.g., GPA) before repair. (Cummings 7e, Ch 67, pp 955–957, 961)

**Stents**: mucosal capillary flow stops at about 20–40 mm Hg where mucosa lies on cartilage, so stents trade support for ischemic ulceration, infection and granulation. Duration: 1–3 weeks for mucosal healing/graft take, 6–8 weeks to splint an adequate framework, months (up to 14) when the framework is deficient and mature scar must form. Montgomery T-tube (hollow, allows phonation, single lumen so obstruction risk), Aboulker stent (fixed to a metal tracheostomy tube), and soft finger-cot stents are the classic options. Solid stents lower aspiration risk. (Cummings 7e, Ch 67, pp 957–958)

**Procedures**: type I (interarytenoid band) usually responds to CO2 laser division plus steroid injection. Joint fixation historically needed arytenoidectomy — Woodman external approach (removes all but the vocal process, which is sutured laterally about 5 mm in women and 6 mm in men) or Ossoff endoscopic laser arytenoidectomy (removes all but the muscular process, risk of perichondritis). Alternatives: lysis of cricoarytenoid adhesions with abduction stenting (mobility returned in about 90% in one report), endoscopic posterior cricoid split with rib graft (90–100% decannulation in children with grades III–IV). A temporarily plugged tracheostomy helps reveal true abduction during evaluation. (Cummings 7e, Ch 67, pp 958–959)

**History sorts the lesion**: solid-only dysphagia suggests a structural lesion — intermittent (ring) vs progressive (peptic stricture, cancer); solid plus liquid dysphagia suggests a motility disorder — intermittent (spasm) vs progressive (achalasia, scleroderma). Up to 30% of distal obstructions are perceived in the neck. Globus is unrelated to (and may improve with) swallowing. Odynophagia points to inflammation (erosive, pill, infectious esophagitis); water brash is reflex salivary hypersecretion, not regurgitation. (Cummings 7e, Ch 68, pp 965–966)

**Endoscopy landmarks and indications**: the Z line (squamocolumnar junction) normally sits at the GEJ (top of gastric folds); in Barrett esophagus the Z line is proximal to the GEJ, and in hiatal hernia the GEJ is proximal to the diaphragmatic pinch. Indications: weight loss, GI bleeding, dysphagia, odynophagia, chest pain, failed empiric therapy, Barrett screening. Manometry: normal LES pressure about 10–45 mm Hg, distal peristaltic amplitude 30–180 mm Hg; high-resolution manometry uses 36 sensors at 1-cm spacing. UES manometry is unreliable (asymmetric pressures), so UES disorders are better defined radiographically. (Cummings 7e, Ch 68, pp 967–969)

**Strictures**: normal esophagus is about 20 mm; dysphagia usually appears below about 15 mm. Peptic strictures cause 60–70% of intrinsic strictures. Treat by dilation (bougie or wire-guided Savary-Gilliard for complex strictures) plus PPI; refractory = failure of two or more dilations (look for ongoing pill/NSAID injury, uncontrolled acid, inadequate diameter) and may benefit from intralesional steroid before dilation. Eosinophilic esophagitis: rings ('feline' esophagus), furrows, white plaques, more than 15 eosinophils/hpf on proximal and distal biopsies; treat with elimination diet, swallowed topical steroid, and careful dilation (deep mucosal tears are common). (Cummings 7e, Ch 68, pp 976–978)

**Esophageal cancer for the head and neck surgeon**: more than half of US cases are now adenocarcinoma (distal/GEJ; white men, GERD, Barrett, obesity), whereas squamous cell carcinoma (tobacco, alcohol, prior head and neck SCC, HPV association) favors the midesophagus. Presentation is rapidly progressive solid dysphagia and weight loss; hoarseness signals RLN invasion. Rich submucosal lymphatics mean most present at an advanced stage. Scleroderma: GI involvement in about 90%, with smooth-muscle fibrosis causing distal aperistalsis and a weak, patulous LES (opposite of achalasia), severe reflux, strictures and Barrett. (Cummings 7e, Ch 68, pp 982–983, 987)

**Indications (ABEA 2007)**: esophageal — dysphagia, symptoms persisting on antireflux therapy, Barrett screening, evaluation/biopsy of radiographic abnormalities, GERD of 5 or more years. Extraesophageal — chronic cough, head and neck cancer panendoscopy/biopsy, moderate–severe LPR, globus. Plus procedures. Other uses: screening head and neck cancer patients (esophagitis about 63%, stricture about 23%, only 13% normal in one series, screened second esophageal primaries found earlier), caustic ingestion follow-up, varices, prebariatric evaluation, flap monitoring. TNE vs sedated EGD: sensitivity about 89%, specificity 97%. IV sedation causes over half of conventional EGD adverse events. (Cummings 7e, Ch 69, pp 993–995)

**Distances from the nasal ala**: esophageal inlet about 18 cm. Aortic arch compression about 24–26 cm (pulsatile, anterolateral). Left mainstem bronchus about 29–30 cm (anterior). Diaphragmatic pinch about 41–43 cm. GEJ about 40 cm. Esophageal body about 18–22 cm long. Gastric rugae extending more than 2 cm above the diaphragmatic impression indicate hiatal hernia. Retroflexion (rotate 180 degrees, deflect tip 210 degrees) shows sliding vs paraesophageal hernia. Normal esophageal transit is under 13 seconds. Scopes are 3.1–5.3 mm (conventional 10–12 mm). (Cummings 7e, Ch 69, pp 993, 995–996)

**Technique and safety**: decongest/anesthetize the wider side (oxymetazoline with 4% lidocaine or 2% tetracaine). Avoid over-anesthetizing the hypopharynx, which causes aspiration and coughing. NPO 3 hours before and 60–90 minutes after. Sit upright, flexed forward, neck extended for nasal passage, then flex the neck and have the patient swallow at the postcricoid level. Resistance at the UES suggests a Zenker diverticulum or hypertonic cricopharyngeus — insufflate and rotate rather than push. Success is 83–99% (failure mainly a tight nose). Epistaxis 0.85–2%. Perforation is extraordinarily rare. Through the channel: biopsy, guidewire for balloon dilation, TEP, PEG, laser, LES botulinum toxin. (Cummings 7e, Ch 69, pp 994–996)

**Epidemiology and side**: annual incidence about 2 per 100,000, men 2–3 times more than women, mostly elderly. Up to 1 in 1000 upper GI studies. About two-thirds are midline, about 25% bulge left and 10% right (left carotid lies more laterally and the cervical esophagus curves left), so open approaches use a left neck incision unless imaging shows a right-sided sac. Other pharyngoesophageal weak points: Laimer triangle (below the cricopharyngeus) and Killian-Jamieson space. Boyce sign = neck swelling that gurgles on palpation. (Cummings 7e, Ch 70, pp 998–999)

**Endoscopic staple diverticulostomy (ESD) details**: Weerda bivalved laryngoscope, telescope inspection and biopsy of any pouch lesion. Traction sutures help with small (under 2–2.5 cm) or large (over 3.5 cm, multiple firings) sacs. The cartridge blade goes in the esophageal lumen and the anvil in the pouch (Operative Techniques in Laryngology places the longer anvil in the esophagus instead). Same-day discharge after 3–4 hours' observation for fever, chest/back pain, emphysema or tachycardia. Clear liquids that night. Routine postoperative esophagram is unnecessary (a residual nonretaining pouch is expected). Limits: kyphosis, cervical osteophytes, small mouth opening, and small (under 2 cm) pouches where the myotomy may be incomplete. For 1–2 cm pouches, myotomy alone may suffice in open surgery. (Cummings 7e, Ch 70, pp 1000–1004)

**Diagnostic bronchoscopy numbers**: topical 1% lidocaine is preferred (no added anesthesia from higher concentration and twice the volume before the 6–8 mg/kg toxic limit). BAL wedges in a segmental bronchus with 20–60 mL aliquots to 100–300 mL total. Complications 0–2.3%, transient fever in up to 30%. Transbronchial biopsy carries about a 5% pneumothorax risk (cryobiopsy higher, about 9.5%). EBUS-TBNA staging sensitivity about 88–93%, equivalent or better than cervical mediastinoscopy, and is now the preferred minimally invasive mediastinal staging tool. Sample nodes over 5 mm. Navigation yield improves with a CT 'bronchus sign'. (Cummings 7e, Ch 71, pp 1007–1010)

**Central airway obstruction toolkit**: the rigid bronchoscope is the instrument of choice (ventilates, core-out with the barrel, large suction, tamponade). Cold techniques — mechanical debulking, microdebrider (long 37–45 cm blades), cryotherapy (no fire risk, ideal for organic foreign bodies, clots and mucus plugs, delayed effect, carcinoids may be cryoresistant). Thermal — Nd:YAG laser (keep under 40 W, 0.5–1 s pulses, fire parallel to the wall), electrocautery, argon plasma coagulation (noncontact, shallow, requires FiO2 below 0.4). Stents: silicone (need rigid scope, migrate more) vs self-expanding metallic. All risk mucus impaction, granulation, migration — survey at about 4–6 weeks. Rigid bronchoscopy removes foreign bodies more reliably than flexible. (Cummings 7e, Ch 71, pp 1010–1014)

topic: Systemic Therapy Foundations in Head & Neck Cancer
text: **HNSCC genomics (TCGA, 279 tumors)**: alterations cluster in cell-cycle (TP53, CDKN2A, MYC — the most commonly altered pathway, present in essentially all tumors), mitogenic (EGFR, RAS, PI3K), differentiation (NOTCH1) and apoptotic pathways. TP53 is the most commonly mutated gene (about 47–72%), occurs early in dysplasia, is tobacco-associated, inversely related to HPV, and disruptive mutations predict worse survival. CDKN2A (9p21, p16/p14ARF) is lost in about 57% of HPV-negative tumors but intact in HPV-positive ones (E7 inactivates Rb). PIK3CA is the most frequently altered oncogene, especially in HPV-positive tumors (about 56%). EGFR is overexpressed in over 90% and predicts worse outcome, but unlike lung cancer it is rarely mutated in the kinase domain — one reason EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors work poorly. HPV-positive tumors carry fewer mutations. (Cummings 7e, Ch 73, pp 1033–1037)

topic: Systemic Therapy Foundations in Head & Neck Cancer
text: **Gene therapy in HNSCC**: strategies replace a defective gene (e.g., adenoviral wild-type p53 — Advexin in US trials, Gendicine approved in China), use conditionally replicating oncolytic viruses that lyse p53-deficient cells (ONYX-015), or suppress oncogenes. Delivery is by direct DNA/RNA injection, nonviral vectors (liposomes, nanoparticles) or viral vectors (adenovirus, AAV, retrovirus, lentivirus). Adenovirus does not integrate and is immunogenic. Retroviruses integrate but need dividing cells. (Cummings 7e, Ch 72, pp 1017–1030)

**Epidemiology numbers**: oral HPV infection (oral rinse PCR) is present in about 7% of the US population and HPV16 in about 1%; prevalence is about 11.5% in men vs 3.2% in women, bimodal by age, higher with tobacco, marijuana, HIV/low CD4 and immunosuppression, and linked to oral-sex partners and earlier sexual debut. Most incident oral infections clear within a year (median about 7 months); men acquire more and clear less. HPV-positive OPSCC rose about 225% (1988–2004), from about 16% to about 70% of oropharyngeal cancers; men outnumber women about 4:1; over 90% of patients are white; about 65% have smoked. HPV16 E6 antibodies can be detectable years before diagnosis. A sexual history does not reliably predict tumor HPV status. (Cummings 7e, Ch 74, pp 1047–1050)

**De-escalation context**: severe late toxicity (mainly dysphagia) occurred in about 43% across three RTOG chemoradiation trials, and dysphagia rises in a dose-response fashion above about 55 Gy to the superior and middle constrictors — the rationale for de-intensification in younger, longer-surviving HPV-positive patients. ECOG 1308 (induction responders given 54 Gy with cetuximab) showed 2-year OS about 94% with less solid-food dysphagia (54% vs 89%); other strategies tested were cetuximab for cisplatin (RTOG 1016 — inferior), radiation alone (NRG HN002), and TORS with risk-adapted adjuvant therapy (ECOG 3311, PATHOS). About 90% of unknown-primary SCCs with HPV-positive nodes arise in the oropharynx; HPV is found in 2–20% of oral cavity and 5–30% of laryngeal/sinonasal SCC without the same prognostic meaning. (Cummings 7e, Ch 74, pp 1049, 1051–1052)

topic: Radiation Therapy Principles for Head & Neck Surgeons
text: **Dose to control disease**: subclinical/microscopic disease needs about 50 Gy, positive margins about 60 Gy in this text (current postoperative practice gives about 66 Gy to positive margins or ENE), and large (T3–T4) tumors about 70 Gy or more in 2-Gy fractions. Tumor control probability depends on both dose and the number of clonogens (volume). (Cummings 7e, Ch 75, p 1057)

topic: Radiation Therapy Principles for Head & Neck Surgeons
text: **IMRT by site**: in nasopharynx, randomized trials showed IMRT equals conventional control and better preserves salivary flow. In sinus cancer IMRT lowers optic nerve dose and severe dry-eye syndrome. In oropharynx, nearly all failures after careful IMRT are in-field in high-dose volumes (marginal misses occur mainly at the match line with an anterior low-neck field). IMRT increases skin dose because of multiple beams unless skin is contoured as an avoidance structure. (Cummings 7e, Ch 75, pp 1063–1065, 1067)

**Radiation context**: carotid rupture and pharyngocutaneous fistula occur almost exclusively after combined surgery and radiation (43 of 46 cases in one series had radical salvage surgery with brachytherapy and/or external beam), are more common with preoperative than postoperative RT, and are rare after definitive RT unless tumor invades the carotid sheath; temporal-bone ORN after nasopharyngeal RT also predisposes. Pseudoaneurysm is the most common angiographic finding, and rebleeding after endovascular treatment occurs in up to about 25%. (Cummings 7e, Ch 75, p 1069)

**Flap perfusion concepts**: widening a random flap's base does not allow a longer flap, because added vessels have the same perfusion pressure — survival length is set by perfusion pressure vs critical closing pressure. Septocutaneous (direct cutaneous) arteries run parallel to the skin and supply large territories. Musculocutaneous perforators supply smaller ones. Four zones of failure: I macrocirculation (pedicle, delay acts here), II capillary (no-reflow, sludging — less if hematocrit under 30%), III interstitial (edema, lymphatic loss), IV cellular. Sympathetic denervation causes vasoconstriction until norepinephrine is depleted at 24–48 hours. Neovascularization begins at 3–4 days and can permit pedicle division by about 7 days. Creep and stress relaxation explain tissue expansion and serial excision. (Cummings 7e, Ch 77, pp 1090–1094)

**Salvage adjuncts**: after thrombectomy and revision, intra-arterial thrombolytics (urokinase/tPA) treat capillary microemboli, because systemic heparin does not dissolve formed thrombus. UW-solution washout helps more during secondary than primary ischemia. Medicinal leeches relieve venous congestion through salivary anticoagulants (hirudin) but carry a risk of Aeromonas hydrophila infection. Hyperbaric oxygen can prolong viability only after the thrombus is cleared. A transcutaneous O2 over 90 mm Hg in a congested flap signals the need for intervention. (Cummings 7e, Ch 77, pp 1096–1098)

**Anastomosis technique**: cut vessel ends cleanly, dilate gently, strip adventitia only near the edge, use a double approximating clamp without tension, place stay sutures at bisecting or trisecting points, pass the needle perpendicular at 1–2 wall thicknesses from the edge, avoid instrumenting the lumen, and irrigate to detect backwalling; venous sutures can be spaced farther apart. Release downstream clamps first. End-to-end and end-to-side have equal patency; couplers speed venous (and some arterial) anastomoses. Vein grafts (usually distal saphenous) add a second anastomosis and higher thrombosis risk. Recipient options in a depleted neck: contralateral neck, transverse cervical system, prior flap pedicles, reverse flow in distal facial or superior thyroid arteries, flow-through flaps (fibula, radial forearm); the internal jugular system may give better venous patency than the external jugular. (Cummings 7e, Ch 78, pp 1111–1116)

**Idiopathic rhinitis is the largest subtype**: idiopathic (formerly vasomotor) rhinitis accounts for roughly 71% of NAR diagnoses and is a diagnosis of exclusion. On longitudinal follow-up up to one-quarter of these patients convert to positive allergy testing, so 'mixed rhinitis' is common and the label should be revisited if symptoms change (Cummings 7e, Ch 39, p 637).

**Pregnancy rhinitis**: nasal congestion that affects about 20% of pregnant women, usually in the later trimesters, and resolves within about 2 weeks of delivery. Smoking is the only known risk factor. It is associated with asthma and reduced quality of life. Hypothyroidism and acromegaly are other hormonal causes (Cummings 7e, Ch 39, p 637).

**Atrophic rhinitis, primary vs secondary**: primary disease occurs mainly in developing, subtropical/temperate regions and is associated with Klebsiella ozaenae (also Staphylococcus, Proteus mirabilis, E. coli). Secondary disease follows surgical overresection (empty nose syndrome), granulomatous disease or radiation. Rhinitis medicamentosa can also be grouped here. Symptoms are paradoxical obstruction, dryness and crusting (Cummings 7e, Ch 39, p 639).

**Occupational rhinitis**: classified as primary occupational rhinitis (new symptoms after starting a job) or work-exacerbated rhinitis (preexisting rhinitis made worse at work). High-molecular-weight agents (>10 kDa, plant, animal, microbial) tend to cause IgE-mediated disease, while low-molecular-weight agents (<10 kDa, diisocyanates, anhydrides, metals) act through less defined, often nonallergic, mechanisms and can be triggered by a single high-dose exposure. Its severity predicts the severity of occupational asthma. Reviewing the safety data sheet for workplace chemicals helps (Cummings 7e, Ch 39, pp 639–640).

**Diagnostic aids**: a validated questionnaire found that onset after age 35, no family history of allergy, no outdoor or cat-triggered symptoms, and symptoms with perfumes/fragrances gave a 96% likelihood of NAR. Cold dry air provocation is more specific for NAR than histamine challenge. Nasal cytology alone cannot separate NAR from AR, but eosinophils suggest NARES, mast cells suggest NARMA and neutrophils suggest NARNE (Cummings 7e, Ch 39, pp 640–641).

**Capsaicin and botulinum toxin**: topical capsaicin, a TRPV1 agonist, desensitizes nociceptive C fibers by Ca2+-mediated afferent atrophy and improved idiopathic rhinitis symptoms for up to 36 weeks in a Cochrane review. Mucosal burning limits tolerance. Botulinum toxin injected into the inferior/middle turbinate heads lowers rhinorrhea only, for up to about 12 weeks (Cummings 7e, Ch 39, pp 637, 641–642).

**Pearls**: NAR typically starts in adulthood without seasonal variation and with less itching and sneezing than AR (except NARES). NAR patients have more acute and chronic rhinosinusitis than AR patients and are more often diagnosed with OSA, of greater severity. Elderly ('senile') rhinitis is mainly bilateral watery rhinorrhea that responds well to ipratropium. Ulceration, heavy crusting or septal perforation points toward vasculitis, granulomatous disease or malignancy (Cummings 7e, Ch 39, p 640).

**Post-vaccine microbiology shift**: only about 0.5–2% of viral acute rhinosinusitis becomes bacterial. After pneumococcal conjugate vaccine was introduced (2000), S. pneumoniae isolates fell from about 43% to 25% while H. influenzae rose from 35% to 41% (M. catarrhalis stable at 13–14%), and beta-lactamase-producing H. influenzae increased. This shift is why the IDSA prefers amoxicillin-clavulanate over plain amoxicillin (Cummings 7e, Ch 40, pp 644–645).

**Adjuncts**: intranasal steroids shorten symptom duration and lower symptom intensity, and saline or topical decongestants may help with symptoms. Oral decongestants are not recommended (poor efficacy, side effects), and antihistamines do not help nonallergic patients (sedating ones may thicken secretions) (Cummings 7e, Ch 40, p 646).

**Age and sinus development**: orbital complications cluster in children younger than about 7, because the ethmoids are the most developed sinuses at birth. Intracranial complications cluster in adolescents, because the frontal sinus first appears radiographically around age 5 and enlarges through puberty. The sphenoid pneumatizes through later childhood and is rarely the source. Overall, complications occur in about 1 per 95,000 pediatric admissions and are more common in males (Cummings 7e, Ch 40, p 647).

**Microbiology of complicated sinusitis**: unlike routine ABRS, complicated cases are often polymicrobial (about 75% in one series), with Streptococcus anginosus (formerly milleri) the most common isolate (about 18.5%), followed by S. aureus (12.4%) and beta-hemolytic streptococci. MRSA appears in about 6% of orbital complications. Peptostreptococcus and Prevotella are the main anaerobes (Cummings 7e, Ch 40, p 647).

**Sequence**: in intracranial complications draw blood cultures, and consider lumbar puncture only after imaging when focal deficits are present (herniation risk). Obtain contrast MRI and a neurosurgery consult when exam or CT suggests intracranial spread. When neurosurgical drainage is planned, coordinate sinus drainage under the same anesthetic. Classic signs of raised ICP: frontal/retro-orbital headache, vomiting, altered mental status, nuchal rigidity and papilledema (Cummings 7e, Ch 40, p 648).

**Outcome data**: mortality is about 40–80%. In a large systematic review, surgical resection and liposomal amphotericin B were each linked to better survival. Diabetes as the host factor predicted better survival, while intracranial involvement and older age predicted worse survival. Orbital exenteration has not clearly added survival benefit in retrospective series, and granulocyte transfusions for neutropenia have only case-series support. CT findings such as bone erosion appear late, and MRI loss of contrast enhancement better maps devitalized tissue (Cummings 7e, Ch 40, p 648).

**Type 2 CRSwNP vs allergic rhinitis**: polyp tissue makes polyclonal IgE that is usually not tied to atopy, unlike the allergen-specific IgE of AR. S. aureus is found in about 60% of CRSwNP. IgE against staphylococcal enterotoxins (SE-IgE) is a risk factor for comorbid asthma and for polyp recurrence after surgery. Epithelial alarmins (IL-25, IL-33, TSLP) start the type 2 cascade (Cummings 7e, Ch 41, p 657).

**Non-type 2 sub-endotypes**: (1) neutrophilic (IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, MPO), (2) Th17/Th22 (IL-17, IL-22, TNF-α) and (3) Th1 (IFN-γ). Mixed endotypes are common. Tissue neutrophilia predicts a poorer corticosteroid response, and no endotype-targeted therapy for non-type 2 disease is proven. TGF-β1 drives early remodeling in CRSsNP, and higher IFN-γ is seen in nonrecurrent polyps (Cummings 7e, Ch 41, pp 657–658).

**Etiologic hypotheses to know**: the original fungal (Alternaria) hypothesis is largely rejected except for AFRS. The staphylococcal superantigen hypothesis explains Western eosinophilic polyps but not CRSsNP or most Asian polyps; superantigens may only modify an existing type 2 response. Biofilms (mostly S. aureus) are linked to recalcitrance, though cause vs effect is unclear. The immune barrier hypothesis (defective mechanical/innate barrier, as in CF) is the broadest unifying model, and the leukotriene/eicosanoid hypothesis covers only an AERD-like subset (Cummings 7e, Ch 41, p 656).

**Ethnic and genetic pearls**: Asian CRSwNP is often Th1/Th17 and neutrophilic, with lower IL-5, less eosinophilia and less asthma than Western CRSwNP. Polymorphisms of the bitter taste receptor T2R38 (expressed on sinonasal epithelium and solitary chemosensory cells, where it boosts ciliary beat and antimicrobial release) may affect CRS susceptibility. Low vitamin D has been linked to deficient Treg activity in CRSwNP (Cummings 7e, Ch 41, pp 652, 655).

**Saline and steroid delivery**: high-volume (>200 mL) saline irrigation carries a strong recommendation (Grade A) as an adjunct but is not monotherapy. High volume beats low-volume sprays; hypertonic saline may improve radiographic scores, while isotonic and hypotonic give similar symptom results. Budesonide irrigations are recommended, especially after ESS (Grade B), and outperformed steroid sprays at 12 months in postoperative patients. Mucosal atomization devices and maxillary antrostomy sinus tubes are options (MAST complications 35%; MAD with about 6% raised intraocular pressure), and the YAMIK catheter is recommended against (Cummings 7e, Ch 42, pp 661–664).

**CRSwNP-specific ICAR grades**: intranasal steroid drops or sprays get a strong recommendation (Grade A, more than 30 RCTs, equally effective). A short oral steroid course (up to 14 days) is an option (Grade A), with benefit lasting about 12 weeks. Doxycycline for 3 weeks reduced polyp size at 12 weeks in one RCT. Leukotriene modifiers are an option (Grade A), with efficacy similar to intranasal steroids, especially for steroid-intolerant patients; montelukast carries rare neuropsychiatric effects and zileuton raises liver enzymes. Aspirin desensitization after ESS is recommended in AERD (Grade B) (Cummings 7e, Ch 42, pp 663–666).

**Alternative topical agents (boards like these)**: 1% baby-shampoo surfactant irrigation disrupts Pseudomonas biofilm but is poorly tolerated (option). Manuka honey (active compound methylglyoxal) has data only in AFRS and gets no recommendation; high MGO doses denude cilia. Xylitol gets no recommendation (insufficient data). Colloidal silver is recommended against, since the FDA rules it unsafe and ineffective. Photodynamic therapy has no human data. Treating comorbid allergy is an option (Grade D), and immunotherapy after ESS is an option in AFRS (Grade C) (Cummings 7e, Ch 42, pp 665–666).

**Who benefits more or less after ESS**: polyps, AFRS and baseline olfactory loss predict larger improvement, and worse baseline SNOT-22 and asthma also go with bigger gains. Obesity and anxiety predict smaller gains. Sex, GERD, migraine, diabetes and trainee participation have no effect. Smoking, female sex, depression, fibromyalgia, migraine, OSA and AERD worsen baseline QOL. Primary ESS patients were about 2.1 times more likely to improve than revision patients in one multicenter study. Delaying surgery more than 5 years after diagnosis has been linked to smaller gains in some, but not all, studies (Cummings 7e, Ch 43, pp 672–673).

**Medical vs surgical outcomes in refractory CRS**: about two-thirds of patients who choose continued medical therapy stay stable or improve, but only about 1 in 4 gain one MCID and 1 in 5 worsen. Patients waiting for ESS on maximal therapy worsened by about 8.5 SNOT-22 points over roughly 7 months, then improved from about 66 to 16 after surgery. ESS outperforms continued medical therapy on QOL, oral antibiotic/steroid use and missed work, and patients who cross over do as well as the surgical cohort (Cummings 7e, Ch 43, pp 670–674).

**2016 appropriateness criteria for ESS**: candidacy is graded appropriate, uncertain or inappropriate from three inputs: the preoperative medical regimen, the Lund-Mackay CT score and the SNOT-22 score. Retrospectively, 'appropriate' and 'uncertain' patients both improved meaningfully while 'inappropriate' patients did not. The criteria set a minimum threshold for offering surgery; they do not mandate surgery (Cummings 7e, Ch 43, p 674).

**Comorbidity outcomes after ESS**: in asthmatic CRS patients, a 22-study review found improved asthma control in 76%, fewer attacks in 85%, fewer hospitalizations in 64%, and less oral (73%) and inhaled (28%) steroid use, but no significant change in FEV1/PFTs. In CF, ESS improves symptoms without improving pulmonary function. Smell improves most in CRSwNP and in patients with worse baseline olfaction. Sleep, depression, fatigue and productivity improve (absenteeism fell from 22 to 3 days per year). ESS becomes more cost-effective than medical therapy by about year 3 (ICER about $5,900/QALY) (Cummings 7e, Ch 43, pp 673–675).

**Balloon catheter dilation evidence**: a 2011 Cochrane review found no convincing evidence favoring balloon dilation over standard ESS. An industry-sponsored noninferiority RCT in limited maxillary/anterior ethmoid disease (posterior ethmoid, sphenoid and frontal disease excluded) showed similar SNOT-20 improvement to 24 months with faster recovery. A 2018 consensus statement agreed on only 2 of 31 statements: balloon dilation can improve short-term QOL in limited CRSsNP, and it can be effective in frontal sinusitis (Cummings 7e, Ch 43, pp 674–675).

**Antrochoanal polyp technique**: removing the intra-antral portion is the key to avoiding failure. Use angled endoscopes and curved powered instruments through a middle meatal antrostomy, and add a small temporary inferior meatal window, a canine fossa/sublabial puncture, or a mega-antrostomy (resecting the mid-inferior turbinate down to the floor) when needed. Caldwell-Luc mucosal stripping is unnecessary (Cummings 7e, Ch 44, p 687).

**Image guidance facts**: an acceptable accuracy is 2–3 mm, so navigation confirms compartments (e.g., posterior ethmoid vs sphenoid) rather than millimeter skull base decisions. Error sources include CT acquisition, fiducial/headset shift, soft-tissue effects during surface registration and operator error. AAO-HNS endorses it for revision surgery, distorted anatomy, extensive polyposis, frontal/posterior ethmoid/sphenoid disease, disease abutting skull base/orbit/optic nerve/ICA, CSF leak or skull base defect, and neoplasms. A meta-analysis found fewer major complications with navigation (RR 0.48), although single-center series disagree (Cummings 7e, Ch 44, p 690).

**Nasolacrimal duct protection**: never dissect anterior to the anterior margin of the middle turbinate, and do not extend middle or inferior antrostomies anteriorly. An inferior meatal antrostomy should be at least 1 cm behind the anterior end of the inferior turbinate attachment region to spare the duct. Symptomatic duct injury (epiphora) is treated with endoscopic dacryocystorhinostomy (Cummings 7e, Ch 44, p 707).

**Bleeding control**: the posterior septal artery, which crosses the sphenoid face below the ostium, is the usual source of major post-ESS bleeding needing return to the OR. For an ICA injury, keep up brain perfusion, use two large-bore suctions, apply crushed muscle (e.g., harvested lateral tongue) over the tear, pack, and move straight to angiography/endovascular care. Repeat angiography in the following weeks to look for delayed pseudoaneurysm or dissection (Cummings 7e, Ch 44, pp 706–707).

**Technical causes of primary ESS failure**: middle turbinate lateralization. A middle meatal antrostomy that misses the natural ostium (recirculation). Maxillary ostial stenosis. Ethmoid adhesions. Incomplete 'central' ethmoidectomy that leaves partitions along the lamina, skull base and middle turbinate. And frontal recess scarring. Misdiagnosed migraine or neuralgia is a nontechnical cause. In a 61,339-patient cohort, 6.65% had revision ESS. Nasal polyps and female sex each raised the odds (aOR about 1.2) (Cummings 7e, Ch 44, p 708).

**Primary polyp surgery principles**: primary polyps are gelatinous and fairly avascular, while revision cases are fibrotic and bloodier. Clear polyps from anterior/inferior until landmarks appear, then do a complete ethmoidectomy with larger maxillary, sphenoid and frontal openings for topical delivery and office debridement. Dissect the posterior frontal recess carefully, because polyps tend to recur there first. Unoperated sinuses get almost no topical steroid penetration. Modified Lothrop and middle turbinate resection are kept for recalcitrant revision disease. Antibiotics plus oral steroids for 7–10 days before surgery can calm purulent or polypoid mucosa and protect reactive airways (Cummings 7e, Ch 44, pp 687, 690, 703).

**AFRS surgery specifics**: bony expansion and erosion often leave dura and periorbita stuck to the overlying mucosa, so avoid or use the microdebrider very carefully near dehiscences. Remove all tenacious allergic mucin, because residual debris drives recurrence and revision. Perioperative systemic steroids help but recurrence follows their withdrawal, so long-term steroid irrigations are preferred (Cummings 7e, Ch 44, p 704).

topic: Facial Pain / Headache vs Rhinogenic Disease
text: **Contact-point surgery criteria**: offer surgery only when a mucosal contact point on endoscopy/CT is shown to drive the pain, for example by clear relief with topical decongestant/anesthetic or a diagnostic block, after neurologic evaluation and failed medical therapy. Contact points are common in pain-free people. One series reported 91% lower intensity and 85% lower frequency, but results vary, surgery can worsen headache, and at least 1 year of follow-up is needed to call it a success (Cummings 7e, Ch 44, p 688).

**Post-ESS care**: check vision and mental status in recovery. Start saline irrigation the day after surgery when no packing is used, use nonopioid analgesia, and give a short steroid burst for asthma, fungal disease or heavy polyposis. The first visit is at about 5–7 days. Remove loose crusts and clots but not adherent ones (removing them damages mucosa and promotes scarring), and fix a lateralizing middle turbinate early. Evidence on debridement frequency is limited (Cummings 7e, Ch 44, pp 705–706).

**Revision series numbers**: middle turbinate lateralization was the most common revision finding (78% in one series), typically after a partial middle turbinectomy. If the middle turbinate must be resected, take nearly all of it and leave only a short lamella at the skull base, or stabilize a floppy turbinate with medialization or spacers. Retained ethmoid cells were found in more than half of revision patients. In revision frontal surgery, residual agger nasi or bulla remnants were present in 79%, residual uncinate in 39% and lateralized middle turbinate in 36% (Cummings 7e, Ch 45, pp 714–715).

**Revision technique rules**: in revision frontal surgery, first remove every residual bony partition. Dilation or drilling only complements this. Avoid balloon-only revision when partitions remain, since retained mucosa can be trapped against the lamina or skull base. For neo-osteogenesis or circumferential scarring, use nonanatomic procedures: Draf III/modified Lothrop, maxillary mega-antrostomy, or transseptal sphenoidotomy (posterosuperior septectomy, full removal of the sphenoid face and drilling of the intersinus septum into one common opening, with optional floor 'nasalization'). Cover exposed bone with mucosal grafts when possible (Cummings 7e, Ch 45, pp 715–716).

**Host factors to screen before revising**: AERD (polyp recurrence 36–96%, aspirin desensitization about 1 month after surgery, once polyps and eosinophilia are controlled). GPA, sarcoidosis and EGPA (surgery can worsen GPA and sarcoid, get rheumatology/immunology input first). CF or PCD. Immunodeficiency (CRS prevalence rises when CD4 falls below 50 cells/mm3). Continued smoking. And poor adherence. Think of atypical adult CF with poorly pneumatized sinuses, Pseudomonas colonization, neo-osteogenesis, GI or non-asthma lung disease, or a family history. Endoscopic medial maxillectomy may suit these patients (Cummings 7e, Ch 45, pp 713–714).

**Unexpected neoplasia and iatrogenic leak**: unsuspected neoplasm turns up in about 0.46% of bilateral inflammatory CRS specimens. Never perform a major oncologic resection on the basis of a frozen section. Refer with a detailed description of attachment sites if needed. An intraoperatively recognized skull base breach should be repaired at once unless intracranial injury needs imaging first. Postoperative clear rhinorrhea calls for β2-transferrin or β-trace testing and early repair because of meningitis risk. The SPA territory can be embolized, but ethmoidal arteries (ophthalmic branches) cannot, and medical lowering of orbital pressure alone is inadequate for orbital hematoma (Cummings 7e, Ch 45, pp 716–717).

**Draf III technical landmarks**: start with a complete anterior (preferably also posterior) ethmoidectomy. Make a septal window from just anterior to the frontal ostium about 2 cm forward and down, but never behind the first olfactory fibers (the posterior limit). Drill the beak and intersinus septum anteriorly almost to the skin, leaving under 1 mm of bone. Bounds are the lacrimal bones laterally, the skull base/first olfactory neuron posteriorly and the nasal skin anteriorly. Do not drill the posterior table (CSF leak risk). The 'outside-in' variant defines the first olfactory neuron and lateral periosteum first and is useful when tumor or scar hides the recess (Cummings 7e, Ch 46, pp 726–727).

**Frontal surgery restraint pearls**: frontal recess opacification alone is not a reason to instrument it; it often clears after the ostiomeatal complex is opened and disease is treated medically. Many chronic frontal cases start with unnecessary recess instrumentation. Forehead pain is usually tension-type headache, and surgery worsens it in about one-third. Three or more episodes of acute frontal sinusitis a year should prompt an immune workup before anatomy is blamed. The frontal ostium usually lies more medial, higher and more anterior than expected, and the sagittal CT is the key view (Cummings 7e, Ch 46, pp 723–724).

**Pneumosinus dilatans**: a rare benign over-expansion of an aerated (not fluid-filled) frontal sinus beyond the normal bony margin. It is usually found because of forehead deformity or mass effect. The proposed mechanism is a one-way ostial valve. Exclude fibrous dysplasia and an underlying dural meningioma. Opening the ostium usually halts expansion and can shrink the sinus (Cummings 7e, Ch 46, p 730).

**Frontal IP**: the frontal sinus is involved in about 1.6–15% of IP. CT focal hyperostosis predicts the attachment site in about 95%, and T2 MRI separates tumor from retained secretions. Most frontal-recess IP can be removed via Draf IIa, but attachment within the recess or sinus needs Draf IIb/III drilling of the pedicle bone. Lateral orbital-roof attachment may need an added transpalpebral approach, and topical 5-FU is an adjunct when margins are uncertain (Cummings 7e, Ch 46, pp 729–730).

**Osteoplastic flap/obliteration pearls**: indications are extensive osteomyelitis, endoscopically inaccessible tumor, loculated disease, or a failed Draf III. A Caldwell-view template underestimates superior and lateral pneumatization, so image guidance or a hook-palpation technique is better. Avoid a high-midline entry hole, where venous channels are large. Strip all mucosa and lightly drill the inner cortex because mucosa follows the foramina of Breschet, otherwise a mucocele forms. Fat (abdominal, ideally left side) is the preferred obliterating material, and an infected anterior wall requires a Riedel procedure. Lynch-Howarth external ethmoidectomy has been abandoned because about one-third stenose (Cummings 7e, Ch 46, pp 730–732).

**Chronic frontal sinusitis bacteriology**: compared with acute disease there are more anaerobes. Besides S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae and M. catarrhalis, previously operated patients often grow MRSA, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Enterobacter (Cummings 7e, Ch 46, p 721).

**Vascular anatomy numbers**: more than 90% of epistaxis is anterior (Kiesselbach plexus: anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine septal, greater palatine and superior labial branches). Woodruff plexus, posterior to the inferior turbinate root and below the horizontal middle turbinate, is formed by sphenopalatine and ascending pharyngeal branches and is a common posterior source. A middle ethmoidal artery exists in about 30%, and the anterior ethmoidal artery hangs below the skull base in a mesentery in up to 25%. The greater palatine artery re-enters the nose through the incisive foramen to supply the anterior floor and septum (Cummings 7e, Ch 47, pp 733–735).

**Resuscitation and coagulopathy numbers**: tachycardia is the earliest sign of acute blood loss. Consider transfusion at hemoglobin of 7 g/dL or lower (8 g/dL with cardiovascular disease or after cardiac/orthopedic surgery). Platelet goals are >50,000/µL with active bleeding and >10,000/µL to prevent spontaneous bleeding. Antiplatelet effects last 7–10 days (NSAIDs reverse more readily with platelets). Use desmopressin for uremia and for von Willebrand types 1 and 2A. Warfarin users make up about 8% of ED epistaxis visits: Cummings reverses only if supratherapeutic, with FFP (vitamin K acts slower and delays re-anticoagulation for about a week). Current practice, including the 2020 AAO-HNSF epistaxis guideline, avoids stopping or reversing anticoagulation unless bleeding is life-threatening, and then uses 4-factor PCC with IV vitamin K rather than FFP. Alcohol lowers fibrinogen. Routine coagulation labs are not needed without suggestive history (Cummings 7e, Ch 47, pp 735–738).

**Packing specifics**: direct packs along the nasal floor, not upward toward the middle turbinate. Absorbable packs (polyurethane foam, hyaluronic acid) are better tolerated but apply little pressure, while nonabsorbable PVA sponges or balloon packs stay 3–5 days and should be moistened before removal. For a posterior pack, pass a 12–14 Fr Foley with a 30-mL balloon until the tip is seen in the oropharynx, inflate with 5–10 mL of water, pull it back into the choana and pad it to prevent alar necrosis. Monitor with pulse oximetry and telemetry (ICU if cardiopulmonary disease); the nasocardiac reflex can cause bradycardia. Do not cauterize both sides of the septum at one sitting (perforation risk) (Cummings 7e, Ch 47, pp 738–740).

**Greater palatine canal injection**: a 25-gauge needle bent 1.5 cm from the tip is passed into the greater palatine foramen just medial to the upper second molar. After aspirating, inject about 1 mL of dilute epinephrine/lidocaine to vasoconstrict the SPA in the pterygopalatine fossa. It controlled posterior epistaxis in about 90%, though about 36% needed a repeat injection. It also improves the ESS field in the posterior ethmoids (Cummings 7e, Ch 47, pp 737–738).

**Other ligations**: endoscopic internal maxillary artery ligation goes through a wide antrostomy and the posterior maxillary wall into the pterygopalatine fossa (two proximal clips, one distal). It risks vidian (dry eye), greater palatine and infraorbital nerve injury. External carotid ligation is a last resort. Anterior ethmoidal artery: always found between the second and third lamellae, and low-lying with a supraorbital ethmoid cell or a deep (high Keros) olfactory fossa. Via a transcaruncular/precaruncular or Lynch approach, the anterior lacrimal crest–AEA–PEA–optic canal distances are about 24–12–6 mm, although the number of foramina varies (Cummings 7e, Ch 47, pp 740–742).

**Outcome and pediatric pearls**: in a UK national study epistaxis carried a 13.9% recurrence rate and measurable 30-day mortality, a marker of comorbidity. Pediatric epistaxis is almost always anterior, from digital trauma, and self-limited. Use moisturization and silver nitrate in cooperative children. Screen children with recurrent severe bleeding for hemophilia or von Willebrand disease, and consider JNA in any adolescent male with unilateral obstruction and bleeding. Routine antistaphylococcal coverage for nasal packing is not supported by evidence: a systematic review of 990 patients found no toxic shock without it (Cummings 7e, Ch 47, pp 733, 740, 742).

**Spontaneous-leak profile in numbers**: anterior spontaneous leaks are 77% female, typically aged 45–65 (mean 57–60), with BMI around 35–38. In one series 82% had elevated BMI, and 72% met modified Dandy criteria for idiopathic intracranial hypertension. In one series empty sella occurred in 100% of spontaneous vs 11% of nonspontaneous leaks. Across series, imaging shows arachnoid pits (79%), empty or partially empty sella (50%), meningoencephalocele (50%) and dural ectasia (35%). A classic history is a diffuse headache that eases when the drip starts and returns when it stops (Cummings 7e, Ch 48, p 747).

**Mimics to exclude**: CSF otorrhea behind an intact tympanic membrane draining down the eustachian tube (look at the middle ear when effusion accompanies a confirmed leak); retained saline irrigation released on head tilt after ESS (stops when irrigations stop); and a ruptured sinus retention cyst after trauma or URI, whose fluid has a yellow tint on white tissue and shows an air-fluid level. The halo sign is falsely positive with tears or saliva. Persistent CSF depletion can cause an orthostatic low-pressure headache (Cummings 7e, Ch 48, pp 748–749).

**Lumbar drain management**: aim for about 10 mL/hour and send daily CSF cell count, protein, glucose and culture. Overdrainage causes low-pressure headache and pneumocephalus from air drawn through the defect; slow or clamp the drain if this happens. Avoid lumbar drains with markedly raised ICP. Routine use does not raise repair success, so keep it for high-flow or tenuous repairs (1–5 days). Conservative care for selected leaks is 1–2 weeks of bed rest with head elevation, stool softeners and no straining or nose blowing (Cummings 7e, Ch 48, pp 753, 756).

topic: Endoscopic CSF Leak Repair / Nasoseptal Flap
text: **Repair technique points**: never push a meningoencephalocele back intracranially; ablate the sac with bipolar or coblation. Strip mucosa within about 5 mm of the defect edges. Never place mucosa intracranially, and orient free mucosal grafts mucosa-side toward the sinus (an intracranial mucocele can result otherwise). Underlay fascia is held by ICP; the 'bath-plug' fat technique is an option. Graft material does not change outcome (meta-analysis of 289 fistulas). Reconstructive ladder: no leak gets a mucosal graft, a low-flow leak gets a multilayer free graft, and a high-flow leak adds a vascularized (nasoseptal) flap (Cummings 7e, Ch 48, pp 754–755).

topic: Endoscopic CSF Leak Repair / Nasoseptal Flap
text: **Outcome numbers**: endoscopic repair succeeds in about 90% of primary and 97% of secondary attempts, while transcranial repair has failure rates above 25% plus craniotomy morbidity (anosmia, seizures, hematoma, brain retraction). Monitor 24 hours in a step-down setting, then avoid strenuous activity, sneezing and coughing for about 6 weeks. For spontaneous leaks, recheck ICP afterward (papilledema, headache, possibly LP opening pressure) and treat with acetazolamide or VP/LP shunt; get endocrinology involved when an empty sella is present (Cummings 7e, Ch 48, pp 753–757).

**Endoscopic medial/inferior decompression technique**: do a wide maxillary antrostomy (back to the posterior wall and down to the inferior turbinate) and a total ethmoidectomy, but leave the most anterior/superior frontal-recess cells alone so prolapsed fat does not obstruct the maxillary or frontal sinus. Remove the lamina from the sphenoid face to the frontal process of the maxilla, up to the frontoethmoid suture, and the floor medial to the infraorbital canal (the lateral limit). For apical compressive optic neuropathy, drill the orbital process of the palatine bone. Incise the periorbita posterior to anterior and lyse fibrous bands. Avoid packing, and tell anesthesia not to mask-ventilate at extubation (pneumo-orbita risk) (Cummings 7e, Ch 49, pp 767–768).

**Post-decompression complications**: do not pack postoperative epistaxis at the bedside because orbital contents are exposed. Return to the OR instead. Retrobulbar hematoma can still threaten vision and may need canthotomy/cantholysis. Give intraoperative and tapered postoperative steroids against edema-related optic neuropathy. Sinusitis or mucocele from herniated orbital fat can appear decades later. SNOT-22 improves at 1 year, so sinonasal function is not harmed long term (Cummings 7e, Ch 49, pp 767–768).

**Endonasal optic canal anatomy**: the canal is formed by two struts of the lesser sphenoid wing and carries the optic nerve and ophthalmic artery. It appears as a superolateral bulge in the sphenoid, or in an Onodi cell when present. The intracanalicular nerve keeps all three meningeal layers with CSF, condensing at the annulus of Zinn. The ophthalmic artery is usually superolateral but runs inferior/inferomedial in about 20%, which is why a sheath incision is made superomedially and carefully (Cummings 7e, Ch 49, p 769).

**Orbital masses reaching endonasal surgery**: the most common benign adult orbital tumor is cavernous hemangioma (cavernous venous malformation, 5–15%), which is well circumscribed, enhancing and T2 bright. Schwannoma and solitary fibrous tumor follow. Orbital pseudotumor can mimic a mass (11%), and lymphoid hyperplasia on biopsy warrants surveillance for lymphoma. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is the most common adult orbital malignancy (about 10%). Lesions medial to the optic nerve, extraconal or intraconal, suit a purely endonasal approach (Cummings 7e, Ch 49, pp 769–770).

**Pedicle-oriented resection and maxillary corridors**: debulk to find the insertion, then limit subperiosteal stripping and bone drilling to the attachment. This gives the same recurrence as full demucosalization with shorter surgery and fewer complications. A modular endoscopic medial maxillectomy runs from type A (middle antrostomy) to type D (endoscopic Sturmann–Canfield, removing the medial anterior maxillary wall). Canfield morbidity: epiphora 12%, premaxillary paresthesia 24%, incisor/canine hypoesthesia 29%. The prelacrimal approach, which preserves the turbinate and nasolacrimal duct ('TuNa-saving'), avoids epiphora but is harder to survey endoscopically. Plan an external or combined approach for an anterior-wall or lateral-recess frontal attachment, extensive supraorbital cell disease, or orbital involvement (Cummings 7e, Ch 50, pp 776–777).

**MRI 'convoluted cerebriform' pattern**: contrast T1 MRI shows alternating parallel folds of cellular epithelium and less cellular stroma, which is highly predictive of IP and separates tumor from retained secretions. Loss of this pattern with infiltrative growth suggests carcinoma ex-IP. The attachment is predicted by focal hyperostosis or a bony strut on CT. Orbital symptoms (epiphora, proptosis, diplopia) should raise suspicion of malignancy (Cummings 7e, Ch 50, p 775).

**Origin and spread**: JNA may be a vascular malformation arising from an incompletely regressed first branchial arch artery (vessels express laminin α2), which explains its mixed internal and external carotid supply. ICA supply is found in about 36% and bilateral supply in about 31%. The epicenter is the pterygopalatine fossa/pterygoid base, with permeative spread into the cancellous basisphenoid. It spreads medially through the sphenopalatine foramen, posteriorly along the vidian canal, laterally through the pterygomaxillary fissure to the infratemporal fossa, and intracranially via the inferior/superior orbital fissures, foramen rotundum or ovale to the parasellar region. True transdural growth is rare (Cummings 7e, Ch 50, pp 777–779).

**Surgical keys and staging**: dissect in the subperiosteal plane with bipolar and drill the involved cancellous basisphenoid and pterygoid root aggressively, which sharply lowers recurrence. Infratemporal fossa, orbital or parasellar extension is not a contraindication to endoscopy, but ICA encasement or residual disease in critical areas after prior surgery argues against a purely endoscopic plan. The UPMC staging system emphasizes residual ICA vascularity after embolization and intracranial route (medial vs lateral to the ICA/cavernous sinus). Some skip embolization for small tumors (clip the IMA early), because it can blur tumor margins (Cummings 7e, Ch 50, pp 779–780).

**Lobular capillary hemangioma ('pyogenic granuloma')**: only about 10% of mucosal head and neck cases are nasal. It typically arises on the anterior septum (Little area) or turbinate heads, with peaks in male adolescents and pregnancy (about 30% of affected women were pregnant).
