It presents with epistaxis (75%) as a red-purple mass usually under 1 cm, with T2 hyperintensity and vivid enhancement. Excise it at the submucosal attachment plane, since debulking or cautery leads to recurrence (0 to over 40% across series). Pregnancy lesions may regress after delivery, and there is no malignant potential (Cummings 7e, Ch 50, pp 783–785).

**Sinonasal schwannoma**: only about 4% of head and neck schwannomas are sinonasal. Most arise from V1/V2 (also sympathetic or pterygopalatine ganglion fibers), most often in the ethmoid, with intracranial extension in up to 8.5%. Histology shows Antoni A areas with Verocay bodies, Antoni B myxoid areas and diffuse S-100. MRI shows a well-circumscribed, intensely enhancing mass with intralesional cysts, and T2 brightness tracks the Antoni B content. Endoscopic resection gives about 3% (or lower) recurrence, and observation is possible for small lesions in unfit patients (Cummings 7e, Ch 50, pp 786–787).

topic: Systemic Disease of the Nose / Sinuses
text: **GPA course and nasal care**: untreated active GPA killed more than 80% within 3 years (mean survival under 6 months). Induction uses steroids plus cyclophosphamide or rituximab (methotrexate for minor disease), and maintenance uses azathioprine, methotrexate or rituximab. About 85–90% enter remission, but about 50% relapse within 5 years. S. aureus nasal carriage independently predicts relapse. Use topical saline/antibiotic irrigations and steroids. CT abnormalities alone are not a surgical indication, and nasal reconstruction should wait until the disease has been inactive for 6–12 months (Cummings 7e, Ch 51, pp 789–790).

topic: Systemic Disease of the Nose / Sinuses
text: **Sarcoidosis and EGPA numbers**: on careful history, 61% of sarcoid patients report nasal symptoms, with obstruction the most common ENT complaint. The mucosa has a 'strawberry skin' look (submucosal granulomas on red mucosa), ACE is raised in about 80%, and biopsy of submucosal nodules has high yield. EGPA is ANCA-positive in only about 40% (p-ANCA/MPO, which goes with renal disease, pulmonary hemorrhage and mononeuritis). It runs prodromal (asthma/atopy), eosinophilic and vasculitic phases, with nasal involvement in 60–70% and polyps in 75%. The older ACR 1990 criteria (now replaced by the 2022 ACR/EULAR criteria) include eosinophilia over 10%, neuropathy, migratory pulmonary infiltrates, sinus abnormality and extravascular eosinophils on biopsy (4 or more: sensitivity 85%, specificity 99.7%). EGPA is treated with steroids, rituximab and mepolizumab (Cummings 7e, Ch 51, pp 790–791).

**Paranasal sinus cholesterol granuloma**: an expansile cyst most often in the frontal (also maxillary) sinus. It probably arises from obstructed, hypoventilated air cells with hemorrhage, hemosiderin and cholesterol crystals that provoke a foreign-body granulomatous reaction. Only about 25% have prior trauma or surgery. It is T1 and T2 hyperintense on MRI, unlike a typical mucocele (T1 variable). Treat by endoscopic marsupialization or excision (Cummings 7e, Ch 51, p 793).

topic: Facial Pain / Headache vs Rhinogenic Disease
text: **ICHD-3 migraine criteria**: migraine without aura needs at least 5 attacks of 4–72 hours with at least 2 of: unilateral, pulsating, moderate/severe, worsened by routine activity. At least 1 of nausea/vomiting or photophobia plus phonophobia must also be present. Migraine with aura needs at least 2 attacks of fully reversible visual, sensory, speech, motor, brainstem or retinal aura (each 5–60 minutes, spreading over at least 5 minutes) followed within 60 minutes by headache. Red flags for expedited workup and admission are mental status change, seizure, acute vision change, neck stiffness, temporal artery tenderness, field loss, diplopia, cranial neuropathy and unilateral rhinorrhea (Cummings 7e, Ch 52, pp 795–796).

topic: Facial Pain / Headache vs Rhinogenic Disease
text: **Treating the mimics**: for mild/moderate migraine, NSAIDs or acetaminophen are first line. Triptans (serotonin agonists that vasoconstrict) are for moderate/severe migraine and are contraindicated in cardiovascular disease; ondansetron can itself cause headache. For TMD (5–10% of people; 82% present with ear pain), use a night occlusal splint, a 2-week NSAID trial (ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily), a soft diet and muscle relaxants, and refer refractory cases to oral surgery; MRI is not routine (Cummings 7e, Ch 52, pp 796–797).

topic: Facial Pain / Headache vs Rhinogenic Disease
text: **Neuropathic facial pains**: Trigeminal neuralgia is brief electric attacks triggered by innocuous stimuli in V divisions, mostly in women over 50, with normal sensation. Get an MRI for MS, CPA tumor or vascular loop; carbamazepine is first line (baclofen, lamotrigine and pimozide are possible alternatives), with microvascular decompression or ablation for refractory cases. Glossopharyngeal neuralgia causes seconds-to-2-minute stabbing pain in the tonsil, tongue base, ear or mandibular angle, triggered by swallowing, coughing or yawning. Image it (demyelination, CPA tumor, carotid aneurysm), and treat with carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine or microvascular decompression (Cummings 7e, Ch 52, p 797).

topic: Facial Pain / Headache vs Rhinogenic Disease
text: **Postherpetic and other chronic pains**: about 30% of people get zoster, and V1 is the most common cranial site. Antivirals within 72 hours shorten the rash but do not prevent postherpetic neuralgia (pain more than 3 months after the rash heals), which is very common after age 50. Treat with 5% lidocaine, 8% (not 0.075%) capsaicin, gabapentin/pregabalin (a 50% pain reduction may take 2–3 months) or TCAs. Persistent idiopathic facial pain is daily pain for more than 2 hours a day over more than 3 months, poorly localized, not in one nerve's distribution and without deficit. It often starts after minor dental or ENT procedures and has psychiatric comorbidity; use low-dose amitriptyline or anticonvulsants, not surgery. Posttraumatic trigeminal neuropathic pain follows injury to the inferior alveolar, lingual or mental nerve (Cummings 7e, Ch 52, pp 797–798).

**Missed cases and late signs**: Many newborn screens refer only at about 35 dB, so mild cCMV-related loss can pass, and loss may begin after the screen. In the Dallas series, three-quarters of the infants with cCMV were found only because they had hearing loss. Outside the newborn window, suspect cCMV in a child with developmental delay, microcephaly and SNHL. Vision problems (strabismus, optic atrophy, chorioretinitis) occur in 10-20% of symptomatic infants, and chorioretinitis can appear late. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nongenetic Hearing Loss", p 517)

**Diagnosis after the newborn window**: Once the first weeks of life have passed, a positive PCR on the stored newborn dried blood spot can confirm that the infection was congenital, though dried-spot PCR is less sensitive than newborn saliva or urine testing. Brain imaging supports the diagnosis: intracranial (periventricular) calcifications, migration defects such as polymicrogyria, ventriculomegaly, white-matter disease and cerebral or cerebellar volume loss. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nongenetic Hearing Loss", p 517)

**Antiviral toxicity**: Ganciclovir and its oral prodrug valganciclovir are given for at least 6 weeks, and some evidence supports up to 6 months. The main toxicity is bone-marrow suppression (neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia), plus kidney and liver toxicity. Animal data raise concern about carcinogenesis or mutagenesis and gonadal toxicity, so blood counts are monitored. Hearing can still worsen after the drug is stopped. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nongenetic Hearing Loss", p 517)

**Other prenatal (TORCH) infections**: Today CMV is the only TORCH agent that causes much congenital hearing loss. *Toxoplasmosis* comes from undercooked meat or cat feces. About 85% of infected infants look well at birth. The classic signs are chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and intracranial calcifications. Treating the infant with pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine (with folinic acid) appears to lower the rate of SNHL. *Congenital rubella*: maternal infection in the first 11 weeks gives about a 90% risk of congenital rubella syndrome (cataracts, heart defects, SNHL). Affected infants can shed virus for up to a year. *Neonatal HSV* rarely causes SNHL, and only alongside severe CNS disease. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nongenetic Hearing Loss", p 516-518)

**Pediatric sudden hearing loss is often nonorganic**: In one series of children presenting with sudden hearing loss, 54% had pseudohypacusis. The mean age was about 10.5 years and most were girls. Among the true organic cases were EVA, multiple sclerosis, herpes virus and acoustic trauma, and the rest were idiopathic. Before starting steroids in a child, check for nonorganic loss: SRT-PTA mismatch, acoustic reflexes or OAEs present despite the claimed loss. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nongenetic Hearing Loss", p 522)

**Noise dose rule**: NIOSH recommends protection above 85 dBA and uses a 3-dB exchange rate: for every 3-dB rise above 85 dBA, the allowable exposure time is cut in half. (The OSHA regulatory limit uses 90 dBA with a 5-dB exchange rate.) Personal music players with earbuds can exceed 100 dBA. A common rule of thumb limits listening to about 60% volume for about 60 minutes a day. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nongenetic Hearing Loss", p 520-521)

**Synergy in the NICU and in oncology**: Cisplatin given together with temporal-bone radiation causes more SNHL than either alone, and the loss can appear years after treatment. In preterm infants under 27 weeks, aminoglycosides for 7 days or more combined with ventilator noise above 80 dB carried about a 68% risk of hearing loss. Macrolide ototoxicity is usually reversible once the drug is stopped. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nongenetic Hearing Loss", p 521, 523)

**Bilirubin and screening**: ANSD makes up as much as 10% of infant hearing loss. In late-preterm and term infants it can be the only sign of acute bilirubin neurotoxicity. Moderate bilirubin elevations in VLBW infants may also matter, and aggressive phototherapy has been linked to less hearing loss. An OAE-only screen will pass these infants. Diagnostic follow-up therefore needs both OAE and ABR, looking for a cochlear microphonic followed by an absent or disorganized ABR. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nongenetic Hearing Loss", p 515, 523)

**Week of developmental arrest (Jackler/Sennaroglu)**: Michel aplasia, 3rd week. Cochlear aplasia, late 3rd week. Common cavity, 4th week. Incomplete partition type I, 5th week. Cochlear hypoplasia, 6th week. IP-II (Mondini), 7th week. The otic placode appears in week 3 and the otocyst in week 4. The semicircular canals form in the order superior, then posterior, then lateral, so the lateral canal is the one most often malformed. The organ of Corti is complete at about week 25. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Inner Ear Anomalies", p 531-535)

**Semicircular canal and IAC anomalies**: Lateral semicircular canal dysplasia is the most common vestibular anomaly and is often called the second most common bony anomaly after EVA. About 40% of ears with a cochlear malformation also have semicircular canal dysplasia. CHARGE classically has absent semicircular canals. Trisomy 21 shows a small bony island of the lateral semicircular canal. A *narrow IAC* (2 mm or less) suggests an absent or hypoplastic cochlear nerve, which must be confirmed with oblique-sagittal MRI. A narrow IAC was found in 30% of syndromic vs 1.2% of nonsyndromic SNHL. A *wide or bulbous IAC* (over 8 mm) goes with X-linked mixed loss and stapes gusher. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nongenetic Hearing Loss", p 525-526) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Inner Ear Anomalies", p 536, 539-540)

**Recurrent meningitis means look at the inner ear**: Mondini/IP malformations, especially those with a dilated basal turn and stapes footplate or modiolar defects, predispose to CSF-perilymph leak and recurrent meningitis. The classic triad is CSF otorrhea (or rhinorrhea through the eustachian tube), a malformed temporal bone and recurrent meningitis. In any child with recurrent meningitis, image the temporal bones. Counsel parents of children with malformed ears about this meningitis risk and pneumococcal vaccination. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Inner Ear Anomalies", p 536, 540, 542)

**Temporal-bone signatures of syndromes**: *BOR* (EYA1, SIX1, SIX5) shows a hypoplastic apical cochlear turn, a funnel-shaped IAC, a facial nerve displaced medial to the cochlea, a patulous eustachian tube and malformed ossicles. *CHARGE* (CHD7 in about 70%) shows absent semicircular canals in essentially all patients, cochlear aperture atresia (about 77%), oval-window atresia (about 81%), dysplastic ossicles and an anomalous facial nerve. *X-linked POU3F4 (DFN3)* shows a dilated IAC, stapes fixation and a perilymph gusher during stapes or CI surgery. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nongenetic Hearing Loss", p 523)

**Congenital PLF in children**: When explored, the leak is usually at the oval window/stapes footplate (about 60%), less often the round window (about 30%). Middle-ear anomalies, especially of the stapes superstructure, are found in about 80%, and fistulas are bilateral about 30% of the time. In a prospective series of 244 children with unexplained SNHL, 6% had a PLF at exploration. Worsening hearing was the main symptom, and 11% had vertigo. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Inner Ear Anomalies", p 540-541)

**Outcome after pediatric exploration**: In a Pittsburgh series of 160 explored ears, hearing stabilized in 83.5% with a confirmed PLF and in 93% with no PLF found, and improved in only 8.7% vs 1.8%. This suggests that much of the apparent 'stabilization' is the natural history (as with EVA). Repair packs the window with fascia, muscle or areolar tissue. Beta-2 transferrin on the leaked fluid is neither fast enough nor reliable enough to use during surgery. Explore only after the etiologic workup is complete and the family has been counseled about the controversy. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Inner Ear Anomalies", p 540-541)

**Implanting malformed cochleae**: Common-cavity ears have an aberrant facial nerve in about 33%, and malformations in general raise the risk of CSF leak or gusher at the cochleostomy. A transmastoid labyrinthotomy approach has been described for common-cavity ears: it gives quick control of a leak and keeps away from an anomalous facial nerve. Taking out the incus widens facial-recess access. Manage a gusher by packing connective tissue around the electrode, with a lumbar drain if needed. Facial nerve monitoring is essential. Vertigo after surgery tends to scale with how much perilymph was lost and is self-limited. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Inner Ear Anomalies", p 541-542)

**Inner-ear and facial-nerve anomalies with atresia**: In 118 children with aural atresia, 22% had inner-ear anomalies and 13% had facial palsy. Every child with facial palsy also had an inner-ear anomaly, sometimes bilateral when the palsy was one-sided. Anterior displacement of the facial nerve at about 6 weeks blocks contact between the stapes and the otic capsule, which explains why congenital stapes malformations go with an aberrant facial nerve. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nongenetic Hearing Loss", p 523)

**Pediatric labeled criteria (and the current update)**: The book's FDA framework: children 12-24 months qualify with bilateral *profound* loss and lack of auditory progress with hearing aids, documented by parent questionnaires such as IT-MAIS. Children 2-17 years qualify with bilateral *severe-to-profound* loss and limited aided benefit (word recognition below about 30%). All need no medical contraindication and enrollment in an auditory-oral rehabilitation program. Labeling has since expanded: some devices are now FDA-approved from 9 months, and off-label implantation earlier than that is done for postmeningitic ossification. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Cochlear Implants in Children", p 549-550)

**Imaging for postmeningitic ears**: CT shows bony labyrinthitis ossificans but can miss the earlier *fibrous (sclerosing)* stage. Heavily T2-weighted MRI showing loss of the normal fluid signal in the cochlea shows that obstruction. Ossification is not a contraindication, but it limits electrode type and insertion depth. In a postmeningitic infant with a firm diagnosis, no response to sound, and early fibrosis or ossification on imaging, many centers shorten or skip the hearing-aid trial and implant before 12 months. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Cochlear Implants in Children", p 550-551)

**Who does well**: Children deafened after about age 5 (postlingual) are excellent candidates if implanted soon. A long gap is harmful: in one reported case, a child implanted 10 years after deafness never gained listening-only speech understanding. Congenitally deaf adolescents who rely on sign language and have little auditory experience are at high risk of not using the device. Consistent hearing-aid users with an oral communication style do best. In multivariate analysis (Geers), the strongest child factor was nonverbal intelligence, and the strongest educational factor was an oral rather than a total-communication program. Children with prior motor or cognitive delays progress more slowly. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Cochlear Implants in Children", p 550, 555)

**Ossified cochlea options**: In about half of postmeningitic children, new bone blocks the round window. Make the cochleostomy anterior to the round window and drill forward until an open scala tympani is found, which usually allows a full insertion. If the scala tympani is completely obliterated: (1) drill a tunnel about 6 mm into the basal turn for a partial insertion (10-12 active electrodes), (2) use a split or double array with the second branch through a cochleostomy just anterior to the oval window, (3) do a Gantz-style drill-out of the basal turn, or (4) insert into the scala vestibuli, which is often ossified too. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Cochlear Implants in Children", p 549, 553)

**Infant temporal bone**: The cochlea is adult-sized at birth. By about 6 months the mastoid antrum and facial recess are developed enough for the standard approach, and growth of the skull after implantation has not caused problems. Two aberrant facial nerve courses threaten CI surgery: a vertical (mastoid) segment displaced laterally and anteriorly, and a nerve running over the promontory or anterior to the round window. A suprameatal (transcanal tunnel) approach that avoids the facial recess has been described for these cases. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Cochlear Implants in Children", p 552-553)

**Ear disease around an implant**: An uninfected middle-ear effusion in an already implanted ear needs no treatment. Treat acute otitis media promptly. Delayed mastoiditis with a postauricular abscess has been handled with incision and drainage plus IV antibiotics, without removing the device. A prior open mastoid cavity is not a contraindication, but it usually calls for mastoid obliteration with blind-sac closure of the canal or reconstruction of the posterior canal wall. Chronic suppurative otitis media or cholesteatoma must be cleared first. Gushers from IP-II or EVA are controlled with a small cochleostomy, tight fascial packing around the electrode, eustachian tube occlusion and, rarely, a lumbar drain. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Cochlear Implants in Children", p 551, 553-554)

**Epidemiology and teratogens**: Microtia occurs in about 0.03% of births. Moderate-to-severe atresia occurs in roughly 1-5 per 20,000. Both are more common in boys, unilateral more often than bilateral, and right-sided more often than left. Most cases are sporadic. Associated conditions include hemifacial microsomia/Goldenhar (oculoauriculovertebral spectrum: epibulbar dermoids, vertebral anomalies), Treacher Collins and Möbius. Teratogens include *isotretinoin*, which causes major malformations in about 25% of first-trimester exposures, with anotia or microtia, a large vestibular aqueduct, CNS and cardiac defects. *Thalidomide* causes ear anomalies in about 20% of affected children, and about 75% of those have moderate-to-profound SNHL. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Anomalies of the External and Middle Ears", p 564, 566, 579-580)

**Atresia severity groups (Altmann)**: Group 1 (mild): a hypoplastic but present canal with a small drum and a normal or small middle ear. Group 2 (moderate): no canal, a partly or completely bony atresia plate, and a small middle ear with deformed contents. Group 3 (severe): no canal and a markedly hypoplastic or absent middle-ear cavity. Atresia is more often bony than membranous. The descending facial nerve is typically displaced anteriorly and laterally, and the chorda tympani often has an anomalous course. The conductive loss is maximal and nonprogressive, with a variable sensorineural component. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Anomalies of the External and Middle Ears", p 564)

**Congenital stapes fixation vs otosclerosis**: A congenital ossicular anomaly gives a *nonprogressive*, flat, moderate-to-severe conductive or mixed loss with a normal drum from early childhood. Otosclerosis gives a *progressive* loss that begins in adolescence or adulthood. Congenital causes include footplate fixation, an ossified stapedius tendon, and incus-stapes nonunion or fibrous union. Absence of the oval window is often found with an inferiorly displaced facial nerve running over the window niche. Before any stapes surgery in a child, image for an X-linked POU3F4 IAC/cochlear defect (bulbous lateral IAC, thin bone between the IAC and the vestibule), because it predicts a perilymph-CSF gusher. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Anomalies of the External and Middle Ears", p 563, 568, 576, 584)

**Congenital cholesteatoma and unilateral atresia burden**: Congenital cholesteatoma behind an atresia plate is reported in up to about 4-7% (most often with canal *stenosis*). Get a CT even if repair is not planned, and repeat it several years later. Cholesteatoma, or chronic suppurative otitis refractory to IV antibiotics, is an indication for surgery even when the anatomy is poor for hearing. In unilateral atresia, about 65% of school-aged children needed extra school services (IEP 48%, speech therapy 48%, FM system 33%). Use a lower threshold for tympanostomy tubes in the normal ear, which is the only hearing ear. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Surgical Management of Microtia and Congenital Aural Atresia", p 597-598)

**Schuknecht A-D classification**: Type A is meatal stenosis from incomplete canalization, which can trap squamous debris and form a canal cholesteatoma. The middle ear is normal, and canalplasty is done if the stenosis is severe. Type B is more extensive canal stenosis with more middle-ear anomalies, also treated by canalplasty with a split-thickness graft. Type C is complete atresia with a well-pneumatized middle ear and a favorable facial nerve, and is the classic atresiaplasty candidate. Type D is complete atresia with poor pneumatization and major ossicular/facial nerve anomalies, and is usually not repaired. Use stricter selection criteria for unilateral than for bilateral cases. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Surgical Management of Microtia and Congenital Aural Atresia", p 611-612)

**Atresiaplasty principles (Jahrsdoerfer anterior approach)**: In bilateral atresia, operate first on the *better-hearing ear with the more favorable anatomy* (the opposite of chronic-ear practice). Also favor an ear with a partial canal or plate, because the remaining bone is a landmark. Drill anterior (toward the TMJ) and superior (toward the middle fossa dura, identified but not exposed), because the facial nerve is least likely to be there. Enter through the attic, thin the atresia plate to eggshell with diamond burrs, and lift it off with picks, because the fused malleus-incus complex is attached to it and transmits drill energy. Make the new canal up to about 15 mm wide. Line it with a thin split-thickness skin graft over a temporalis-fascia drum, use a silastic disc to keep the graft medial, and create a generous meatus. Keeping the native ossicular chain gives better hearing and fewer revisions than ossiculoplasty. If no stapes or oval window is found, stop the procedure. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Surgical Management of Microtia and Congenital Aural Atresia", p 610-614)

**Demographics and grading**: In Brent's series of 1200 patients, 58% were right-sided, 32% left-sided and 9% bilateral, and 63% were male. Associated findings were facial asymmetry (36.5%), facial nerve weakness (15%) and cleft lip or palate (4%). Up to 40% of children called 'isolated microtia' actually have hemifacial microsomia and need craniofacial, ophthalmic and dental review. Grade I is a small ear with most landmarks present. Grade II is a smaller ear with poorly defined scapha, fossa and antihelix. Grade III is a peanut- or sausage-shaped vestige with a lobule. Grade IV is anotia. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Surgical Management of Microtia and Congenital Aural Atresia", p 595)

**Brent first-stage details**: Harvest the 6th-7th rib synchondrosis for the base and the 8th and floating 9th ribs for the helix, from the side *opposite* the ear, because the rib curvature gives better projection. Keep a 3-4 mm upper rim of the 6th rib and spare the rectus abdominis to reduce chest-wall deformity. Carve the framework about 3 mm smaller than the template (film traced from the normal ear) to allow for skin thickness. Place it level with the normal ear, at the same distance from the lateral canthus, with its long axis tilted about 30 degrees (parallel to the nasal dorsum). Coapt the skin with suction drains, not bolster sutures. Later stages include lobule transposition, elevation with a postauricular graft, and tragus construction, at least 2-3 months apart. Atresiaplasty follows the auricle so that the skin is undisturbed, unless a porous polyethylene/TPF reconstruction is used. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Surgical Management of Microtia and Congenital Aural Atresia", p 600-603, 609)

**Complications and salvage**: Small areas of flap loss heal with local care. Larger cartilage exposure needs a temporoparietal fascia flap with a full-thickness skin graft (or an innominate fascia flap if the TPF has already been used). Infection may show only as mild redness and swelling, and is treated with IV antibiotics and catheter irrigation under the flap. Pleural tears during rib harvest are closed over a catheter under positive pressure, and a chest tube is needed only if the visceral pleura is injured. Indications for a prosthetic ear include family preference, a low hairline, prior radiation or cancer resection, poor soft tissue, coagulopathy and failed reconstruction. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Surgical Management of Microtia and Congenital Aural Atresia", p 601, 608-609)

**Imaging in children and nuclear scans**: In young children, bone erosion on CT may be absent because the tympanic bone is underdeveloped. Loss of fat planes below the temporal bone and in the parapharyngeal space and infratemporal fossa is the key CT sign of skull-base involvement. Technetium-99m bone scan is sensitive but stays positive indefinitely, so it cannot show when to stop therapy. Gallium-67 tracks active inflammation and has been used, with ESR, to decide when to stop, though relapses have occurred after a normal gallium scan. About 62% of adult cases followed tap-water ear irrigation within the preceding 2 weeks. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the External Ear", p 626-627)

**Pediatric antibiotic choices**: Classic IV regimens are an antipseudomonal penicillin plus an aminoglycoside (with drug levels and audiograms monitored), or ceftazidime alone, with imipenem or aztreonam as alternatives. Fluoroquinolones are not labeled for routine pediatric use because of arthropathy in juvenile animals. However, the AAP (2006) lists NOE among the appropriate pediatric indications, and only reversible arthralgia has been seen. Children who respond early may need only 2-3 weeks of treatment, compared with 4-6 weeks or more in adults. Hyperbaric oxygen is reserved for refractory disease. Surgery is limited to debridement of granulation tissue, sequestra and abscesses, and biopsy to exclude cancer. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the External Ear", p 627)

**Neomycin contact dermatitis and chronic otitis externa**: If AOE gets worse on neomycin-containing drops, with more redness, itching and excoriation, suspect allergic contact dermatitis. Neomycin is the most common topical sensitizer. Stop the neomycin and switch to a fluoroquinolone (with or without steroid) drop. Avoid other aminoglycoside drops, which cross-react with neomycin. Chronic otitis externa (itch-scratch cycle) responds to frequent cleaning plus topical fluorinated steroids. The differential includes otomycosis, seborrheic dermatitis, psoriasis, contact dermatitis and canal carcinoma. Long-standing disease can cause *pachyderma*, a thickened, stenotic canal with a blunted anterior sulcus, which requires canalplasty with a split-thickness graft. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the External Ear", p 624-625, 628)

**Perichondritis vs auricular hematoma**: Perichondritis follows high (helical or scaphal) piercing, acupuncture, surgery, burns or frostbite. It is usually caused by *P. aeruginosa* or *S. aureus*, spares the lobule (which has no cartilage), and in children needs IV antipseudomonal therapy. Drain any collection, because suppuration destroys cartilage and leaves a cauliflower ear. A traumatic hematoma or seroma (wrestling, boxing) is aspirated or incised under sterile conditions, followed by a contoured bolster sutured through the ear and frequent rechecks for reaccumulation. Relapsing polychondritis also spares the lobule, but it is recurrent and bilateral, involves the nose, larynx or trachea and joints, and is treated with steroids. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the External Ear", p 628-629)

**Earlobe keloid after piercing**: The keloid usually sits on the medial (posterior) lobule with a core along the piercing tract to a small lateral opening. Excise the whole core sharply. Close the lateral defect simply and the medial defect in two layers, injecting triamcinolone into the subcutaneous tissue before closure. Follow with a few weekly triamcinolone injections to reduce recurrence. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the External Ear", p 630)

**Topical regimen**: Keratosis obturans is usually bilateral and seen in young and middle-aged patients. Removing a long-standing cast can be painful and may need repeated sessions. Between debridements, agents that slow epithelial turnover or soften the keratin reduce how fast it builds up: steroid drops, mineral oil, acetic-acid rinses, a betamethasone-urea preparation, and topical 5-fluorouracil. Under the cast the canal skin looks shiny, red and atrophic. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the External Ear", p 622)

**Natural history of post-AOM effusion**: After treatment, 30-70% of children still have middle-ear effusion. The mean duration is about 23 days, and only 6-26% still have fluid 3 months after the acute episode. Do not retreat an asymptomatic child for persistent effusion, because this drives resistance. Most children still have fluid at a 10-14-day visit, so that visit is useful only if symptoms persist. A 2-3-month check identifies chronic OME. 'Relapse' (the same signs within 4 days of finishing therapy) counts as treatment failure. 'Recurrence' at 5-14 days is usually a new infection. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otitis Media and Eustachian Tube Dysfunction", p 695-696, 702-703)

**Epidemiology and risk factors**: AOM incidence peaks at 6-13 months, and the first episode most often occurs around 6 months. By age 3, children fall into roughly equal thirds: no infections, occasional infections, and otitis-prone. In one cohort, 46% had 3 or more episodes and 16% had 6 or more by age 3. An early first episode predicts recurrent disease and may signal an underlying anatomic or immune defect (submucous cleft, immunoglobulin subclass deficiency). Risk factors are male sex, genetic susceptibility, daycare (31% of daycare children had tubes vs 11% cared for at home), parental smoking, pacifier use, not breastfeeding, supine bottle feeding, and the respiratory season. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otitis Media and Eustachian Tube Dysfunction", p 657, 661, 663-664, 667, 670, 728)

**Tympanocentesis and myringotomy indications**: Perform diagnostic tympanocentesis, followed by myringotomy for drainage, in these situations: a toxic or critically ill child; a suppurative complication (mastoiditis, facial palsy, labyrinthitis, meningitis), where a tube is also placed; failure of appropriate antibiotics with persistent pain or fever; AOM that develops while the child is already taking an effective antibiotic; neonatal AOM; and an immunocompromised host. Severe otalgia is also an indication for myringotomy. Randomized trials showed that routine myringotomy, alone or added to antibiotics, did not improve outcomes, and myringotomy with placebo did worse than antibiotics. The incision should span both inferior quadrants. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otitis Media and Eustachian Tube Dysfunction", p 694-695, 724-725)

**Prevention for the otitis-prone child**: Offer the conjugate pneumococcal vaccine and annual influenza vaccine (both reduce AOM). Address modifiable risks: smoke exposure, pacifier use, and large-group daycare. For early-onset or severe recurrent disease, look for an underlying cause: submucous cleft palate, nasopharyngeal obstruction or tumor, allergy, sinusitis, and humoral or cellular immune defects. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otitis Media and Eustachian Tube Dysfunction", p 696-697)

**Retained tube removal and refractory otorrhea**: Consider removing a retained tube at about age 6 or older when the other ear has been disease-free for a year or more (ET function is usually symmetric in children, but not in adults). Also consider removal for recurrent otorrhea, chronic otorrhea, or a tube embedded in refractory granulation tissue. Freshen the edges and patch the defect (paper or Steri-Strip). Tubes retained for 2 years or more in children 7 years or older have high complication rates. For otorrhea that fails drops, culture the aspirate: the usual AOM organisms are found in winter and in infants, Pseudomonas in summer and in older children. Most refractory cases clear with culture-directed IV antibiotics, without mastoidectomy. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otitis Media and Eustachian Tube Dysfunction", p 729-731)

**Barotrauma prevention in children**: Functional ET obstruction causes symptoms only on *descent*, when active swallowing is needed to open the tube. Infants often cry on descent, which inflates the ear. Children who already have bilateral effusion usually have no pain when flying and need no preparation. For a child with ETD or recurrent AOM but no effusion, give an oral decongestant before the flight and oxymetazoline sprays just before descent. Children with tubes in place have no problem. Avoid scuba diving in children with chronic ETD or otitis because of the risk of severe vertigo. Obstructive ETD is common around puberty, especially in girls, and is typically worse on waking. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otitis Media and Eustachian Tube Dysfunction", p 699-701)

**Pediatric patulous ET**: Patulous ET is uncommon in children. It is usually idiopathic or follows rapid weight loss or interruption of tensor veli palatini innervation (surgery or trauma), and in adolescents it is usually self-limited with growth. Confirm it with the patient sitting: the drum moves with breathing, and the tympanogram trace fluctuates with respiration (exaggerated by sniffing with one nostril occluded), with the fluctuation stopping on breath-holding. Tympanostomy tubes may help, through coexisting obstruction, or may worsen symptoms. Irreversible bulking or caustic treatments are discouraged. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otitis Media and Eustachian Tube Dysfunction", p 699-700)

**Pediatric presentation and mimics**: In a Pittsburgh series of 72 children, half were 3 years old or younger. The common findings were otalgia (86%), postauricular tenderness (81%), pinna protrusion and postauricular redness (71%) and fever (71%). Only about two-thirds had a visible middle-ear effusion, because mastoid infection can persist after the middle ear clears. Differentiate it from perichondritis or otitis externa spreading behind the ear, which *obliterate* the postauricular crease, whereas the crease is usually preserved in early mastoiditis with periosteitis. A postauricular lymph node (from a scalp infection or insect bite) is discrete, mobile and nontender, with a normal middle ear. A subperiosteal abscess is fixed, poorly defined, tender and pushes the pinna down and forward. Sagging of the posterosuperior canal wall suggests osteitis. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Complications and Sequelae of Otitis Media", p 788-791)

**Microbiology and spread routes**: The organisms were S. pneumoniae 32%, P. aeruginosa 29% (more often with prior otorrhea or recurrent AOM) and S. pyogenes 19%, with anaerobes in about 11%. TB and atypical mycobacteria are rare causes. Coalescent pus can drain back through the aditus (and resolve), break through the lateral cortex (subperiosteal abscess), track into the zygomatic root (pre- or supra-auricular abscess), go through the tip deep to the SCM (*Bezold abscess*), extend posteriorly into the occipital bone (*Citelli abscess*, calvarial osteomyelitis), or pass medially into petrous cells (petrositis). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Complications and Sequelae of Otitis Media", p 789-791)

**Pediatric petrositis facts**: Only about 30% of people have a well-pneumatized petrous apex, and the apex does not pneumatize before about age 3. Acute petrositis (pneumococcus, H. influenzae, GAS) is now rare. Chronic petrous osteomyelitis from CSOM or cholesteatoma (Pseudomonas, Proteus, TB) is more common and does not need pneumatized cells, because it spreads by thrombophlebitis or osteitis. The full Gradenigo triad (retro-orbital pain from V1, otorrhea, CN VI palsy) is often incomplete, and abducens palsy is a late sign. Suspect it when purulent drainage persists after a simple mastoidectomy. All four Pittsburgh cases resolved with IV antibiotics and cortical mastoidectomy without opening the apex. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Complications and Sequelae of Otitis Media", p 796-797)

**Schuknecht classification and portal of entry**: Labyrinthitis is classified as serous (toxic, no bacteria in the labyrinth), suppurative (otogenic bacterial invasion), or meningogenic (spread from the subarachnoid space), with labyrinthitis ossificans as the end stage. The usual tympanogenic portal is the round window, less often the oval window, a congenital defect, a fracture or a surgical defect. Serous labyrinthitis is common in otitis media and hits the cochlea (basal turn, high frequencies) more than the vestibule. This explains the high-frequency bone-conduction loss seen in ears with chronic otitis media. In a child with recurrent meningitis after AOM, look for a CSF/perilymph fistula at the oval or round window and repair it. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Complications and Sequelae of Otitis Media", p 797-798, 830)

**Pediatric staging and follow-up**: Preserve the posterior canal wall in children whenever possible. When the drum is preserved or reconstructed, plan a second look (exploratory tympanotomy with or without mastoidotomy) at about 6 months, because older CT/MRI could not replace it. Non-EPI DWI MRI now reduces the need for routine second-look surgery in selected patients. Control the underlying ET dysfunction with cartilage tympanoplasty and/or tubes, and treat adenoid, allergy or sinus disease. Follow for 5-7 years, and examine the *opposite* ear regularly for new retractions. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Complications and Sequelae of Otitis Media", p 817-818)

**CSOM without cholesteatoma in children**: Pseudomonas was isolated in 38 of 40 children with CSOM, often with S. aureus. Treat in steps: aural toilet with daily suction and a topical quinolone, then add an oral agent, then admit for a parenteral antipseudomonal beta-lactam (ceftazidime, or, when S. aureus is also present, the book's ticarcillin-clavulanate, which is no longer marketed in the US and is usually replaced by piperacillin-tazobactam) with daily aspiration and drops. This usually avoids mastoidectomy. Surgery is reserved for failures, cholesteatoma or complications. Persistent drainage despite this regimen suggests hidden cholesteatoma. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Complications and Sequelae of Otitis Media", p 784, 830) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otitis Media and Eustachian Tube Dysfunction", p 677)

**Pediatric chronic perforation and tympanoplasty timing**: A dry perforation ventilates the ear but removes the protective middle-ear gas cushion, so the ear is exposed to water contamination and nasopharyngeal reflux. Pediatric myringoplasty or tympanoplasty succeeds in about 80% of children older than about 5-6 years. One series favored repair after age 6 rather than delaying further, to limit inner-ear damage. Tube-related perforations needing tympanoplasty were about 2.4% in the Pittsburgh trials, and higher with long-term tubes. Weigh contralateral ear status and ET function when timing repair. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Complications and Sequelae of Otitis Media", p 772-773)

**Blue eardrum and tympanosclerosis**: In a child, a blue drum is most often an ordinary effusion. Middle-ear cholesterol granuloma is a rare sequela of chronic OME and is not caused by blood (so 'idiopathic hemotympanum' is a misnomer). The differential includes a dehiscent high jugular bulb and glomus tympanicum or jugulare. Myringosclerosis is common after recurrent otitis, healed perforations and tubes, and does not affect hearing. Tympanosclerosis involving the ossicles takes years to develop and is rare in young children (only 20% of cases were in people 30 years old or younger). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Complications and Sequelae of Otitis Media", p 818-820)

**Unexpected facial palsy after ear surgery**: The facial nerve is most often injured at the second genu, then at the anterior epitympanum. If the patient wakes with a paralysis, wait about 2 hours for local anesthetic to wear off and loosen the mastoid dressing. If the nerve was clearly seen and intact (or only its sheath was breached and decompressed), do not explore. If immediate complete paralysis follows surgery in which the nerve was *not* identified, exploration is mandatory, and it can be planned for the next day. At exploration, decompress several millimeters proximal and distal to the injury. A frayed sheath with intact contents needs decompression only. A transected nerve is freshened and repaired primarily or with an interposition graft. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Facial Paralysis in Children", p 863)

**Electrodiagnostic timing**: MST and ENoG are useful from about 3 days to 2-3 weeks, because a cut nerve still conducts distally for 48-72 hours. EMG fibrillations appear at only 10-21 days, but volitional motor-unit potentials on EMG mean the nerve is intact despite an absent ENoG response (deblocking). Fisch's criteria for surgical exposure are ENoG 10% or less of normal within 6 days for trauma, within 2 weeks for Bell palsy, and despite drainage and antibiotics for AOM. Gantz found no benefit from middle fossa decompression after 14 days. Incomplete palsy with ENoG above 10% after day 14 gives about 90% satisfactory recovery. Complete palsy with ENoG of 10% or less in the first 14 days gives under 50%. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Facial Paralysis in Children", p 857-858)

**Pediatric fracture-related facial palsy**: In a series of 1015 children with head injury, 71 had temporal bone fractures and 21% of these had facial paralysis. Transverse fractures cause palsy in up to 50%. Children can keep good tone and eye closure despite a transected nerve, so examine carefully. With immediate complete palsy, follow with serial ENoG. Stable function above 10% for 5 days predicts a good outcome, while rapid decline is an indication to explore. Decompress from the meatal segment to the stylomastoid foramen: translabyrinthine if hearing is dead, combined transmastoid-middle fossa if hearing is intact. Be prepared for grafting (sural or great auricular nerve), TM, ossicular and CSF repair. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Facial Paralysis in Children", p 862-863)

**Reinnervation timing**: Repair a sharp transection by tension-free direct anastomosis as early as possible. Distal branches can be found with a stimulator only within about 72 hours. In a contaminated facial wound, tag the distal stumps and repair within about 3 weeks, which gives results equal to immediate repair. Repair can still succeed for several months, but results are poor after 1 year because of distal fibrosis and muscle atrophy. In congenital paralysis, or when muscle is absent, defer dynamic reconstruction until facial growth is complete or use muscle transfer. In children the lower lid usually keeps good tone and ectropion is rare. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Facial Paralysis in Children", p 863, 865-866)

**Stapes surgery in children and in OI**: Pediatric stapedectomy is safe and effective. Many surgeons wait until the child can take part in the decision (because of the small risk of a dead ear) and until otitis media has settled. Waiting too long, however, risks obliterative footplate disease. In osteogenesis imperfecta, the crura are fragile and may be fractured, the malleus may be fractured or ankylosed to the scutum, and the footplate thickened. Stapedectomy is possible but the long-term results are worse, so handle the ossicles very gently. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the Labyrinthine Capsule", p 870-872)

**Pediatric Ménière disease is rare**: Ménière disease accounted for only about 2.9% of children evaluated for vertigo. More than half of pediatric vertigo was due to otitis media, vestibular neuronitis, benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood or migraine. Still consider Ménière disease when vertigo comes with aural fullness, fluctuating hearing loss and tinnitus. Children with vestibular symptoms plus SNHL after temporal bone trauma (especially oval window involvement) may have a perilymph fistula, and the vertigo may improve after repair even though the SNHL rarely does. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the Labyrinthine Capsule", p 869, 874)

**Postmeningitic ossification specifics**: Bacteria spread from the meninges through the cochlear aqueduct, which opens into the basal turn of the scala tympani near the round window. That is where ossification is most severe, and it keeps advancing for years. The risk is highest after *S. pneumoniae* meningitis, in males, and when intracranial pressure was raised. Early fibrous or osteoid obliteration is missed on CT and is seen as loss of fluid signal on high-resolution T2 fast-spin-echo MRI. Monitor postmeningitic children with progressive loss closely with imaging, so they can be implanted before the cochlea ossifies. Basal-turn drill-out allows insertion in ossified cochleae. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the Labyrinthine Capsule", p 873-874)

**Pediatric fracture specifics**: Temporal bone fractures occur in 18-40% of skull fractures. Only about 2.5-5.6% violate the otic capsule, and fewer than 20% of pediatric fractures leave permanent SNHL. Facial palsy occurs in 5-33% of children with temporal bone fractures (less often than in adults, possibly because the skull is less ossified). CSF fistula occurs in 10-30% of children, similar to adults. Hemotympanum is seen in 20-65% of temporal bone fractures and TM perforation in 20-50%. In one series of 115 children with traumatic facial weakness, *55% had an upper-motor-neuron (central) cause*, with lower-face predominance and preserved emotional movement. Older head CTs missed up to a third of fractures. Battle sign appears at 4-5 days. Never irrigate a traumatized ear. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Injuries of the Ear and Temporal Bone", p 884-888, 890, 892) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the Labyrinthine Capsule", p 869)

**Immediate complete traumatic palsy**: Electrical tests are misleading for the first 48-72 hours, so obtain high-resolution CT and an audiogram and explore as soon as the patient is stable. Remove bone spicules, incise the sheath, and graft immediately if the nerve is lacerated. The nerve is usually injured in the perigeniculate/horizontal segment. Use transmastoid exposure for the perigeniculate region to the stylomastoid foramen, translabyrinthine exposure when hearing is gone, and middle fossa exposure for the labyrinthine/IAC segment when hearing and the ossicular chain are intact. For delayed or incomplete palsy, follow with serial electrical testing. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Injuries of the Ear and Temporal Bone", p 892)

**Traumatic perforation details**: Common mechanisms are an open-hand slap, a blast or firecracker, water impact (diving, water-skiing), a cotton swab, and irrigation of hard cerumen. The loss is usually 20-40 dB conductive. For a fresh perforation, the inverted edges can be unfolded and supported on Gelfoam. If edges have epithelialized, mechanical freshening with a fat or paper myringoplasty healed 87% vs 67% with trichloroacetic acid cautery. A *paper patch test* helps separate the perforation's share of the loss from ossicular injury: if hearing does not improve with the patch, suspect discontinuity. CT shows incus or malleus dislocation in about 90%. Explore urgently for SNHL with vertigo (stapes subluxation or a round window tear, sealed with tissue) or for immediate facial paralysis. Defer elective tympanoplasty in children with active ET problems. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Injuries of the Ear and Temporal Bone", p 881-883)

**Aural foreign bodies and button batteries**: Children commonly put beads, paper, food and insects in the ear canal. A neglected object causes otorrhea and granulation that can mimic chronic mastoid disease and will not clear with antibiotics until it is removed. A button battery in the ear canal is an emergency: current leak and alkaline electrolyte cause liquefactive necrosis, so remove it immediately and *never irrigate*. Use general anesthesia for a wedged object or an uncooperative child, because a sudden movement risks TM and ossicular injury. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Injuries of the Ear and Temporal Bone", p 880-881)

**Acute auricular trauma**: Irrigate lacerations and avulsions copiously. Cover exposed cartilage with local flaps or skin grafts, reconstruct the canal and meatus first, and align the helical rim and tragus precisely. Partial avulsions usually survive because the blood supply is rich. A complete avulsion can be reattached immediately (microvascular when feasible; leeches or anticoagulation help venous congestion; avoid pressure dressings and cool the part). If reattachment is impossible, the cartilage can be de-skinned and banked in a postauricular pocket. Treat a hematoma by aspiration or incision with a through-and-through bolster or stent. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Injuries of the Ear and Temporal Bone", p 879-880)

**Temporal bone fibrous dysplasia management and leukemia**: Fibrous dysplasia starts around age 10. It is monostotic in about 70%, and CT shows ground glass with the otic capsule 'floating'. *Never irradiate it*: radiation raises the sarcoma risk about 400-fold, against a baseline malignant change of about 1 in 200. Treat conservatively and recontour bone only for function or deformity. For canal stenosis, transcanal canalplasty restenosed in 89%, whereas postauricular canalplasty with (usually canal-wall-down) mastoidectomy, an oversized canal, skin grafting and a meatoplasty had no restenosis. *Leukemia* involves the temporal bone in about 20% (infiltration, hemorrhage, infection) and can present as otitis or mastoiditis. It is treated by treating the leukemia. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Ear and Temporal Bone", p 905-908)

**Epidemiology**: In adults about 90% of primary tracheal tumors are malignant, whereas in children about 80% are benign. SCC and adenoid cystic carcinoma together make up roughly 75% of primary malignancies. Tracheal SCC is smoking-related (about 90%), with synchronous or metachronous respiratory tract cancers in about 30%. An SCC centered on the membranous wall should raise concern for invasion from an esophageal primary. (Cummings 7e, Ch 112, p 1719)

**CT clues**: A lesion that is intraluminal, smooth, well circumscribed and under 2 cm favors a benign tumor. Calcification suggests carcinoid, chondroma or chondrosarcoma, and intense homogeneous enhancement suggests carcinoid. Size over 2 cm, an irregular surface, circumferential or long-segment involvement, mediastinal extension and nodes favor malignancy. CT underestimates submucosal spread, especially in ACC. Because ACC pushes structures aside rather than invading them, loss of fat planes predicts invasion poorly. (Cummings 7e, Ch 112, p 1721) (Cummings 7e, Ch 112, p 1722)

**Staging and bronchoscopy**: There is no AJCC/UICC staging system for tracheal tumors. A proposed SEER-based TNM uses T1 = confined to the trachea and <2 cm, T2 = confined and >2 cm, T3 = beyond the trachea but not into adjacent organs, and T4 = into adjacent organs. Rigid bronchoscopy is preferred for subtotal obstruction because it ventilates, cores out and tamponades. Carcinoids bleed briskly and are best biopsied rigidly in the OR. (Cummings 7e, Ch 112, p 1720) (Cummings 7e, Ch 112, p 1722) (Cummings 7e, Ch 112, p 1723)

**Secondary tracheal involvement**: Of the cancers that invade the trachea directly, only lung and thyroid cancer offer cure by resection. For thyroid cancer, options include shaving versus segmental resection. Complete resection gave about 78% 5-year survival versus 44% for incomplete resection in one series. Esophageal, mediastinal and head and neck cancers invading the trachea are treated palliatively. Anaplastic thyroid cancer and lymphoma involving the trachea should not be resected. (Cummings 7e, Ch 112, p 1720) (Cummings 7e, Ch 112, p 1721)

**ACC follow-up**: ACC can recur locally or distantly up to 30 years after treatment. Surveillance bronchoscopy is advised annually for life. Its apparently better 5-year survival than SCC (SEER about 74% vs 13%) may partly reflect slow tumor growth rather than cure. (Cummings 7e, Ch 112, p 1719) (Cummings 7e, Ch 112, p 1724)

**Cervical teratoma**: This is a germ cell tumor with all three germ layers. It is usually detected on prenatal ultrasound as a mixed mass with calcification, cysts and fat; calcification within a neonatal neck mass strongly suggests teratoma. Rapid growth can obstruct the airway, and prenatal evidence of airway compression may call for an EXIT procedure. Associations include cleft lip/palate, trisomies 13 and 21, Klinefelter and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndromes, and cardiac defects. Dermoid cysts, by contrast, have only ectoderm and mesoderm, sit in the midline, and are mostly diagnosed before age 3. (Cummings 7e, Ch 113, p 1734)

**Non-SCC unknown primary**: When a neck node shows adenocarcinoma or undifferentiated carcinoma, stain for thyroglobulin, PAX8, TTF-1 and calcitonin to look for a thyroid primary. If these are negative and the node is in levels I-III, suspect a salivary primary (neck dissection with or without parotidectomy). Nodes in levels IV-V point to an infraclavicular source (lung, esophagus, kidney, ovary, cervix, prostate). (Cummings 7e, Ch 115, p 1765)

**Melanoma of unknown primary**: About 2-3% of melanomas present without a primary. Stage for stage, these patients do better than those with a known primary, possibly because of immune regression. Treatment is comprehensive neck dissection with adjuvant RT and/or immunotherapy, plus full skin surveillance. (Cummings 7e, Ch 115, p 1765)

**Yield numbers**: PET/CT found the primary with about 62% sensitivity and 82% specificity in a 190-patient series. A stepwise approach for p16-positive nodes has a reported 80-90% detection rate: direct laryngoscopy, then ipsilateral palatine tonsillectomy with frozen section, then ipsilateral base-of-tongue resection (TORS) if the tonsil is negative. A diagnosis of SCC arising in a branchial cyst requires strict criteria, including no primary found after 5 years of follow-up. In adults, assume a cystic node is metastasis from a Waldeyer ring primary. (Cummings 7e, Ch 115, p 1765) (Cummings 7e, Ch 115, p 1773)

**US pearls**: A comet-tail artifact indicates inspissated colloid, a benign finding. In a multinodular gland, biopsy the nodule with the most suspicious features rather than simply the largest one, unless all nodules look very low risk. (Cummings 7e, Ch 114, p 1741)

**Nodal US and surveillance**: Suspicious nodes are round, hypoechoic, have lost the echogenic hilum, and contain microcalcifications or cystic change. Nodal spread mainly involves levels III, IV and VI, but can reach level II along the superior thyroid pedicle and level V along the transverse cervical vessels. Neck US is the most sensitive imaging test for recurrence; a patient is called disease free only when US is negative and tumor marker (thyroglobulin) is undetectable. (Cummings 7e, Ch 114, p 1742) (Cummings 7e, Ch 114, p 1744)

**Normal node size on US**: Normal nodes are ovoid and hypoechoic, have an echogenic hilum, and usually measure 5-6 mm or less in short axis. Jugulodigastric (Kuttner) nodes behind the submandibular gland can reach about 15 mm short axis and still be normal if the hilum is preserved. Intraparotid nodes are normal because the parotid encapsulates late in embryogenesis, and a hilum distinguishes them from tumors. (Cummings 7e, Ch 114, p 1747)

**Risk numbers**: Dissect in the periadventitial plane with proximal and distal control, and dissect the bifurcation last. Routine shunting is not advised. In Anand's 1181-case review, ICA ligation carried about 66% CNS morbidity and 46% mortality, versus 3% after simple repair. Contemporary stroke rates are 2% or less. Cranial nerve injury occurs in about 24% (vagus 11%, hypoglossal 10%, SLN 5%), and risk rises about 1.5-fold for each 1 cm closer to the skull base. If embolization is used, operate 24-48 h later; embolization stroke risk is 0-2%. Consider balloon test occlusion for large tumors. (Cummings 7e, Ch 115, p 1760)

**RT and observation**: Fractionated RT gives about 94-97% local control. It stops growth but shrinks only about a quarter of tumors. Its risks include carotid atherosclerosis and radiation-induced malignancy, so it is usually reserved for older or poor-risk patients. Untreated carotid PGLs grow slowly. Jansen found a median doubling time of about 7 years, and Farr's older estimate was about 2 cm per 5 years, but serial-imaging series show growth nearer 1 mm per year, and many tumors do not grow at all. About one third of observed patients develop new cranial neuropathies. (Cummings 7e, Ch 115, p 1761)

**Neurogenic tumor pathology**: Schwannomas are encapsulated and show Antoni A (dense spindle, Verocay bodies) and Antoni B (loose) areas. FNA is diagnostic in only about 20%. Asymptomatic tumors without a deficit can be observed. Resection usually costs the nerve of origin, although enucleation can sometimes spare function. Neurofibromas are unencapsulated and intertwined with the nerve. In NF1 they are multiple and have a higher malignant transformation risk. Lifetime MPNST risk in NF1 is up to about 13%. (Cummings 7e, Ch 115, p 1763) (Cummings 7e, Ch 115, p 1764) (Cummings 7e, Ch 115, p 1772)

**HL survivorship**: After about 15-20 years, deaths from second cancers and coronary disease exceed deaths from HL. Cumulative second-cancer risk is about 25% at 30 years, including head and neck mucosal cancers (RR about 3-5), thyroid cancer, breast cancer in young women, and lung cancer in smokers. MI mortality is about 2.5-fold higher. These risks drive the move to omit or reduce RT in nonbulky early disease. (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1779) (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1780)

**Salivary MALT lymphoma**: MALT accounts for 60-70% of salivary lymphomas (DLBCL 20-30%), usually in the parotid, and is linked to Sjogren syndrome and hepatitis C with cryoglobulinemia. At least one third involve multiple glands, and relapse in other extranodal sites is common (at least one third), so follow-up is lifelong. Stage I-IIE disease is treated with involved-field RT (24-30 Gy). (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1784)

**ENB and SNUC outcomes**: For esthesioneuroblastoma, combined surgery and RT beats either alone (SEER 5-year OS about 73% vs 68% surgery vs 35% RT). Late recurrences more than 10 years out require long follow-up. Regional failure (high level II, retropharyngeal) is common, so elective neck RT is favored (0/11 regional failures with elective RT vs 44% without). SNUC behaves far worse. Single-modality therapy carries about 3-fold higher mortality than combined therapy, and about 27% fail regionally by 2 years, which again supports elective neck treatment. (Cummings 7e, Ch 117, p 1802) (Cummings 7e, Ch 117, p 1803)

**Nomenclature**: AAO-HNS/AHNS terms are radical, modified radical (preserves one or more of SAN, IJV, SCM), selective (levels listed, e.g., SND II-IV), and extended. The 2010-2011 international symbolic system writes the side, then ND, then the levels and the nonlymphatic structures removed. For example, L ND (I-V, SCM, IJV, CN XI) is a radical dissection and R ND (II-IV) is a lateral SND. (Cummings 7e, Ch 118, p 1810) (Cummings 7e, Ch 118, p 1811)

**Carotid involvement**: Carotid ligation historically carried about 30% mortality and 45% neurologic morbidity. Selective resection with saphenous vein interposition and flap coverage can be done with about 12% CVA risk. Assess beforehand with balloon test occlusion: 30 minutes of occlusion with induced hypotension and neuro exams, with or without xenon CT/SPECT perfusion. Prior embolic symptoms call for preoperative stenting or endarterectomy if the vessel is to be preserved. (Cummings 7e, Ch 118, p 1823) (Cummings 7e, Ch 118, p 1824)

**Outcome numbers**: After SND I-III, neck recurrence is about 5% for pN0, 10% for a single node without ECS, and 24% for multiple nodes or ECS (lower with RT). In selected cN+ patients, SND achieved about 94% regional control. Macroscopic ECS carries about 44% neck recurrence versus 25% for microscopic ECS, and multilevel disease has much higher recurrence than single-level disease. (Cummings 7e, Ch 118, p 1825) (Cummings 7e, Ch 118, p 1826)

**Other nerve rates**: In large series, injury rates are about 1.3% for the marginal mandibular nerve (lip asymmetry on long follow-up 4-23%), 0.4% for the hypoglossal nerve, 0.6% for Horner syndrome, and up to 8% for the phrenic nerve in one series. Phrenic injury shows as hemidiaphragm elevation and is usually transient. Protect the marginal branch with the Hayes Martin maneuver (ligate the facial vein and retract it superiorly), and protect the phrenic nerve by preserving the fascia over the anterior scalene. First-bite syndrome after parapharyngeal or deep-lobe surgery reflects sympathetic disruption (about 10% overall, 20% after vagal PGL excision). (Cummings 7e, Ch 119, p 1836) (Cummings 7e, Ch 119, p 1837)

**Fistula, lymphedema and veins**: After TORS with neck dissection, intraoperative orocervical communication was found in up to 29% of cases, but only about 4% became fistulas when they were closed and reinforced; concurrent and staged neck dissection give similar fistula rates. Fistula after salvage laryngectomy reaches about 50%, and vascularized flap reinforcement reduces this. Neck/facial lymphedema occurs externally in 17-36%, and internal lymphedema causes dysphagia; refer for lymphedema therapy. The IJV stays patent in about 86% after MRND, less with infection, catheters or RT. (Cummings 7e, Ch 119, p 1833) (Cummings 7e, Ch 119, p 1834) (Cummings 7e, Ch 119, p 1835)

**Ballistics**: High-velocity missiles (>610 m/s, military rifles about 760 m/s) create a temporary cavity up to 30 times the missile diameter, so viscera can be injured without direct contact. Shotguns are low velocity (about 300 m/s), but at close range the shot mass acts like a rifle injury. Birdshot (≤3.5 mm) seriously injures to about 12 m, whereas buckshot pellets act like handgun bullets to about 150 m. Remove wadding from the wound. In Ordog's classification, mortality ranges from 0% for type 0 (skin) to 85-90% for type III (point blank). Use MRI for retained pellets only when the metal is known to be nonferromagnetic. (Cummings 7e, Ch 120, p 1840) (Cummings 7e, Ch 120, p 1841) (Cummings 7e, Ch 120, p 1842)

**Vascular exposure**: Approach zone I injuries on the right through a median sternotomy and on the left through a left anterior thoracotomy. For zone III ICA bleeding, use Foley/Fogarty balloon tamponade, or pass a No. 4 Fogarty through a shunt beyond the injury. Mandibulotomy or endovascular embolization may be needed. Ligate ECA branches and veins freely, but if both IJVs are injured, repair one. Ligate the CCA/ICA only for irreparable injury or a comatose patient with fixed pupils. In a hematoma, find the carotid by tracing the facial or superior thyroid artery retrograde. (Cummings 7e, Ch 120, p 1843) (Cummings 7e, Ch 120, p 1848)

**Toxic adenoma and toxic MNG**: A toxic adenoma is usually ≥3 cm with suppression of the rest of the gland. It rarely remits, so treat with lobectomy (after a thionamide and Lugol) or RAI; ethanol ablation is an option. Toxic MNG appears late in long-standing goiter, usually in women over 50, and never remits. RAI is generally first line; surgery reduces volume faster but more often causes hypothyroidism. Iodine loads (contrast, amiodarone) can trigger thyrotoxicosis in autonomous nodular glands (Jod-Basedow). (Cummings 7e, Ch 121, p 1862)

**Thyroiditis spectrum**: Painless (silent) thyroiditis affects both sexes and has no viral prodrome. Thyrotoxicosis lasts 2-6 weeks, then hypothyroidism for 2-8 weeks, and about half later develop chronic autoimmune thyroiditis. The postpartum form behaves the same way. RAI-induced thyroiditis flares 1-2 weeks after treatment. Amiodarone causes either iodine-induced hyperthyroidism (in nodular glands) or a destructive thyroiditis, and about 2% of patients on interferon-alpha develop thyrotoxicosis. Exogenous hormone use shows no goiter, low uptake and low thyroglobulin. In de Quervain thyroiditis, treat with salicylates 2.4-3.6 g/day or NSAIDs, and use prednisone about 40 mg/day for 3-4 weeks for severe pain. (Cummings 7e, Ch 121, p 1861) (Cummings 7e, Ch 121, p 1862)

**ENT manifestations of hypothyroidism**: Hoarseness comes from mucopolysaccharide infiltration of the vocal folds. Bilateral edematous but mobile folds should prompt a TSH, and the voice almost always recovers with replacement alone. About 30-40% of adults with myxedema have bilateral SNHL, with conductive loss from ET edema and effusion. Vertigo occurs in about two thirds. About 10% of Hashimoto hypothyroidism is transient. Hypothyroidism develops in about 31% after neck RT for Hodgkin lymphoma, so monitor laryngectomy and irradiated patients. (Cummings 7e, Ch 121, p 1864)

**Rare thyroid malignancies**: The most common metastasis to the thyroid is renal cell carcinoma. About 1% of lung cancers metastasize to the thyroid yet account for about 20% of thyroid metastases; consider thyroidectomy for palliation of slow primaries. Primary thyroid SCC is under 1% of thyroid cancers; exclude an aerodigestive primary, resect aggressively and give adjuvant RT. Incidental DTC appears in up to 1% of neck dissection specimens, and malignancy in about 1.5% of TGDCs, which a Sistrunk procedure usually treats adequately. (Cummings 7e, Ch 115, p 1773) (Cummings 7e, Ch 122, p 1888)

**Numbers**: ATC is about 1% of thyroid cancers, is rare before age 50, and up to 80% arise with coexisting DTC (dedifferentiation; BRAF about 40%, RAS 30%, TP53 50%). More than 60% have lateral nodes and more than 50% have distant metastases at presentation. Debulking is not supported. With resection plus RT and chemotherapy, median OS was about 22 months versus 6.5 months for unresectable disease. Dabrafenib plus trametinib gave about a 69% response in BRAF V600E tumors. (Cummings 7e, Ch 122, p 1887)

**Normocalcemic PHPT**: Calcium (total and ionized) is persistently normal with elevated PTH. Diagnose it only after excluding secondary causes, especially vitamin D deficiency (which can mask hypercalcemic PHPT) and renal calcium leak (thiazide trial). It is considered an early form of PHPT. Monitor and operate on progression. (Cummings 7e, Ch 123, p 1902)

**Sestamibi mechanics**: Tc-99m sestamibi is retained by mitochondria-rich parathyroid tissue. Images at about 10 minutes and 2 hours show parathyroid activity persisting after the thyroid washes out, and SPECT improves detection of small glands. Sestamibi is weak for multigland hyperplasia, and thyroid nodules or nodes can cause false positives. 4D-CT finds more than half of glands missed by sestamibi and US. For intraoperative PTH, draw the post-excision sample at 10-15 minutes (not earlier, because handling causes a spike). A 50% drop predicts cure. Postoperative hypocalcemia peaks at about 48 h. (Cummings 7e, Ch 123, p 1904) (Cummings 7e, Ch 123, p 1905) (Cummings 7e, Ch 123, p 1906)

**Imaging and labs**: CT or MRI shows extraocular muscle enlargement in about 70% of patients: fusiform 2-8-fold belly enlargement sparing the tendons, bilateral in 90%, inferior and medial recti most often. Patients under 40 tend toward fat expansion and those over 60 toward muscle swelling. Apical crowding without much proptosis carries the highest risk of compressive optic neuropathy. TRAb is detected in about 98% of untreated Graves patients. Grading systems are NOSPECS, EUGOGO CAS (active if ≥3/7 initially or ≥4/10 on follow-up), and VISA. (Cummings 7e, Ch 125, p 1919) (Cummings 7e, Ch 125, p 1920)

**Epitympanic compartments**: The ossicles, ligaments and mucosal folds seal the attic from the mesotympanum except for the anterior and posterior tympanic isthmi, so attic ventilation is fragile. Prussak space lies between the pars flaccida and the malleus neck. Pars flaccida cholesteatomas spread posteriorly into the posterior epitympanum, aditus and antrum. The supratubal recess, anterior to the attic, lies right next to the geniculate ganglion and first genu, and its bony 'cog' must be removed to clear disease safely. The geniculate ganglion is dehiscent under the middle fossa floor in about 25%. (Cummings 7e, Ch 126, p 1934) (Cummings 7e, Ch 126, p 1935)

**Board landmarks**: The temporal line is about 5 mm below the lowest middle fossa floor. The tympanomastoid suture leads to the stylomastoid foramen, at the anterior end of the digastric groove. The cochlear aqueduct marks the inferior limit of translabyrinthine drilling and protects CN IX-XI. The long process of the incus has a single nutrient vessel and no collateral supply, so it necroses first. The facial nerve is most often injured just proximal to the second genu and in its vertical segment. (Cummings 7e, Ch 126, p 1929) (Cummings 7e, Ch 126, p 1931) (Cummings 7e, Ch 126, p 1934)

**EAC tumor and infection routes**: The canal is about 2.5 cm long: the outer third is cartilaginous (hair, sebaceous and ceruminous glands) and the inner two thirds bony (thin skin). Tumor escapes through the fissures of Santorini (to the superficial parotid), the foramen of Huschke (an anteroinferior ossification defect, to the infratemporal fossa and deep parotid), and the bony-cartilaginous junction, which is also where granulation tissue of necrotizing otitis externa appears. These routes explain why EAC carcinoma needs en bloc lateral temporal bone resection. (Cummings 7e, Ch 126, p 1931)

**Hillocks of His**: The first arch hillocks form the tragus, helical root and superior helix, and the second arch hillocks form the antihelix, antitragus, lobule and inferior helix. The EAC comes from the dorsal first branchial cleft. A meatal plug normally recanalizes, and failure to do so causes canal atresia or stenosis with a risk of canal cholesteatoma. Preauricular pits and sinuses come from defects in hillock fusion. (Cummings 7e, Ch 126, p 1931)

**Tube anatomy**: The ET runs at about 45 degrees from the middle ear to the torus tubarius. The bony proximal third lies in the petrous bone, and the distal two thirds are fibrocartilaginous and closed at rest. The isthmus (narrowest point) is classically placed at the bony-cartilaginous junction, although histologic studies put it just inside the cartilaginous portion. The tensor veli palatini opens the tube by pulling its lateral membranous wall. The ICA lies medial to the tympanic orifice, where the bone may be dehiscent. (Cummings 7e, Ch 126, p 1932)

**Hair cell and neuron counts**: There are about 3,500 IHCs in one row and about 12,000 OHCs in three rows. About 30,000 spiral ganglion neurons sit in Rosenthal canal. Type I neurons (about 90-95%) are myelinated and bipolar, and many contact each single IHC. Type II neurons (about 5-10%) are unmyelinated, and each contacts many OHCs. Mechanotransduction depends on tip links and TMC1/TMC2 channels: K+ enters from endolymph (+80 mV endocochlear potential), depolarization opens basolateral Ca2+ channels, and glutamate is released at ribbon synapses. (Cummings 7e, Ch 127, p 1940) (Cummings 7e, Ch 128, p 1949) (Cummings 7e, Ch 128, p 1951) (Cummings 7e, Ch 128, p 1952)

**Efferents and binaural nuclei**: The olivocochlear bundle has about 1,600 fibers. Medial olivocochlear efferents (myelinated, mostly crossed, from the medial superior olive region) synapse on OHCs, suppress cochlear gain, and protect against noise. Lateral olivocochlear efferents (unmyelinated, mostly uncrossed, from the lateral superior olive) synapse on type I afferent dendrites beneath IHCs. The MSO encodes interaural time differences (low frequencies), and the LSO encodes interaural level differences (high frequencies) with MNTB inhibition. Primary auditory cortex lies on the transverse gyri of Heschl and is tonotopic. (Cummings 7e, Ch 127, p 1941) (Cummings 7e, Ch 127, p 1943) (Cummings 7e, Ch 127, p 1944)

**Fallopian canal**: In the IAC the facial nerve has no epineurial sheath, only arachnoid. The labyrinthine segment is the shortest and narrowest and lies in a vascular watershed between vertebrobasilar and external carotid supply. The nerve gains its fibrous sheath at the geniculate ganglion, where the GSPN leaves through the facial hiatus. The tympanic segment is dehiscent over the oval window in about 55% of ears. (Cummings 7e, Ch 126, p 1934) (Cummings 7e, Ch 126, p 1935)
